title: Do you need a crown after a root canal? Why root-filled teeth break and when a filling is enough
desc: Does a root-canal-treated tooth need a crown? The difference between front and back teeth, fillings, onlays and crowns, when to place the permanent restoration and how to stop the tooth from breaking.
seoTitle: Do you need a crown after a root canal? | Dent32
seoDesc: Does a root-canal-treated tooth need a crown? Front versus back teeth, fillings, onlays and crowns, and how to stop the tooth from breaking.
lead: Root canal treatment clears infection from inside a tooth, but it doesn’t strengthen the tooth from the outside. Decay, old fillings and the access opening made to reach the canals remove a good part of the tooth, so molars and premolars in particular often need a crown or onlay covering the top of the tooth after treatment. Front teeth with little tooth loss can usually be restored with a well-placed filling. The decision depends on where the tooth is and how much sound tooth is left.

sections.h: Why do root-filled teeth break more easily?
sections.html:
Most teeth that need root canal treatment have already had a large cavity, a deep filling or a crack. During treatment an opening is made through the top of the tooth to reach the canals. As a result, the cusps (the raised points of the biting surface) can be left as thin walls.

Back teeth carry most of the chewing load. Thin walls can crack on a hard mouthful or when you clench at night. If a fracture runs below the gum line, the tooth may not be saveable, so the aim is to protect the tooth before it breaks. A root-filled tooth can also darken over time; we cover this in dead teeth and discolouration.

sections.h: What is usually done for which tooth?
sections.html:
SituationUsual restoration
Front tooth, small access cavity onlyComposite (white) filling
Front tooth with a large filling or discolourationCrown or veneer; internal whitening if needed
Premolar with sound wallsOnlay or crown; sometimes a filling
MolarUsually an onlay or full crown
Most of the tooth is missingFibre post (support inside the root) + crown
In short

Because of the chewing load, back teeth are usually protected with an onlay or crown after root canal treatment. For front teeth with little tooth loss a filling may be enough. The permanent filling or crown shouldn’t be delayed for long after treatment.

sections.h: Filling, onlay or crown: what’s the difference?
sections.html:
• Composite filling: Closes the access cavity and small defects in one visit. It can be enough for front teeth and premolars with sound walls. See white (composite) fillings.
  • Onlay (partial crown): A piece made in the laboratory or digitally that covers only the weak cusps. Sound parts of the tooth are not cut away, so it preserves more tooth than a full crown.
  • Full crown: Covers the whole visible part of the tooth. It is chosen when tooth loss is large or the tooth has cracked before. Zirconia and e.max are the most common options; we compare them in types of dental crowns.
  • Fibre post: If very little of the tooth is left above the gum, a post placed in part of the root canal gives the filling and crown something to hold on to. Not every root-filled tooth needs one.

sections.h: When should the permanent filling or crown be placed?
sections.html:
At the last root canal visit the tooth is usually sealed with a temporary filling. Temporary fillings wear and can leak over time; if bacteria in saliva get back into the cleaned canals, the success of the treatment is put at risk. That’s why the permanent filling or crown should be placed within the time your dentist gives you, often within a few weeks. We explain how long temporary fillings last in how long does a temporary filling last.

Until the crown is fitted, avoid chewing hard or sticky foods on that side. A few days of tenderness after treatment is normal; see pain after root canal treatment.

sections.h: What happens if you don’t get a crown?
sections.html: Not every root-filled tooth without a crown will break, but in back teeth the risk of fracture rises noticeably. Studies show that molars protected with a crown or onlay after root canal treatment stay in the mouth longer. If a vertical crack extends into the root, the tooth may need to come out, and more involved treatment such as an implant or bridge then becomes necessary. We explain how we decide in extraction or root canal treatment.

• Don’t put off the permanent filling or crown.
  • If you clench or grind, wear a night guard. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • A root-filled tooth has no nerve sensation, so decay can progress without pain; regular check-ups and X-rays matter for that reason.
  • Clean around the edges of the crown with floss or an interdental brush. See how to floss.
  • Don’t bite very hard things such as nutshells, ice or fruit stones with a root-filled tooth.

sections.h: Planning after root canal treatment at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At the end of root canal treatment we explain which restoration suits your tooth, based on how much tooth is left, and set out the options in a written treatment plan. You can read how long zirconia and e.max crowns take in how many days a zirconia crown takes.

faq.q: Is a crown compulsory after root canal treatment?
faq.a: Not for every tooth. For front teeth with little tooth loss a filling may be enough. Molars and premolars usually need an onlay or crown because of the chewing load.

faq.q: How long after a root canal should the crown be placed?
faq.a: Once the tooth has settled, within the time your dentist gives you, often within a few weeks. Leaving a temporary filling for a long time can let the canals become reinfected.

faq.q: Zirconia or e.max for a root-filled tooth?
faq.a: Both can be used. Zirconia is often chosen for back teeth because of its strength, and e.max for front teeth because of how it lets light through. Clenching habits and how much tooth is left also affect the choice.

faq.q: How long does a root-filled tooth last?
faq.a: With good root canal treatment and a timely permanent restoration, a root-filled tooth can last for many years. Its lifespan depends mainly on how much tooth is left, the restoration, clenching and whether new decay develops.

faq.q: Why can a root-filled tooth decay without pain?
faq.a: Because the nerve tissue has been removed, the tooth doesn’t react to cold, heat or sweet things. Decay can progress without pain, so regular check-ups are important.

title: How long does a temporary filling last? What to do if it falls out and whether you can eat on it
desc: Why are temporary fillings used and how many days or weeks do they last? When you can eat after a temporary filling, what to avoid, and what to do if it wears down or falls out.
seoTitle: How long does a temporary filling last? | Dent32
seoDesc: Why are temporary fillings used and how long do they last? When you can eat, what to avoid, and what to do if one wears down or falls out.
lead: A temporary filling protects a tooth for a short time until the permanent treatment and is usually designed to last from a few days to a few weeks. It is used between root canal appointments, while watching how the nerve responds after deep decay, or while a permanent filling or crown is being made. Some wear of the surface is normal; if it falls out completely or the tooth starts to hurt, contact the clinic within a few days, or, for a tooth in the middle of root canal treatment, the same or next day if possible.

sections.html:
• Between root canal visits: It protects the medicine placed in the canals and keeps saliva out of them. See root canal treatment.
  • For deep decay: If decay has come very close to the nerve, the dentist may wait for a while to see whether the nerve settles.
  • While a crown or onlay is made: It covers the tooth between the impression and fitting the permanent piece.
  • In an emergency: It can be placed at the first visit to ease pain and seal the tooth.

sections.h: How long does a temporary filling last?
sections.html:
Temporary filling materials are made to be easy to remove, so they aren’t as strong as permanent fillings. They generally do their job for anywhere from a few days to a few weeks. Some materials last longer, but what really counts is the time your dentist gives you.

If a temporary filling is left too long, it can start to leak at the edges, the tooth can crack or new decay can develop underneath. In a tooth having root canal treatment, this can mean the cleaned canals become reinfected. So try not to postpone your follow-up appointment; we explain why the permanent restoration matters in do you need a crown after a root canal.

In short

Temporary fillings are made to last from a few days to a few weeks. Some wear of the surface is normal. If it falls out completely or pain starts, call the clinic, and don’t delay the permanent treatment beyond the time your dentist gives you.

sections.h: When can you eat after a temporary filling?
sections.html:
Some temporary filling materials set with moisture in the mouth. That’s why you’re usually asked not to eat for at least an hour, or for as long as your dentist says. If you’re still numb, it’s also wise to wait until the numbness wears off so you don’t bite your cheek or tongue; see how long dental numbness lasts.

Food / habitWith a temporary filling
Soft meals, soup, yoghurtFine; chew on the other side if you can
Chewing gum, Turkish delight, toffee, fruit leatherAvoid; they can pull the filling out
Nuts, hard crusts, iceAvoid; they can break the filling and the tooth
Very hot or very cold drinksMay cause sensitivity; choose lukewarm
BrushingBrush as usual, gently over the area
FlossingFloss, but pull the floss out sideways instead of lifting it up

• Normal: The surface wearing down or getting lower, a slightly rough feel, mild sensitivity for the first day or two, a clove-like taste with some materials.
  • Call the clinic: The filling falling out completely, a clear feeling of a hole in the tooth, pain on biting because the filling is too high.
  • Get seen the same or next day: Throbbing pain, swelling of the gum or face, fever. See dental abscess and can a toothache cause a fever.

sections.h: What to do if your temporary filling falls out
sections.html:
1. Don’t panic; it’s usually not an emergency.
  2. Rinse with lukewarm water and gently brush the tooth to clear food debris.
  3. Don’t chew on that side; keep away from sugary and sticky foods.
  4. Call the clinic. In a tooth having root canal treatment, the filling should be replaced the same or next day if possible; otherwise an appointment within a few days is enough.
  5. Temporary filling kits sold in pharmacies can bridge a day or two until you see the dentist, but they don’t replace the material your dentist places.

We cover what to do when a permanent filling or crown comes out in my filling fell out or my crown came off.

faq.q: How many days does a temporary filling last?
faq.a: It’s usually made to last from a few days to a few weeks. What counts is the time your dentist gives you; don’t delay the permanent treatment beyond it.

faq.q: When can I eat after a temporary filling?
faq.a: Usually after at least an hour, or as long as your dentist says. If you’re still numb, it’s safer to wait until the numbness wears off.

faq.q: My temporary filling has worn down. Is that normal?
faq.a: Some wear of the surface is normal. If the filling falls out completely, you feel a clear hole in the tooth or pain starts, call the clinic.

faq.q: Will my tooth be harmed if the temporary filling falls out?
faq.a: If it’s replaced quickly, there’s usually no problem. In a tooth having root canal treatment it should be replaced the same or next day if possible, so the canals aren’t exposed to saliva.

faq.q: Can I chew gum with a temporary filling?
faq.a: No. Gum and sticky foods can pull a temporary filling out.

title: When should you brush your teeth after eating? Brushing straight away, and before or after breakfast
desc: Is brushing right after a meal harmful, and how long should you wait? Acidic foods, brushing before or after breakfast, the bedtime brush, and what to do after vomiting or reflux.
seoTitle: When should you brush your teeth after eating? | Dent32
seoDesc: Is brushing right after a meal harmful, and how long should you wait? Acidic foods, brushing before or after breakfast, and the bedtime brush.
lead: You don’t always need to wait before brushing after a meal. Waiting matters mainly after acidic foods and drinks: oranges, lemonade, fruit juice, fizzy drinks, salads with vinegar or wine soften the enamel for a while, and brushing hard at that point can wear it. In that case waiting around 30–60 minutes and rinsing with water in the meantime is enough. After a non-acidic meal there’s no harm in brushing straight away. The most important brush of the day is the one before bed.

sections.html:
When acid levels in the mouth rise, the surface of the enamel softens for a while. Saliva gradually neutralises the acid and puts minerals back into the enamel. Brushing with a hard brush and an abrasive toothpaste straight after acid can remove a tiny amount of the softened surface. Repeated every day, this can contribute to dental erosion; we cover it in detail in dental erosion and enamel wear.

There’s no exact figure for the waiting time; most sources suggest between 30 minutes and an hour. Rinsing with water, drinking water or chewing sugar-free gum during this time helps saliva do its job faster.

sections.h: When to brush, depending on what you had
sections.html:
What you ate or drankWhen to brush
A non-acidic meal (e.g. rice, meat, cooked vegetables)You can brush straight away
Citrus, fruit juice, fizzy or energy drinksWait 30–60 minutes; rinse with water first
Salad with vinegar or lemon, picklesWait 30–60 minutes
WineDrink water; brush after waiting
Sweets, sugary snacksRinse with water; clean thoroughly at your next brush
Vomiting or refluxDon’t brush straight away; rinse with water, then wait
In short

If you’ve had something acidic, wait about half an hour to an hour before brushing and rinse with water in the meantime. After non-acidic meals you can brush straight away. The most important brush is the one before bed.

There’s a case for both. Brushing before breakfast clears the plaque built up overnight and leaves a fluoride layer on the teeth; if you have acidic things like orange juice or tomatoes at breakfast, this order suits you better. If you prefer to brush after breakfast and your breakfast is acidic, waiting about half an hour is enough.

What matters most is brushing at least twice a day, for two minutes each time, with a fluoride toothpaste. Choose whichever order is easier to turn into a habit.

sections.h: Why the bedtime brush matters most
sections.html:
Saliva flow drops during sleep, and with it saliva’s protective effect, so teeth are more vulnerable to decay at night. Make the last brush of the day just before bed and have nothing but water afterwards.

  • After brushing, spit out the toothpaste but don’t rinse with lots of water; the fluoride left on your teeth keeps protecting them. See is fluoride harmful.
  • Clean between your teeth with floss or an interdental brush before the bedtime brush. See how to floss.
  • Children given milk or juice in a bottle at night have a higher risk of decay; see baby bottle tooth decay.

sections.h: After vomiting, reflux or pregnancy sickness
sections.html: Stomach acid affects enamel more strongly than acids in food. After vomiting or reflux, rinse your mouth with water instead of brushing straight away; wait a while, then brush with a soft brush. If you have reflux often, tell both your doctor and your dentist. For sickness during pregnancy, see dental treatment during pregnancy.

sections.h: Good technique matters as much as timing
sections.html:
• Use a soft or medium brush; hard brushes and pressing too hard can lead to gum recession.
  • Hold the brush at about 45 degrees to the gum and use small movements. Details: how to brush your teeth properly.
  • Replace your brush or electric brush head about every three months. See when to replace your toothbrush.
  • After meals when you can’t brush, rinsing with water or chewing sugar-free gum helps. See is sugar-free gum good for your teeth.

sections.h: If you wear braces, aligners or a night guard
sections.html: If you wear clear aligners, brush your teeth after eating before putting them back in; otherwise food stays trapped between the aligner and your teeth for hours. If you’ve had something acidic, rinse with water first. With fixed braces, the area around the brackets needs cleaning after every meal. See living with braces and how to clean night guards and clear aligners.

sections.h: Care advice at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At check-ups we look together at your brushing technique, the brush you use and your eating habits, and if there are signs of enamel wear or gum recession we explain the cause.

faq.q: Is it bad to brush straight after eating?
faq.a: Not after a non-acidic meal. After acidic food or drinks, because enamel softens for a while, waiting about 30–60 minutes is better.

faq.q: Should I brush before or after breakfast?
faq.a: Either is fine. If your breakfast includes acidic things, brushing before is better; if you brush after, wait about half an hour. What matters is brushing at least twice a day.

faq.q: Should I rinse with water after brushing?
faq.a: Spitting out the toothpaste is enough; rinsing with lots of water reduces the fluoride left on your teeth. Not rinsing is especially protective after the bedtime brush.

faq.q: Can I brush after vomiting?
faq.a: Rather than brushing straight away, rinse with water, wait a while and then brush with a soft brush.

faq.q: Can I drink water after brushing at night?
faq.a: Yes, water is fine. Just avoid eating or drinking anything else.

title: Is sugar-free gum good for your teeth? Decay, dry mouth and the effect on your jaw
desc: Does chewing sugar-free gum help your teeth, and can it replace brushing? Xylitol, how long to chew, the effect on the jaw joint, and gum with fillings, crowns and braces.
seoTitle: Is sugar-free gum good for your teeth? | Dent32
seoDesc: Does sugar-free gum help your teeth, and can it replace brushing? Xylitol, how long to chew, the jaw joint, and gum with crowns and braces.
lead: Chewing sugar-free gum for 15–20 minutes after a meal increases saliva flow, and that extra saliva helps neutralise acid in the mouth and wash away food debris. That makes sugar-free gum a useful stopgap for your teeth when you can’t brush. But it doesn’t replace brushing and flossing. Gum with sugar raises the risk of decay. Chewing gum for long periods and often can also tire the jaw joint and muscles.

sections.html:
Chewing stimulates the salivary glands. Saliva buffers the acid that rises after eating, carries calcium and phosphate to the enamel and clears food debris. This helps shorten the acidic phase in which decay begins.

Being sugar-free is what matters here. Sugary gum keeps feeding the bacteria in the mouth and has the opposite effect. Gums sweetened with xylitol, sorbitol or maltitol don’t increase acid production by bacteria; there are studies suggesting xylitol can also reduce bacterial growth, but on its own it doesn’t prevent decay.

QuestionAnswer
Does it replace brushing?No; it’s only a stopgap
How long should you chew?15–20 minutes after a meal is enough
Gum with sugar?Raises the risk of decay
Chewing all day?Can tire the jaw joint and muscles
For dry mouth?Can bring relief by increasing saliva
For bad breath?Masks it temporarily; doesn’t fix the cause
In short

Chewed for 15–20 minutes when you can’t brush after a meal, sugar-free gum helps your teeth by increasing saliva. It doesn’t replace brushing and flossing. If your jaw hurts, limit gum.

sections.h: When does chewing gum make sense?
sections.html:
• You’ve eaten out and can’t brush.
  • While waiting to brush after an acidic drink; see when to brush after eating.
  • For dry mouth caused by medicines or not drinking enough; see causes of dry mouth.
  • When you have few chances to drink water, such as long meetings or journeys.

For bad breath, gum only freshens things up for a while. If the smell is persistent, a cause such as the gums, the tongue surface or food trapped between teeth should be looked for; see causes of bad breath.

Chewing for a short time causes no problems for most people. But chewing gum for hours every day can tire the chewing muscles and the jaw joint. If you have jaw pain, clicking or tiredness in the morning, or you clench your teeth at night, cutting down on or stopping gum can help. See jaw joint pain and clicking and teeth grinding and night guards.

Natural mastic gum contains no sugar either, but because it’s firm it can work the jaw muscles harder.

sections.h: Gum with fillings, crowns, braces and dentures
sections.html:
• Permanent fillings and crowns: Sugar-free gum usually causes no problems. If you notice a crown or filling sticking to the gum, get it checked; its edge may be loosening.
  • Temporary fillings and crowns: Don’t chew gum; it can pull them out. See how long a temporary filling lasts.
  • Fixed braces: Gum can stick to brackets and wires; follow your dentist’s advice. See living with braces.
  • Clear aligners: Don’t chew gum with the aligners in.
  • Dentures: Gum can stick to the surface of the denture.

• In large amounts, sorbitol, xylitol and maltitol can cause wind and diarrhoea in some people.
  • Xylitol is poisonous to dogs; keep gum where pets can’t reach it.
  • Gum isn’t suitable for young children because of the risk of swallowing and choking.
  • People with phenylketonuria should check the sweeteners on the label.
  • Always put used gum in the bin, not on the pavement or under a desk.

sections.h: Care based on your decay risk at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At the examination we assess your decay risk by looking at your diet, saliva flow and previous fillings, and plan brushing, flossing and fluoride use around you. We explain how decay starts in signs and stages of tooth decay.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Does sugar-free gum replace brushing?
faq.a: No. When you can’t brush it helps by increasing saliva, but plaque is only removed by a brush and floss.

faq.q: How long should I chew gum after a meal?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes is enough. Chewing for hours brings no extra benefit for your teeth and can tire the jaw muscles.

faq.q: Does xylitol gum prevent decay?
faq.a: Xylitol doesn’t increase acid production by bacteria, and some studies have found it helps reduce decay risk. But on its own it doesn’t prevent decay or replace brushing, flossing and fluoride.

faq.q: Can chewing gum cause jaw pain?
faq.a: It can if you chew for long periods and often. People with jaw joint pain or a clenching habit should limit gum.

faq.q: Can I chew gum with fillings?
faq.a: Sugar-free gum usually causes no problems with permanent fillings. Don’t chew gum if you have a temporary filling or temporary crown.

title: Are dental X-rays harmful? Radiation doses, X-rays in pregnancy and for children
desc: How much radiation is in a dental X-ray, and is it harmful? Periapical, panoramic and CBCT doses compared with everyday life, pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and how often X-rays are needed.
seoTitle: Are dental X-rays harmful? Radiation, pregnancy, children | Dent32
seoDesc: How much radiation is in a dental X-ray? Periapical, panoramic and CBCT doses, pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and how often X-rays are needed.
lead: Dental X-rays are among the lowest-dose forms of medical imaging. A small film of one tooth involves less radiation than a person receives from natural background in a single day; a panoramic film is equivalent to a few days of natural radiation. Even so, like any radiation, it shouldn’t be repeated unnecessarily, so an X-ray is taken only when it will help with diagnosis or the treatment plan. Even during pregnancy, a necessary dental X-ray can be taken with suitable precautions.

sections.h: How much radiation is in a dental X-ray?
sections.html:
Radiation dose is measured in microsieverts (µSv). The figures below are approximate and vary with the equipment, the area imaged and the settings. For comparison, a person receives on average 2,000–3,000 µSv a year from natural background (soil, air, space), or roughly 6–8 µSv a day.

ImageApproximate doseComparison
Periapical or bitewing film (digital)Under 5 µSvLess than a day of natural radiation
Panoramic film10–25 µSvA few days of natural radiation
Small-field dental CBCTTens of µSvFrom a few days to a few weeks
Large-field dental CBCTA hundred µSv or moreA few weeks of natural radiation
Long-haul flightTens of µSvFor comparison
In short

Dental X-ray doses are very low: a small tooth film is less than a day of natural radiation, and a panoramic film equals a few days. Even so, X-rays are taken only when needed; bringing a recent X-ray with you can avoid a repeat.

Decay between teeth, infection at the root tips, bone loss and impacted teeth can’t be seen by eye during an examination. X-rays show these problems early, while they can still be solved with smaller, simpler treatment. We explain why decay between teeth is noticed late in decay between teeth, and the types of X-ray in dental X-rays and CBCT.

sections.h: Can you have a dental X-ray when pregnant?
sections.html:
Routine check-up X-rays can be left until after the birth. But if an X-ray is needed for diagnosis because of pain, an abscess or an injury, it can be taken during pregnancy with suitable precautions. In a dental X-ray the beam is aimed at the mouth; the dose reaching the abdomen is extremely low. An untreated dental infection can be a greater risk to mother and baby.

If you are pregnant or think you might be, always say so before the X-ray. Details: dental treatment during pregnancy.

sections.h: Can you have an X-ray while breastfeeding?
sections.html: Yes. Dental X-rays don’t affect breast milk, and there’s no need to pause breastfeeding afterwards. See dental treatment while breastfeeding.

Children are more sensitive to radiation than adults, so how often X-rays are taken and the area covered are kept even more limited. A child at high risk of decay may need bitewings to see decay between teeth, or a panoramic film to check the order of eruption or a missing tooth. These X-rays have very low doses, and their benefit outweighs the problems a delayed diagnosis can cause. See when baby teeth fall out.

sections.h: How often should X-rays be taken?
sections.html:
There is no fixed interval that applies to everyone. How often you need X-rays depends on your age, your risk of decay and gum disease, your symptoms and the treatment planned. An adult at low risk of decay may have bitewings years apart, while a tooth having root canal treatment or an implant may need a few small films during the procedure.

  • If you’ve had X-rays at another clinic recently, bring a digital copy; it avoids an unnecessary repeat. See records when changing dentist.
  • You are entitled to ask why an X-ray is needed.
  • Depending on the clinic, a lead apron or thyroid collar may also be used; you can ask for one.

Digital sensors capture images with a lower dose than old film X-rays, and the image can be looked at on screen straight away. An intraoral scanner is not an X-ray: it scans the surface of the teeth with light to take a digital impression and involves no radiation. See digital dentistry.

If an X-ray is needed, we explain beforehand why and which image is enough, and look at the images on screen together with you during the examination. We also take recent images you bring into account.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Do dental X-rays cause cancer?
faq.a: Dental X-ray doses are very low; a small tooth film is less than a day of natural radiation. Even so, unnecessary repeats are avoided and X-rays are taken only when needed.

faq.q: How many days of radiation is a panoramic X-ray?
faq.a: Roughly, a panoramic film is equivalent to a few days of natural background radiation. The dose varies with the equipment and settings.

faq.q: Can I have a dental X-ray while pregnant?
faq.a: Routine X-rays can wait until after the birth; an X-ray needed because of pain, an abscess or an injury can be taken with suitable precautions. Tell the clinic you are pregnant before the X-ray.

faq.q: How many dental X-rays a year are safe?
faq.a: There’s no fixed number. How often depends on your age, decay risk, symptoms and planned treatment, and is decided by your dentist.

faq.q: Is a dental CBCT scan harmful?
faq.a: A dental CBCT has a higher dose than a panoramic film but a much lower dose than a medical CT scan. It’s used when a two-dimensional film isn’t enough, such as for implant planning.

title: What happens if you don’t replace an extracted tooth? Teeth shifting and chewing
desc: Is it a problem not to replace an extracted tooth? Neighbouring and opposing teeth shifting, bone loss, chewing and cleaning, whether every gap needs filling, and the options.
seoTitle: What happens if you don’t replace an extracted tooth? | Dent32
seoDesc: Is it a problem not to replace an extracted tooth? Teeth shifting, bone loss, chewing, whether every gap needs filling, and the options.
lead: The gap left by an extracted tooth often causes no problems in the first months; changes are slow and quiet. Over time the teeth on either side can tilt into the gap, the tooth in the opposite jaw can drift towards it, and the jawbone where the tooth was becomes thinner. These changes can make a later implant or bridge harder. Not every gap needs to be filled, but the decision should be made by looking at the whole mouth, ideally before the tooth is taken out.

sections.h: Do neighbouring and opposing teeth shift?
sections.html:
Teeth stay in place partly through contact with their neighbours and with the teeth in the opposite jaw. When a tooth is removed, the tooth behind can tilt forwards and the tooth in front can drift into the gap. The tooth in the opposite jaw, with nothing to meet, can gradually over-erupt towards the gap. These movements happen over months and years, usually without being noticed.

New gaps open up between tilted teeth; food gets caught there and cleaning becomes harder. This can set the stage for decay and gum problems. See food getting stuck between teeth.

After a tooth is removed, the bone that held its root is no longer stimulated and gradually becomes thinner and lower. This change is fastest in the first months after extraction. Thin bone can make placing an implant harder and may call for extra procedures such as bone grafting. See bone grafts and sinus lifts. So if you’re considering an implant, it helps to discuss timing before the extraction; details in when can you get an implant after an extraction.

ChangeWhen it showsConsequence
Bone thinningFrom the first monthsExtra procedures may be needed for an implant
Neighbouring teeth tiltingOver months and yearsFood trapping, harder cleaning
Opposing tooth over-eruptingOver yearsLess room for a bridge or implant
Chewing on one sideStraight awayExtra load on the other side
Gap at the frontStraight awayAppearance and speech affected
In short

If the gap from an extracted tooth is left, neighbouring teeth can tilt, the opposing tooth can over-erupt and the bone thins. These changes are slow but can make later treatment harder. Not every gap needs filling; the decision is made by looking at the whole mouth.

sections.h: If several back teeth are missing
sections.html: When several back teeth are missing, the biting load shifts onto the front teeth. Over time the front teeth can fan forwards, gaps can open between them and the remaining teeth can wear faster. Chewing becomes less efficient, and some people start to avoid hard foods. A step-by-step plan for the whole mouth is described in full mouth rehabilitation.

sections.h: Does every gap need to be filled?
sections.html: No. Gaps left by wisdom teeth aren’t filled. In some people, a missing last molar may cause no problems for years if the bite is balanced and the opposing tooth is stable. Gaps from teeth taken out as part of orthodontic treatment are closed by the treatment. Whether a gap should be filled is decided together, based on your bite, the opposing tooth, appearance and what you want.

• Implant: Replaces the missing tooth without touching the neighbouring teeth and keeps stimulating the bone. See how long implant treatment takes.
  • Bridge: Made by crowning the teeth on either side; a sensible option if those teeth already have large fillings or crowns. See implant or bridge and how long a dental bridge lasts.
  • Adhesive bridge: Used especially for front teeth, with wings bonded to the back of the neighbouring teeth and little drilling. See a single missing tooth.
  • Partial denture: A removable solution when several teeth are missing and fixed options aren’t suitable.
  • Space maintainer for children: Used if a baby molar is lost early, so the space for the adult tooth doesn’t close. See when baby teeth fall out.

sections.h: Planning for missing teeth at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
If a tooth needs to come out, we discuss the options for the gap, the timings and the approximate cost before the extraction and set them out in a written treatment plan. For teeth that have been missing for a long time, we assess the neighbouring and opposing teeth and decide on the right option with you.

faq.q: What happens if I don’t replace an extracted tooth?
faq.a: Over time the neighbouring teeth can tilt into the gap, the opposing tooth can over-erupt and the bone thins. These changes are slow but can make a later implant or bridge harder.

faq.q: How long does it take for teeth to shift after an extraction?
faq.a: It varies from person to person. Changes usually happen over months and years without being noticed; bone thinning is fastest in the first months.

faq.q: Does a missing last molar need replacing?
faq.a: Not always. If the bite is balanced and the opposing tooth is stable, the gap may cause no problems for years. The decision is made at the examination, looking at the whole mouth.

faq.q: Can an implant be placed where a tooth has been missing for years?
faq.a: Often, yes. If the bone has thinned, extra procedures such as bone grafting may be needed; this is assessed with a CBCT scan.

faq.q: Can shifted teeth be corrected?
faq.a: In some cases, tilted or over-erupted teeth can be corrected with orthodontic treatment to reopen the space, followed by an implant or bridge.

title: When can you get an implant after a tooth extraction? Same day, weeks or months later
desc: How long after an extraction can an implant be placed? Same-day implants, early and delayed placement, waiting after bone grafting, timing with an infected tooth and temporary teeth while you wait.
seoTitle: When can you get an implant after a tooth extraction? | Dent32
seoDesc: How long after an extraction can an implant go in? Same-day, early and delayed placement, waiting after bone grafting and temporary teeth.
lead: When an implant can be placed after an extraction doesn’t come down to a single time frame. If the bone and gum are suitable, the implant can go in at the same visit as the extraction; in most cases there’s a wait of a few weeks for the gum to heal or 2–4 months for the bone to partly fill in. With infection, significant bone loss or a bone graft, this can extend by several months. The right timing is best planned with a CBCT scan before the tooth is taken out.

sections.html:
TimingWhen?Suitable for
Same-day (immediate) implantAt the same visit as the extractionNo acute infection, intact bone walls, enough bone
Early implant4–8 weeks or 2–4 months after extractionCases where the gum or bone needs to partly heal
Delayed implant3–6 months or more after extractionInfection, significant bone loss, bone grafting
In short

If the bone and gum are suitable, an implant can be placed the same day as the extraction. In most cases there’s a wait of a few weeks to a few months; with infection or a bone graft the wait is longer. Timing is planned with a CBCT scan before the extraction.

sections.h: Who can have an implant on the day of extraction?
sections.html:
With a same-day implant the tooth is removed and the implant is placed in the socket at the same visit. This needs no acute infection around the tooth, intact bone walls and enough bone for the implant to grip. Especially for front teeth, a temporary tooth can sometimes be fitted the same day too. We cover this option in detail in same-day implants.

A same-day implant shortens overall treatment time and avoids an extra surgical visit, but it isn’t right for everyone. Forcing it when conditions aren’t suitable can put the implant’s fusion with the bone at risk.

• Infection: If there’s a large cyst at the root tip or an active abscess, the area is allowed to heal first. See dental abscess.
  • Bone loss: If much of the bone around the tooth has been lost, a bone graft may be placed first. See bone grafts and sinus lifts.
  • Upper molars: If the roots are close to the sinus, the sinus floor is assessed; a sinus lift is done if needed.
  • General health: Uncontrolled diabetes, some medicines and smoking can slow healing. See who can have implants and implants for people on osteoporosis medication.

If the implant won’t be placed straight away, bone graft material can be put in the socket at extraction and covered with a membrane. This helps limit bone thinning after the extraction, and the implant is usually placed 3–6 months later. We explain why bone thins when a gap is left for a long time in what happens if you don’t replace an extracted tooth.

sections.h: When is the permanent tooth fitted after the implant?
sections.html: After an implant is placed, there’s usually a wait of 2–3 months in the lower jaw and 3–6 months in the upper jaw for it to fuse with the bone. If a bone graft was used, this can take longer. In some cases a temporary tooth can be fitted on the implant the same day. We go through the whole process step by step in how long implant treatment takes.

sections.h: What about the gap while you wait?
sections.html:
For back teeth the waiting time usually causes no problems. For front teeth there are several temporary options so you aren’t left with a gap:

  • A removable temporary tooth (a small temporary denture).
  • A temporary tooth set into a clear aligner-style retainer.
  • A temporary tooth bonded to the neighbouring teeth.
  • Where suitable, a temporary tooth on a same-day implant.

sections.h: The first days after the extraction
sections.html: While you wait for the implant, it’s important that the extraction site heals well. In the first days you need to protect the clot, not smoke and avoid strenuous exercise. See after a tooth extraction, when you can exercise after an extraction and smoking after an implant.

sections.h: Planning extractions and implants at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
For a tooth that needs to come out, we plan together after the examination and imaging whether the implant will be placed the same day or later. We share the waiting time, temporary tooth options and the approximate cost in writing.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many days after an extraction can an implant be placed?
faq.a: If conditions are suitable, the same day. In most cases the wait is a few weeks to 2–4 months, or 3–6 months or longer with infection or a bone graft.

faq.q: Can an implant be placed on the same day as an extraction?
faq.a: Yes, if there’s no acute infection, the bone walls are intact and there’s enough bone. Suitability is decided by examination and a CBCT scan.

faq.q: If I wait too long, can I still have an implant?
faq.a: Usually yes, but if the bone has thinned, extra procedures such as bone grafting may be needed. That’s why it helps to discuss timing before the extraction.

faq.q: Can an implant be placed the same day in an infected tooth?
faq.a: With an active abscess or a large cyst, the area is usually allowed to heal first. For small, controlled infections the decision depends on the examination.

faq.q: Will I have a gap at the front while waiting for an implant?
faq.a: You don’t have to. A removable temporary tooth, a temporary tooth in a retainer or a temporary tooth bonded to the neighbouring teeth can be used.

title: How long does a dental bridge last? Cleaning under a bridge and when it needs replacing
desc: How many years does a dental bridge last on average, and what shortens its life? Cleaning under the bridge, smell and movement, when a bridge needs replacing and the options when it does.
seoTitle: How long does a dental bridge last? | Dent32
seoDesc: How long does a dental bridge last, and what shortens its life? Cleaning under it, smell and movement, and when a bridge needs replacing.
lead: A well-planned, well-cared-for dental bridge usually lasts ten years or more, and many stay in the mouth much longer. What decides a bridge’s lifespan most is the health of the teeth that support it: decay or gum disease starting in those teeth, more than the bridge material, is what leads to replacement. That’s why cleaning under and around the bridge every day is the most important habit for making it last.

sections.html: A bridge is made by crowning the teeth on either side of the gap and joining a false tooth (pontic) between those crowns to replace the missing tooth. The pontic sits on the gum but isn’t attached to it, so the area underneath needs special cleaning. We compare bridges and implants in implant or bridge.

• Decay in a supporting tooth: Decay starting at the edge of a crown is the most common reason a bridge needs replacing. If it progresses, root canal treatment may be needed.
  • Gum disease: Plaque building up under the bridge can lead to gum inflammation and bone loss. See how to treat gum inflammation.
  • Clenching and grinding: Can crack the porcelain or loosen the bridge. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • Hard foods: Biting nutshells, ice or fruit stones with a bridge can break the porcelain.
  • Long bridges: Bridges that carry several missing teeth on few supporting teeth are under more load.

sections.h: Get your bridge checked if you notice these
sections.html:
SignPossible cause
Smell or bad taste from under the bridgePlaque build-up, decay under a crown
Sensitivity to hot or cold in a supporting toothGap at the edge, decay, gum recession
The bridge moving or flexing when you biteCement washing out, a problem in a supporting tooth
A dark line at the edge of a crownGum recession or a metal framework
A crack or chip in the porcelainClenching, hard biting
Bleeding or swollen gumsGum inflammation
In short

A bridge usually lasts ten years or more. Its lifespan depends most on the health of the supporting teeth; cleaning under the bridge every day and regular check-ups are the key habits. If you notice a smell, movement or sensitivity, get it checked without waiting.

We explain the causes of smell and darkening in pain and smell from a crowned tooth and dark gums around a crown.

sections.h: How to clean under a bridge
sections.html:
Ordinary floss can’t pass under a bridge, so one of these tools is used:

  • Floss threader: A flexible loop for pulling ordinary floss under the bridge.
  • Super floss: A special floss with one stiff end and a spongy middle section, well suited to wiping under a bridge.
  • Interdental brush: Used if there’s enough space between the bridge and the gum.
  • Water flosser: Helps rinse out debris under the bridge, but doesn’t replace floss on its own. See electric brushes and water flossers.

Wipe under the pontic from front to back a few times, then clean the sides of the supporting teeth facing the bridge. For technique, see how to floss.

• A small porcelain chip: Can sometimes be repaired in the mouth with composite.
  • The bridge coming off: If the bridge and supporting teeth are sound, it can be re-cemented. Keep the bridge and bring it to the clinic; don’t try to fix it with household glue. See my filling fell out or my crown came off.
  • Decay in a supporting tooth: Usually the bridge has to be removed, the tooth treated and a new bridge made.

sections.h: Options when a bridge needs replacing
sections.html: When a bridge needs replacing, depending on the supporting teeth, a new bridge can be made, or an implant can be placed in the gap and the neighbouring teeth crowned separately. Zirconia is the most common material; we cover the habits that affect its lifespan in how long zirconia crowns last. Options for a single missing tooth are in a single missing tooth.

sections.h: Bridge check-ups at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At check-ups we examine the edges of the bridge, the supporting teeth and the gums, using X-rays if needed. We show you in your own mouth how to clean under the bridge with the tool that suits you.

faq.q: How long does a dental bridge last on average?
faq.a: A well-planned, well-cared-for bridge usually lasts ten years or more, and many last much longer. The health of the supporting teeth matters most.

faq.q: Is it normal for a bridge to smell?
faq.a: No. It usually comes from plaque under the bridge or decay at the edge of a crown, and should be checked.

faq.q: How do you clean under a bridge?
faq.a: With a floss threader, super floss or an interdental brush of the right size. A water flosser helps but isn’t enough on its own.

faq.q: My bridge came off. Can it be put back?
faq.a: If the bridge and supporting teeth are sound, it can usually be re-cemented. Keep the bridge and bring it to the clinic; don’t use household glue.

faq.q: Does a bridge or an implant last longer?
faq.a: Both can last many years. An implant doesn’t involve the neighbouring teeth, while a bridge’s lifespan depends on the health of the supporting teeth. The choice depends on your mouth.

title: Can receding gums grow back? What can be done to stop gum recession
desc: Do receded gums grow back on their own? Stopping gum recession, why teeth look longer after a scale and clean, gum grafts, sensitivity on exposed roots and care at home.
seoTitle: Can receding gums grow back? Stopping gum recession | Dent32
seoDesc: Do receded gums grow back on their own? Stopping gum recession, gum grafts, sensitivity on exposed roots and caring for your gums at home.
lead: Receded gums don’t grow back to where they were on their own, but recession can usually be stopped from getting worse, and in some cases an exposed root can be covered again with a gum graft. The first step is finding the cause, such as hard brushing, gum disease, thin gum tissue or clenching. Teeth looking longer after a scale and clean is usually not recession but swollen gums healing and returning to their normal level.

sections.html:
• Brushing hard or pressing too hard: Can wear the gum away, especially around canines and premolars.
  • Gum disease: Tartar and plaque gradually push back the gum and the bone beneath it. See bleeding and receding gums.
  • Thin gum tissue: Some people naturally have thin gums that are more prone to recession.
  • Clenching and grinding: Can contribute to wear at the neck of the tooth and recession. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • Tooth position: Gums are thinner over crowded teeth or teeth that sit towards the outside of the bone.
  • Smoking: Speeds up gum disease and masks its signs. See how smoking affects teeth and gums.

Gum tissue doesn’t regrow on its own where it has been lost. Toothpastes, oil pulling or herbal mixtures said online to bring gums back don’t restore lost tissue. But with the right care and treatment, recession can usually be stopped from progressing. That matters at least as much as regaining tissue, because as recession advances the bone supporting the root can be affected too.

In short

Receded gums don’t grow back on their own, but once the cause is found and dealt with, recession can usually be stopped. Where suitable, an exposed root can be covered again with a gum graft. Teeth looking longer after a scale and clean is usually a sign of healing.

sections.h: Why do teeth look longer after a scale and clean?
sections.html: Tartar and plaque cause gum inflammation and swelling. Swollen gums cover part of the tooth and look higher than their true level. After cleaning, the inflammation settles, the gum tightens and sits where it should be; the gaps between teeth can then look wider and the teeth longer. This doesn’t mean the cleaning caused recession; it means loss that was already there has become visible. See does scaling damage enamel.

sections.h: What can be done to stop recession?
sections.html:
CauseWhat helps
Hard brushingSoft brush, correct technique, electric brush with a pressure sensor
Gum diseaseScale and clean, deep cleaning if needed, regular check-ups
ClenchingNight guard
Thin gums, progressing recessionGum graft to thicken the gum
Tooth positionOrthodontic treatment in some cases

For brushing technique, see how to brush properly and electric or manual toothbrush. If there are deep pockets, we explain the treatment in gum pocket treatment.

sections.h: When is a gum graft done?
sections.html: A gum graft involves placing a small piece of tissue, usually taken from the palate, at the area of recession. The aim is to cover an exposed root, thicken thin gums to stop recession progressing or improve appearance. How much of the root can be covered depends on how deep the recession is and on the level of the bone and gum between the teeth. If there’s little bone loss between neighbouring teeth, coverage is usually better. Details: gum grafts and pink aesthetics.

sections.h: Sensitivity and decay on exposed roots
sections.html: Root surfaces aren’t covered by enamel, so they can be sensitive to cold, heat and brushing and decay more easily than enamel. Desensitising toothpastes, fluoride care and, if needed, a filling or varnish on the root surface help. See sensitivity to hot and cold and is fluoride harmful.

sections.h: Gum assessment at Dent32 in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At the examination we record the depth of recession and gum pocket measurements, and explain the cause and the options that suit you. By repeating the measurements at check-ups, we track together whether the recession has stopped.

faq.q: Does gum recession go away on its own?
faq.a: Lost gum doesn’t grow back on its own. But once the cause is dealt with, recession can usually be stopped from progressing.

faq.q: Can gum recession be treated?
faq.a: Yes. Dealing with the cause stops the recession, and where suitable an exposed root can be covered again with a gum graft.

faq.q: Does a scale and clean cause gum recession?
faq.a: No. After cleaning, swollen gums heal and return to their normal level, which can make teeth look longer.

faq.q: Is there a toothpaste that regrows gums?
faq.a: No toothpaste or herbal mixture restores lost gum tissue. Desensitising and fluoride toothpastes help protect exposed roots.

faq.q: Which toothbrush should I use with receding gums?
faq.a: A soft brush and gentle technique. Electric brushes with a pressure sensor can help prevent pressing too hard.

title: When can you exercise after a tooth extraction? Showers, saunas, swimming and flying
desc: How many days after an extraction can you exercise or lift weights? Exercise after wisdom tooth removal, hot showers, Turkish baths and saunas, swimming, flying, and what to do if bleeding restarts.
seoTitle: When can you exercise after a tooth extraction? | Dent32
seoDesc: How soon after an extraction can you exercise or lift weights? Wisdom tooth removal, hot showers, saunas, swimming, flying and renewed bleeding.
lead: In the first 24–48 hours after an extraction, avoid strenuous exercise: when your heart rate and blood pressure rise, the clot in the socket can be disturbed and bleeding can restart. After a simple extraction, gentle walking is fine from the first day; you can usually return to moderate exercise after 2–3 days and to hard training after 3–5 days. After a surgical extraction such as an impacted wisdom tooth, this can extend to about a week. Turkish baths and saunas should also wait for the first few days.

sections.h: Why take a break from exercise after an extraction?
sections.html:
The blood clot that forms in the socket is the foundation of healing. Intense exercise raises blood pressure, which in the first days can restart bleeding or dislodge the clot. If the clot is lost early, a painful condition called dry socket can develop. See dry socket (alveolar osteitis).

Holding your breath and clenching your teeth while lifting also put pressure on the extraction site. If you’re taking painkillers in the first days, tiredness and dizziness can make exercise harder too.

sections.h: What you can do, and when
sections.html:
ActivitySimple extractionSurgical / wisdom tooth extraction
Gentle walkingFrom the first dayAfter 1–2 days
Light exercise, yoga (no head-down poses)After 2–3 daysAfter 4–5 days
Running, weights, intense cardioAfter 3–5 daysAfter about 1 week
Contact sports (football, basketball, combat sports)After about 1 week, with a mouthguardAfter 1–2 weeks, with your dentist’s approval
SwimmingAfter 2–3 daysAfter about 1 week
Turkish bath, sauna, very hot bathAfter 2–3 daysAfter about 1 week

These times are a general guide; your dentist may give you a different time depending on how difficult the extraction was and whether you have stitches.

In short

Avoid strenuous exercise for the first 24–48 hours after an extraction. After a simple extraction you can return to light exercise after 2–3 days and to hard training after 3–5 days; after surgical extractions it’s about a week. Stop if the area throbs or bleeds while you exercise.

A short shower at a normal temperature is fine on the day of the extraction. Very hot, long baths, Turkish baths and saunas widen the blood vessels and can increase bleeding; avoid them for the first few days, or about a week after surgical extractions. Don’t apply heat to the outside of your face on the first day; for swelling, cold can be applied to the outside of the cheek at intervals in the first 24 hours.

Swimming takes physical effort, so it’s treated like strenuous exercise. As the socket is an open wound in the first days, it’s usual to wait a few days before the pool or sea. Try not to swallow water or swish it around the extraction site.

sections.h: Can you fly after an extraction?
sections.html: Flying usually causes no problems after a simple extraction. If an upper molar was removed with roots close to the sinus and your dentist has said there is an opening between the sinus and the mouth, follow the time your dentist gives you for flying and blowing your nose hard. You may be asked to sneeze with your mouth open. If you have a trip planned, mention it before the extraction.

sections.h: Things to watch when you return to sport
sections.html:
• Drink plenty of water, but don’t use a straw in the first days; the sucking can disturb the clot.
  • Drink protein shakes and sports drinks from a glass; after acidic or sugary drinks, rinse gently with water.
  • Try not to clench your teeth when lifting.
  • Stop if the extraction site starts to throb or bleed during training.
  • Wear a mouthguard for contact sports. See mouthguards for sport.

1. Stay calm and sit down, keeping your head slightly raised.
  2. Fold a clean piece of gauze, place it on the extraction site and bite firmly for 30 minutes.
  3. Don’t rinse or spit.
  4. If the bleeding doesn’t ease in that time, or pain gets worse a few days later, call the clinic.

We cover all of the aftercare in after a tooth extraction and when stitches come out in stitches after a tooth extraction.

faq.q: How many days after an extraction can I exercise?
faq.a: After a simple extraction you can usually return to light exercise after 2–3 days and to hard training after 3–5 days. After surgical extractions it’s about a week.

faq.q: Can I go for a walk after a tooth extraction?
faq.a: Gentle walking is fine from the first day after a simple extraction.

faq.q: When can I exercise after wisdom tooth removal?
faq.a: As it’s a surgical extraction, it’s usual to wait about a week before strenuous exercise. Light activity can start after a few days.

faq.q: Can I go to a sauna or Turkish bath after an extraction?
faq.a: Not for the first few days, or about a week after surgical extractions; heat can increase bleeding.

faq.q: Can I fly after a tooth extraction?
faq.a: Usually yes after a simple extraction. If there’s a sinus issue after an upper molar extraction, follow the time your dentist gives you.

title: Can a toothache cause a fever? What to do if you have a fever and facial swelling
desc: Why might you have a fever with toothache, and can a dental abscess cause one? What to do at home with a fever and swollen cheek, the role of painkillers and antibiotics, and when to see a dentist.
seoTitle: Can a toothache cause a fever? | Dent32
seoDesc: Can toothache or a dental abscess cause a fever? What to do with a fever and swollen cheek, the role of antibiotics and when to see a dentist.
lead: Toothache on its own doesn't cause a fever; a fever can be a sign that an infection (abscess) has developed at the root of the tooth or in the gum. Throbbing pain is then often accompanied by swelling of the cheek or gum, feeling unwell and a tender lump under the jaw. Painkillers bring the temperature and pain down for a while but don't treat the source of the infection. If you have toothache with a fever, see a dentist the same day or the next day at the latest.

sections.h: Why might you get a fever with toothache?
sections.html:
When decay reaches the nerve of a tooth, the nerve gradually dies and an infection can develop at the tip of the root. The body may respond to this infection with a fever. A similar picture can be seen with gum inflammation around a partly erupted wisdom tooth and with advanced gum disease.

What these infections have in common is that they don't fully clear until the source is dealt with. Even if the pain eases for a few days, the infection can carry on quietly. We explain more in dental abscess and facial swelling and wisdom tooth gum infection.

sections.h: What to do, depending on your symptoms
sections.html:
SymptomLikely causeWhat to do
Brief twinges with hot or cold; no feverSensitivity or early decayBook an appointment within a few days
Throbbing pain, worse at night; no feverInflamed nerveExamination within a day or two
Pain + mild fever + swollen gumDental abscessExamination the same or next day
Swelling around a wisdom tooth, difficulty opening the mouthPericoronitisExamination the same or next day
Swelling spreading to the eye or neck, trouble swallowing or breathing, high feverSpreading infectionGo to A&E without waiting
In short

Toothache with a fever usually means there is an infection in the tooth or gum. Painkillers bring relief but don't treat the source; the infection needs to be cleared. So with a toothache and fever, see a dentist without delay.

sections.h: What you can do at home until you see a dentist
sections.html:
• You can take painkillers at the dose on the leaflet; paracetamol and ibuprofen also bring a temperature down. We explain which may suit you in which painkiller is best for toothache.
  • Drink plenty of fluids and rest.
  • Apply a cold compress to the outside of the cheek, on and off.
  • Don't put heat on the swelling, as it can help the infection spread.
  • Don't put aspirin on the gum; it burns the tissue.
  • Don't try to burst the swelling with a needle or your fingers.

Antibiotics are a decision for the dentist after an examination, when there are signs of the infection spreading or a fever and feeling generally unwell. The real treatment is clearing the source of the infection: draining the abscess, root canal treatment or, if necessary, removing the tooth. Starting an old course of antibiotics you have at home can temporarily mask the problem and delay treatment. We cover this in detail in do antibiotics and painkillers cure toothache.

A baby's temperature may rise slightly while teething, but a high fever shouldn't be put down to teething and should be checked by a doctor. See teething in babies. In older children, an abscess from a decayed baby tooth can also cause a fever and a swollen cheek; even though it's a baby tooth, it needs treatment. See baby bottle tooth decay.

sections.h: Is a fever normal after a tooth extraction?
sections.html: A slight rise in temperature can occur on the first day after an extraction. If pain gets worse a few days later and comes with a fever, a bad smell or a bad taste, let your dentist know. We describe the usual course of healing in after a tooth extraction and dry socket.

Dent32 is open seven days a week. If you call with toothache and a fever or facial swelling, we try to see you at the earliest possible time. For nights and public holidays, see emergency dentists in Beylikdüzü.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Can a toothache cause a fever?
faq.a: Toothache on its own doesn't cause a fever. A fever can mean an infection (abscess) has developed at the root of the tooth or in the gum, which needs an examination.

faq.q: How long does a fever from a dental abscess last?
faq.a: The fever can keep coming back until the source of the infection is cleared. Once the abscess is drained or root canal treatment has started, it usually settles within a day or two.

faq.q: Are painkillers enough for a toothache with fever?
faq.a: Painkillers lower the temperature and pain for a while, but they don't treat the infection. You should see a dentist the same day or the next day at the latest.

faq.q: My face is swollen from a tooth. Can I use a warm compress?
faq.a: Don't put heat on the swelling. A cold compress on the outside of the cheek, on and off, can help; if the swelling spreads to the eye or neck, go to A&E without waiting.

faq.q: Do babies get a fever when teething?
faq.a: Their temperature may rise slightly; a high fever shouldn't be put down to teething and should be checked by a doctor.

title: Why is toothache worse at night? What to do when tooth pain starts at night
desc: Why does toothache get worse at night and start throbbing when you lie down? What helps you get to sleep with tooth pain, painkillers and compresses, what to avoid and seeing a dentist the next day.
seoTitle: Why is toothache worse at night? | Dent32
seoDesc: Why does toothache get worse at night and throb when you lie down? What helps you sleep, painkillers, compresses and what to avoid.
lead: There are several reasons toothache gets worse at night: lying down increases blood flow to the head and raises the pressure inside an inflamed tooth, there are fewer distractions so the pain feels stronger, and painkillers taken during the day wear off. In some people, clenching during sleep adds to the pain. Raising your head on an extra pillow, taking painkillers as directed and using a cold compress on your cheek can help you through the night. Throbbing pain that gets worse at night usually means the tooth's nerve is inflamed, so you should be seen the next day.

sections.h: Why does toothache get worse at night?
sections.html:
• Lying down: When you lie flat, more blood flows to your head. Because the inside of a tooth is enclosed by hard tissue, pressure in an inflamed nerve rises easily and the throbbing gets worse.
  • No distractions: During the day, work, conversation and moving about keep pain in the background; in the quiet of the night it feels more intense.
  • Painkillers wearing off: Medicine taken during the day may lose its effect around midnight.
  • Clenching: Clenching during sleep puts extra load on a tooth that is already sensitive. See teeth clenching and grinding.
  • Blocked sinuses: Lying down can increase sinus pressure, which may feel like pain in the upper back teeth. See can sinusitis cause toothache.

1. Sleep with your head raised on an extra pillow or two.
  2. Before bed, take a painkiller at the dose on the leaflet. See which painkiller is best for toothache.
  3. Apply a cold compress to the outside of your cheek for 15–20 minutes at a time.
  4. Rinse gently with warm salt water; if food is stuck between your teeth, floss carefully. See food getting stuck between teeth.
  5. Avoid very hot, very cold and sugary food and drinks before bed.
  6. Don't chew on the painful side.

We cover other things you can do at home, and what to avoid, in how to relieve toothache.

sections.h: What night-time pain can tell you
sections.html:
What the pain is likeLikely causeWhen to be seen
A twinge with cold that passes in secondsSensitivity, early decayWithin a few days
Throbbing that starts on its own and wakes youInflamed nerveThe next day
Worse when biting, tooth feels “raised”Inflammation at the root tipThe next day
With jaw and temple pain in the morningClenchingWithin a few days
Pain with a fever or facial swellingAbscessThe same day; see can toothache cause a fever
In short

Toothache that gets worse at night usually means the tooth's nerve is inflamed; lying down raises the pressure inside the tooth. Raising your head, painkillers at the right dose and a cold compress can help you through the night. Even if the pain settles, get seen the next day.

sections.h: What to avoid with night-time toothache
sections.html:
• Don't put aspirin on the gum or the tooth; it burns the tissue.
  • Don't take more than the recommended dose of painkillers or mix different ones at random.
  • Don't start an old course of antibiotics you have at home. See do antibiotics cure toothache.
  • If there is swelling, don't put heat on your cheek.
  • Don't rub alcohol or cologne on the tooth.

sections.h: What if the pain has gone by morning?
sections.html: It's common for pain that was severe at night to ease by morning, but that doesn't mean the problem has gone. Inflammation in the nerve can progress and come back a few days later with stronger pain or swelling. Seen early, a tooth can often be saved with simpler treatment. We explain when root canal treatment is needed in root canal treatment.

Dent32 is open seven days a week; if toothache starts at night, you can call in the morning and ask for a same-day appointment. For nights and public holidays, see emergency dentists in Beylikdüzü, and for weekends, weekend dental clinic.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Why is toothache worse at night?
faq.a: Lying down increases blood flow to the head and raises the pressure inside an inflamed tooth; there are also fewer distractions, so pain feels stronger, and daytime painkillers wear off.

faq.q: How can I sleep with toothache?
faq.a: Raise your head on an extra pillow, take a painkiller at the dose on the leaflet before bed and use a cold compress on your cheek. Avoid very hot, cold and sugary things before bed.

faq.q: Do I need to go to A&E for toothache that starts at night?
faq.a: If there's no fever, no swelling spreading to the face or neck and no trouble swallowing or breathing, seeing a dentist the next day is usually enough. If you have any of these, go to A&E without waiting.

faq.q: My toothache had gone by morning. Should I still go?
faq.a: Yes. Pain that gets worse at night is often a sign of an inflamed nerve and can come back more strongly a few days later; it's easier to save the tooth if it's seen early.

faq.q: Is heat or cold better for toothache at night?
faq.a: A cold compress on the outside of the cheek usually helps more. Don't use heat if there is swelling.

title: When are stitches removed after a tooth extraction? Dissolvable stitches, stitches coming loose and aftercare
desc: When are stitches removed after an extraction, and when do dissolvable stitches fall out? What to do if one comes out early, and how to eat, brush and rinse with stitches.
seoTitle: When are stitches removed after a tooth extraction? | Dent32
seoDesc: When are stitches removed after an extraction, and when do dissolvable ones fall out? What if one comes out early, and eating and brushing.
lead: Stitches placed after a tooth extraction come in two types: dissolvable stitches usually loosen and fall out on their own within 7–14 days, while non-dissolvable stitches are mostly removed at a check-up after 7–10 days. If a stitch comes out a day or two early and there's no bleeding, it's usually nothing to worry about. Not playing with the stitches with your tongue or fingers, not rinsing for the first 24 hours, then rinsing gently with warm salt water and avoiding chewing on that side all help healing.

sections.h: Why are stitches placed after an extraction?
sections.html: Not every extraction needs stitches. They are used after surgical extractions where the gum has been opened, such as an impacted wisdom tooth, when several neighbouring teeth are removed, or when it's important to control bleeding and keep the clot in place. Stitches hold the edges of the gum together so the wound heals more neatly. For the procedure itself, see wisdom teeth and tooth extraction in Beylikdüzü.

sections.h: What to expect with each type of stitch
sections.html:
Dissolvable stitchesNon-dissolvable stitches
When do they come out?Usually loosen or fall out on their own within 7–14 daysMostly removed at a check-up after 7–10 days
Is a check-up needed?If your dentist asksYes, an appointment to remove them
Does removal hurt?Not removedQuick; usually no anaesthetic needed, just a slight tugging feeling
If one comes out earlyUsually fine if there's no bleedingUsually fine if there's no bleeding; let your dentist know
In short

Dissolvable stitches usually fall out on their own within 7–14 days; non-dissolvable ones are removed after 7–10 days. Don't play with them, don't rinse on the first day, then rinse gently with warm salt water. A stitch that comes out early is usually not a problem if there's no bleeding.

sections.h: A stitch came out early or the wound opened: what to do
sections.html:
It's normal for the ends of dissolvable stitches to loosen within a few days and for some to fall out. If there's no bleeding and the edges of the wound have started to close, you usually don't need to do anything.

  • If it bleeds, fold a clean piece of gauze, place it over the wound and bite on it firmly for 30 minutes without lifting it.
  • If the bleeding doesn't stop, if there's a noticeable gap or if pain is increasing, call your dentist.
  • Don't try to cut or pull out a loose or dangling stitch yourself; if it's poking you, your dentist can trim it.

1. For the first 24 hours, don't rinse, spit or drink through a straw; it's important not to disturb the clot.
  2. From the next day, rinse gently with warm salt water after meals; let the water move around your mouth and then let it fall into the sink.
  3. Brush your other teeth as normal, and be very gentle with a soft brush around the stitches for a few days.
  4. Eat soft, lukewarm food for a few days and don't chew on that side.
  5. Stay off cigarettes for as long as you can, as smoking slows healing. See what smoking does to teeth and gums.
  6. Don't probe the stitches with your tongue or fingers.

We explain what to know about bleeding, swelling and eating in the first days in after a tooth extraction.

sections.h: Is white tissue in the socket normal?
sections.html: Two or three days after an extraction, a soft whitish-yellow layer may appear over the wound. This is usually healing tissue and is normal; it doesn't mean infection. If pain increases rather than easing over a few days, and there's a bad taste or smell and the socket looks empty, it may be a dry socket. See what is dry socket.

sections.h: When to let your dentist know
sections.html:
• Bleeding that doesn't stop despite 30 minutes of pressure
  • Pain that increases after the third day
  • Increasing swelling, a fever or marked difficulty opening your mouth
  • Numbness that lasts longer than a day

These are not common, but if you notice them, calling your dentist straight away makes healing easier.

After an extraction at Dent32, we tell you in writing what type of stitches you have, when they will dissolve or be removed and when your check-up is. If anything worries you, just call.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many days after an extraction are stitches removed?
faq.a: Non-dissolvable stitches are usually removed at a check-up after 7–10 days. Dissolvable stitches aren't removed; they loosen or fall out on their own within 7–14 days.

faq.q: What if dissolvable stitches don't fall out?
faq.a: If a stitch is still bothering you after two weeks, your dentist can easily remove it at a check-up; don't try to pull it out yourself.

faq.q: A stitch fell out early. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Usually not, if there's no bleeding and the edges of the wound have started to close. If it bleeds, press on gauze for 30 minutes; if it doesn't stop, call your dentist.

faq.q: Does it hurt to have stitches removed?
faq.a: Removing stitches is a simple procedure that takes a few minutes; it usually needs no anaesthetic and feels like a slight tug.

faq.q: Can I brush my teeth with stitches?
faq.a: Yes. Brush your other teeth as normal, be very gentle around the stitches with a soft brush for the first few days, and rinse gently with warm salt water from the next day.

title: What can you eat after teeth whitening? The “white diet” and sensitivity
desc: What can you eat in the first 48 hours after whitening, and when can you have tea, coffee or smoke again? The white diet list, sensitivity after whitening and how to make the result last.
seoTitle: What can you eat after teeth whitening? | Dent32
seoDesc: What can you eat in the 48 hours after whitening, and when are tea, coffee and smoking OK? The white diet, sensitivity and making results last.
lead: For the first 24–48 hours after teeth whitening, teeth are more prone to picking up colour from food and drink, so a “white diet” of light-coloured foods is recommended during that time. Water, milk, yoghurt, white cheese, chicken, fish, rice and pasta are fine; tea, coffee, cola, red wine, tomato-based and dark sauces, dark fruit and smoking are best avoided. Some mild sensitivity can occur in this period too; avoiding very hot and very cold things makes it easier. Sensitivity usually settles within a few days.

sections.h: Why do teeth stain more easily after whitening?
sections.html: As whitening gel breaks down the colour molecules inside the tooth, it leaves the enamel temporarily a little more porous and dehydrated. Saliva restores the balance within a few days. In those first days, pigments in dark food and drink can work their way into the tooth more easily, and some of the newly gained shade can be lost.

sections.h: What to eat and avoid in the first 48 hours
sections.html:
OK to eat (white diet)Best avoided
Water, sparkling water, milkTea, coffee, cola, energy drinks
Yoghurt, white cheeseRed wine, cherry and pomegranate juice
Chicken, turkey, white fishTomato purée and sauce, soy sauce, ketchup
Rice, pasta (plain or with a white sauce), potatoesCurry, turmeric and dark spices
Boiled cauliflower, peeled apples and pears, bananasBlackberries, blueberries, strawberries, beetroot
White bread, oatsChocolate, dark desserts, coloured sweets
Cigarettes, shisha and other tobacco
In short

For the first 24–48 hours after whitening, stick to light-coloured foods and avoid tea, coffee, cola, red wine, tomato and dark sauces, dark fruit and smoking. Mild sensitivity is common; avoid very hot and cold things, and it usually settles within a few days.

sections.h: When can you drink tea and coffee again?
sections.html:
You can go back to tea and coffee after the first 48 hours. To make the result last longer:

  • Drink dark drinks through a straw where you can.
  • Rinse your mouth with water afterwards.
  • Have them at set times rather than sipping all day.
  • Stopping or cutting down on smoking makes the biggest difference. See what smoking does to teeth and gums.

We explain why teeth pick up colour again over time in why teeth go yellow.

Some people have short-lived, twinging sensitivity after whitening. It mostly settles on its own within a few days.

  • Avoid very hot and very cold food and drink for a few days.
  • You can use a desensitising toothpaste (such as one containing potassium nitrate).
  • With home whitening, if sensitivity increases, take a day or two off the gel and ask your dentist.
  • If sensitivity lasts more than a week or is marked in one tooth, have it checked.

You can read about other causes of sensitivity in sensitivity to hot and cold.

sections.h: The white diet with home whitening
sections.html: Home whitening with custom trays usually runs for two to three weeks. During that time, following the same rules for a few hours after each session, cutting down on dark drinks and avoiding smoking makes a clear difference to the result. We compare in-clinic and home whitening in teeth whitening: in the clinic or at home.

• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and use whitening toothpastes in moderation. See whitening toothpaste.
  • Have a scale and polish every six months.
  • Don't try DIY methods such as lemon or baking soda. See whitening teeth at home.
  • If needed, a short top-up treatment can be done at intervals your dentist suggests.

After whitening at Dent32, we give you written guidance on what to watch for in the first days. You can read about the process in teeth whitening in Beylikdüzü.
