At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How long should I follow the white diet after whitening?
faq.a: Usually for the first 24–48 hours, when teeth are more prone to picking up colour from food and drink.

faq.q: When can I drink coffee after whitening?
faq.a: After the first 48 hours. Using a straw and rinsing with water afterwards helps keep the result.

faq.q: Can I smoke after teeth whitening?
faq.a: Not in the first 48 hours; smoking is one of the quickest ways to undo the result of whitening.

faq.q: My teeth are sensitive after whitening. Is that normal?
faq.a: Short-lived sensitivity is common and usually settles within a few days. Avoid very hot and cold things, and have it checked if it lasts more than a week.

faq.q: Can I have milk and yoghurt after whitening?
faq.a: Yes. Light-coloured foods such as milk, yoghurt and white cheese are fine on the white diet.

title: How to clean a night guard, clear aligners and retainers: odour, yellowing and storage
desc: How should you clean a night guard, clear aligners or a retainer, and can you use toothpaste or hot water? Dealing with odour, yellowing and white deposits, and storing it properly.
seoTitle: How to clean a night guard, clear aligners and retainers | Dent32
seoDesc: How to clean a night guard, clear aligners or a retainer, and can you use toothpaste? Dealing with odour, yellowing and deposits, and storage.
lead: Night guards, clear aligners and retainers should be rinsed in cold or lukewarm water every time you take them out and gently brushed at least once a day with a separate soft brush and a non-abrasive cleaner such as unscented liquid soap. Toothpaste can scratch the surface and make it cloudy, and hot water can warp the plastic. Cleaning tablets suitable for appliances can be used a few times a week. Once clean and dry, the appliance should be kept in its ventilated case.

sections.html:
1. Rinse the appliance in cold or lukewarm water as soon as you take it out; it's easier to clean before saliva dries.
  2. Using a soft brush kept just for the appliance, gently brush the inside and outside with unscented liquid soap or a cleaner your dentist recommends.
  3. Rinse thoroughly.
  4. Let it air-dry, then put it in its ventilated case.
  5. Brush your teeth before putting it back in; a clean appliance over dirty teeth keeps bacteria against your teeth for hours.

DoDon't
Rinse in cold or lukewarm waterUse hot or boiling water; the plastic can warp
Use a separate soft brushBrush with toothpaste; it scratches and clouds the surface
Use unscented liquid soap or appliance cleaning tabletsSoak in bleach, alcohol or alcohol-based mouthwash
Store it in a ventilated case once dryWrap it in a napkin; it easily ends up in the bin
Wash the case once a week tooLeave it where pets can reach it
In short

Rinse your appliance every time you take it out and brush it once a day with a separate soft brush and a non-abrasive cleaner. Avoid hot water, toothpaste, bleach and alcohol-based mouthwash. Store it in a ventilated case once it's dry.

sections.h: Why do appliances smell or turn yellow?
sections.html:
The most common causes are a layer of bacteria building up on the surface and minerals from saliva. If the appliance isn't brushed regularly, this layer thickens and white, chalky deposits can form over time. Tea, coffee and coloured drinks taken with the appliance in will stain it too.

  • Drink only water while wearing clear aligners; take them out for anything else.
  • Brush your teeth before putting the appliance in.
  • Cleaning tablets made for appliances help with white deposits; if they're stubborn, ask your dentist.
  • If the smell persists despite cleaning, have your mouth checked for a source too. See bad breath.

• Clear aligners (orthodontic treatment): Worn 20–22 hours a day, so they need the most care. Don't put them back in after eating without brushing first. See clear aligners or braces.
  • Retainers: Keep teeth in place after treatment; if one cracks or becomes loose, let your dentist know promptly. See how long to wear a retainer.
  • Night guards: Used for clenching and grinding; clean in the morning and leave to dry. See clenching and night guards.
  • Sports mouthguards: Rinse and dry after every use. See mouthguards for sport.

sections.h: When should an appliance be replaced?
sections.html: Clear aligners are changed at set intervals as part of the treatment plan. Night guards and retainers can last a long time with good care, but cracks, holes, marked wear or a poor fit should be checked at your next appointment. If it's hard to put in or doesn't feel as snug as before, your teeth may have moved.

Always put your appliance in its case when you take it out; appliances wrapped in a napkin at restaurants are lost all the time. If you can't brush, rinse the appliance and your mouth with water and do a proper clean at the first chance.

At Dent32 we look at your night guard or retainer at check-ups and assess how it fits and how worn it is. We explain who needs a night guard in teeth clenching and night guards in Beylikdüzü.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Can I clean my night guard with toothpaste?
faq.a: It's best not to. The abrasives in toothpaste scratch and cloud the surface, and scratches make it easier for bacteria to build up. Use unscented liquid soap or a cleaner made for appliances.

faq.q: Can I wash clear aligners in hot water?
faq.a: No. Hot or boiling water can warp them. Use cold or lukewarm water.

faq.q: How do I remove white spots from my retainer?
faq.a: These are usually deposits of minerals from saliva. Regular brushing and appliance cleaning tablets help; if they're stubborn, ask your dentist.

faq.q: Can I drink anything other than water with aligners in?
faq.a: Only water while you're wearing them. Other drinks can stain them, and sugary drinks held against the teeth under the aligners raise the risk of decay.

faq.q: What should I do if my appliance smells?
faq.a: Brush it more regularly, brush your teeth before putting it in and use cleaning tablets a few times a week. If the smell persists, have your mouth checked for a source.

title: Can you strengthen tooth enamel? Does enamel grow back, and how fluoride and toothpastes help
desc: Does tooth enamel repair itself, and can worn enamel grow back? Ways to strengthen enamel: fluoride toothpaste, fluoride varnish, diet and saliva, and the treatments available when enamel is lost.
seoTitle: Can you strengthen tooth enamel? | Dent32
seoDesc: Does tooth enamel repair itself, and can worn enamel grow back? Strengthening enamel with fluoride, diet and saliva, and treatments for enamel loss.
lead: Tooth enamel contains no living cells, so enamel that has chipped or worn away doesn't grow back. However, the surface of enamel loses and regains minerals every day, and you can tip that balance in your favour with fluoride, saliva and a sensible diet. Early mineral loss, which looks like chalky white spots, can be stopped this way and can even harden again. Enamel that has been lost can only be replaced with treatments such as fillings, bonding or crowns.

sections.h: Enamel loses and regains minerals every day
sections.html:
When we eat or drink something sugary or acidic, acid in the mouth dissolves calcium and phosphate from the enamel (demineralisation). Within minutes to an hour, saliva neutralises the acid and returns those minerals to the enamel (remineralisation). Fluoride speeds up this process and makes the rebuilt surface more resistant to acid.

When acid attacks are very frequent or saliva is reduced, the balance tips towards loss: first white spots, then decay or wear. We explain this process in how to spot tooth decay and dental erosion.

MethodWhat it doesNote
Fluoride toothpasteSupports remineralisation and makes enamel more resistant1450 ppm for adults; spit, don't rinse
Fluoride varnish at the clinicLeaves high-strength fluoride on the surfaceFor children and adults at higher risk of decay
High-fluoride toothpaste from your dentistExtra protection for at-risk teethOn prescription, as advised
Toothpastes with calcium phosphate or hydroxyapatiteExtra mineral supportAlongside fluoride, not instead; the evidence is developing
Sugar-free gum (after meals)Increases salivaAbout 20 minutes
Cutting down on how often you have acid and sugarReduces mineral lossFrequency matters more than amount
In short

Lost enamel doesn't grow back, but the enamel surface loses and regains minerals every day. Fluoride toothpaste, enough saliva and fewer acidic and sugary snacks keep that balance and can stop early white spots. Chipped or worn enamel is restored with fillings, bonding or crowns.

• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste; the bedtime brush is the most important.
  • After brushing, spit the toothpaste out and don't rinse with lots of water, so the fluoride stays on the surface.
  • Have acidic drinks (cola, fruit juice, energy drinks) with meals and finish them quickly; don't sip them all day.
  • Wait about half an hour after something acidic before brushing.
  • Use a soft brush and don't press hard. See how to brush properly.
  • Drink water during the day, and if your mouth is dry, look into the cause. See dry mouth.

Dull, chalky white spots on the tooth surface, especially near the gum line, are often early mineral loss. At this stage fluoride and good care can stop the process; the spot hardens and doesn't progress, and sometimes becomes less noticeable. White spots present from development or caused by fluorosis are a different matter. We explain the difference in white spots on teeth. The same approach applies to spots seen after braces.

In children, the enamel of baby teeth and newly erupted adult teeth loses minerals more easily. Fluoride toothpaste in the right amount for their age, fluoride varnish at the clinic and fissure sealants on the grooves of the back teeth give effective protection. See fluoride and fissure sealants for children. We answer questions about fluoride safety in is fluoride harmful.

sections.h: What if enamel has already been lost?
sections.html: Enamel lost to decay, chipping or marked wear doesn't come back. Small losses are restored with bonding or a filling; larger ones may need a veneer or crown. If there's sensitivity, desensitising toothpastes and in-clinic treatments can help. See what is dental bonding and tooth sensitivity.

At check-ups at Dent32 we record early white spots and signs of wear, and, depending on your decay risk, advise on fluoride varnish and products you can use at home.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Does tooth enamel repair itself?
faq.a: Enamel has no living cells, so chipped or worn enamel doesn't regrow. But its surface loses and regains minerals every day, and fluoride supports that regain.

faq.q: Can worn enamel grow back?
faq.a: No. Further wear can be stopped, and the lost part can be restored with bonding, a filling or a crown if needed.

faq.q: Is there a toothpaste that strengthens enamel?
faq.a: Fluoride toothpastes make enamel more resistant to acid. Toothpastes with calcium phosphate or hydroxyapatite can be used for extra support, but not instead of fluoride.

faq.q: Do white spots on teeth go away?
faq.a: Spots caused by early mineral loss can be stopped and can harden with fluoride and good care. Developmental or fluorosis spots need different treatment.

faq.q: Is it bad to brush straight after an acidic drink?
faq.a: Enamel is temporarily softer straight after acid; it's better to wait about half an hour and rinse with water in the meantime.

title: How often should you replace your toothbrush? After illness, storage and electric brush heads
desc: How often should you change your toothbrush or electric brush head? Signs a brush is worn out, whether to replace it after being ill, and how to store and clean it properly.
seoTitle: How often should you replace your toothbrush? | Dent32
seoDesc: How often should you change your toothbrush or electric brush head? Signs of wear, replacing it after illness, and storing it properly.
lead: It’s generally advised to replace your toothbrush about every 3–4 months, or sooner if the bristles splay or flatten earlier. The same applies to electric brush heads. Worn bristles don’t sit well against the tooth surface and gum line, so they remove plaque less effectively. How long a brush lasts depends not only on the calendar but also on how you brush and how you store it. In this article we cover the signs that it’s time for a new brush and practical ways to keep it clean.

sections.h: How often should you replace a toothbrush?
sections.html:
BrushWhen to replace itNote
Manual brush (adult)About every 3–4 monthsSooner if the bristles splay earlier
Electric brush headAbout every 3 monthsWhen the coloured indicator bristles fade
Child’s brushCheck more oftenWears faster because children chew it
People wearing bracesCheck more oftenWires and brackets wear bristles down quickly
Interdental brushWhen the wire bends or the bristles flattenShort-lived; keep a few spares
In short

Replace your toothbrush about every 3–4 months, and don’t wait if the bristles have splayed sooner. Rinse it under running water after use, let it dry upright in the open air, and don’t share it. If a brush splays within a month or two, you are probably pressing too hard.

sections.h: Signs it’s time for a new brush
sections.html:
• The bristles are splayed outwards, flattened or bent.
  • The coloured indicator bristles on an electric brush head have faded halfway.
  • There is build-up or discolouration between or at the base of the bristles that won’t rinse out.
  • The brush smells unpleasant even after rinsing.
  • The brush fell on the floor or in the sink, or someone else used it by mistake.

Looking for these signs is more reliable than going by the calendar. To make it easy to remember, many people change their brush at the start of each season.

sections.h: If your brush splays within a month or two
sections.html: A brush whose bristles splay within a few weeks usually means you are pressing too hard. Hard brushing doesn’t remove more plaque; instead it irritates the gum line and over time can contribute to gum recession and wear at the necks of the teeth. Holding the brush lightly, like a pen, and brushing with small circular movements without pressing is enough. Electric brushes with a pressure sensor warn you when you press too hard. For more, see how to brush properly and bleeding and receding gums.

sections.h: Should you replace your toothbrush after flu or a throat infection?
sections.html:
There is no strong evidence that replacing your brush after an illness stops you from getting ill again; a healthy immune system usually copes with the small number of microorganisms that may remain on a brush. Still, if the brush is already old, or someone at home has a weakened immune system, replacing it is a sensible and inexpensive precaution. While someone is ill, it’s also a good habit to keep their brush apart from the others.

We discuss whether to go to a dental appointment when you are unwell in can you have dental treatment when you’re ill.

sections.h: How should you store a toothbrush?
sections.html:
• After brushing, rinse the brush thoroughly under running water and shake off the excess.
  • Store it upright, in the open, where it can air-dry on its own.
  • Don’t put a closed cap or case on a wet brush; a damp environment helps microorganisms multiply. When travelling, use a cap with ventilation holes.
  • Make sure family members’ brush heads don’t touch each other.
  • A toothbrush is personal; don’t share it, even within the family.
  • Closing the toilet lid when you flush and keeping brushes as far from the toilet as possible is a simple precaution.

sections.h: Do you need to disinfect your toothbrush?
sections.html: Healthy people don’t need to disinfect their toothbrush regularly; rinsing it under running water and letting it dry is enough. Boiling water, the microwave and the dishwasher can damage the bristles and handle. If you want to dip your brush in mouthwash, use a clean cup and fresh liquid each time; sharing one cup between several brushes can carry microorganisms from one to another. If you are having treatment that affects your immune system, talk to your doctor about toothbrush care. For more on daily mouthwash use, see can you use mouthwash every day.

sections.h: What to look for in a new toothbrush
sections.html: For most people, a soft-bristled brush with a small head that reaches the back teeth comfortably is a good choice. Hard bristles don’t clean better and can wear down gums and enamel. Manual and electric brushes are both effective when used correctly; an electric brush can make things easier for people with limited dexterity and for those wearing braces. We compare them in electric toothbrushes and water flossers. Don’t forget to clean between your teeth, where a brush can’t reach, with floss or interdental brushes.

At check-ups at Dent32 we look at where plaque is being left behind and at the condition of your gums together with you, and talk about your brushing technique and whether your brush suits you.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How often should I replace my toothbrush?
faq.a: About every 3–4 months. If the bristles have splayed or flattened sooner, replace it straight away.

faq.q: When should I change my electric toothbrush head?
faq.a: About every 3 months, or when the coloured indicator bristles fade. A head with splayed bristles should be replaced sooner.

faq.q: Should I replace my toothbrush after being ill?
faq.a: There is no strong evidence that it prevents reinfection. If the brush is already old, or someone at home has a weakened immune system, replacing it is a sensible precaution.

faq.q: Should I keep a cap on my toothbrush?
faq.a: Not while it’s wet. Let it dry upright in the open air, and use a ventilated cap when travelling.

faq.q: Can I disinfect my toothbrush in boiling water?
faq.a: It isn’t advised, as boiling water damages the bristles. Rinsing it under running water after use and letting it dry is enough.

title: Can you go to the dentist when you’re ill? Colds, flu, cold sores and when to reschedule
desc: Should you go to a dental appointment with a cold, flu, a fever or a cold sore? When to postpone and when not to wait, the medicines to mention, and looking after your teeth while you recover.
seoTitle: Can you go to the dentist when you’re ill? | Dent32
seoDesc: Should you go to the dentist with a cold, flu, fever or cold sore? When to postpone, when not to wait, and the medicines to mention.
lead: If you don’t have a fever and feel reasonably well, a mild cold usually isn’t a reason to miss a check-up or a short procedure. With flu or a similar contagious infection with fever, a stomach bug, or a blistering cold sore on your lip, it is better to postpone planned dental treatment for a few days, both for your own comfort and for others at the clinic. If you have toothache or swelling, though, call the clinic without waiting, even if you are ill. If you’re unsure, simply let the clinic know before your appointment.

sections.h: When to go and when to postpone
sections.html:
SituationAppointmentNote
Mild cold, no feverCheck-ups and short procedures are usually fineLong procedures can be hard with a blocked nose; let the clinic know
Seasonal allergy (hay fever)You can goIt isn’t contagious; plan ahead for a blocked nose
Flu or a similar contagious infection with feverPostpone planned treatmentUntil you have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without medicine and feel well
Active cold sore on the lipPostpone planned treatmentUntil it has crusted over and healed, usually 1–2 weeks
Stomach bug, vomitingPostponeUntil you have fully recovered
Fever together with toothache or swellingDon’t wait; call the clinicThe tooth may be the cause of the fever
In short

With a mild cold and no fever, check-ups and short procedures can usually go ahead. With flu and a fever, a stomach bug or an active cold sore, postpone planned treatment until you have recovered. If you have toothache or swelling, call the clinic without waiting, even if you are ill.

sections.h: Going to an appointment with a mild cold
sections.html:
During dental treatment your mouth stays open for a long time and you need to breathe mostly through your nose. If your nose is completely blocked this can be uncomfortable, and frequent coughing and sneezing mean the procedure has to be paused. So while a check-up, a scale and polish or a small filling is usually fine, it may be more comfortable to postpone a long procedure such as root canal treatment for a few days.

  • Call the clinic before your appointment, explain how you are, and decide together.
  • Wearing a mask in the waiting area protects other patients.
  • Bring tissues, and agree on a hand signal for when you need a break.
  • If you use a decongestant nasal spray on your pharmacist’s advice, tell your dentist.

sections.h: Why postpone if you have flu or a fever?
sections.html: During an illness with a fever your body is tired; sitting in the chair for a long time, keeping your mouth open and recovering afterwards can all be harder. Dental instruments also create a spray of water and air, so respiratory infections can pass more easily to other patients and the team. That is why planned treatment is done once you have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine and feel generally well. To postpone, simply let the clinic know.

sections.h: Can you have dental treatment with a cold sore?
sections.html:
It’s advisable to postpone planned dental treatment while you have a blistering or open cold sore on your lip. Stretching the lips during treatment can irritate the sore, slow healing and make it easier for the virus to spread to other areas. Once the cold sore has crusted over and healed, usually within 1–2 weeks, treatment can go ahead safely. If something can’t wait, such as pain, the dentist will take the necessary precautions and treat you.

Cold sores appear on the outer edge of the lip and are contagious. Mouth ulcers, which appear inside the mouth on the cheek or inner lip, are not contagious and usually don’t stop treatment. We explain the difference in mouth ulcers.

sections.h: Tell your dentist about your medicines
sections.html: Tell your dentist about any painkillers, fever reducers, decongestants and antibiotics you are taking for your illness. Some decongestant cold remedies can raise your heart rate and blood pressure, which is important to know when planning local anaesthesia. If you are already taking an antibiotic, whether you need anything further for your tooth is assessed with that in mind. For more, see antibiotics for toothache and which painkiller is best for toothache.

sections.h: If you have toothache while you are ill
sections.html: If you have toothache or swelling in your gum or cheek, being ill is not a reason to put off treatment; call the clinic and describe what is happening. Sometimes the tooth itself is the source of the fever; we explain this in can a toothache cause a fever. On the other hand, an ache in the upper back teeth during a cold or sinusitis often comes from the sinuses and eases as the illness passes; see can sinusitis cause toothache.

sections.h: Your teeth during and after an illness
sections.html:
• Keep brushing twice a day while you are ill.
  • Most throat lozenges and syrups contain sugar; choose sugar-free ones where possible and rinse your mouth with water afterwards.
  • Don’t brush straight after vomiting; stomach acid temporarily softens enamel. Rinse with water first and wait about half an hour before brushing. See dental erosion.
  • Breathing through your mouth dries it out; drink water often. See dry mouth.
  • If your toothbrush is old, replace it once you have recovered. See how often to replace your toothbrush.

If you need to postpone your appointment because you are ill, just call or WhatsApp Dent32. If you have pain or swelling, mention it, and we will plan the most suitable time together based on your situation.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Can I go to the dentist with a cold?
faq.a: If you don’t have a fever and feel well, check-ups and short procedures can usually go ahead. With a blocked nose, postponing a long procedure may be more comfortable; let the clinic know before your appointment.

faq.q: Can I have dental treatment with a fever?
faq.a: Planned treatment is postponed until you have been fever-free for at least 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine. If you have toothache or swelling along with the fever, call the clinic without waiting.

faq.q: Can I go to the dentist with a cold sore?
faq.a: Planned treatment is postponed while a cold sore is blistering or open. Once it has crusted over and healed, treatment can continue.

faq.q: Can I have a local anaesthetic while taking cold medicine?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. Tell your dentist which medicines you are taking, especially decongestants, so the anaesthetic can be planned accordingly.

faq.q: Should I replace my toothbrush after being ill?
faq.a: There is no strong evidence that it prevents reinfection; if the brush is old or someone at home has a weakened immune system, replacing it is a sensible precaution.

title: Which painkiller works for toothache? Paracetamol, ibuprofen and what to watch out for
desc: Ibuprofen or paracetamol for toothache? Which painkiller suits whom, should aspirin go on the tooth, do antibiotics stop the pain, and when is it risky to wait with painkillers?
seoTitle: Which painkiller works for toothache? | Dent32
seoDesc: Ibuprofen or paracetamol for toothache? Which painkiller suits whom, aspirin on the tooth, antibiotics, and when it's risky to just wait.
lead: The painkillers most often used for toothache, and shown to work in studies, are anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen, and paracetamol. Paracetamol is usually the safer choice for people with stomach or kidney problems, those on blood thinners and pregnant women. But painkillers only buy time: the decay, inflammation or abscess causing the pain won't go away without treatment. This article explains which medicine suits whom and when waiting becomes risky.

sections.h: Which painkiller is used for toothache?
sections.html:
Active ingredientHow it worksCaution
IbuprofenReduces pain and inflammation togetherMay be unsuitable with stomach or kidney disease, blood thinners and in pregnancy
NaproxenSimilar to ibuprofen, longer-lastingSame cautions as ibuprofen
ParacetamolReduces pain and fever, not inflammationTake care with liver disease and regular alcohol use; don't exceed the daily maximum
AspirinA painkiller, but increases bleedingAvoid before an extraction and in children; never place it on the tooth or gum

Most toothache comes from inflammation inside or around the tooth, so anti-inflammatories (ibuprofen, naproxen) give many people clearer relief than paracetamol. Studies have shown that ibuprofen and paracetamol taken together work well for dental pain; check with your pharmacist or doctor before combining them.

In short

For toothache, an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen or paracetamol is usually used. Which suits you depends on your stomach, kidneys, liver and other medicines; never exceed the dose on the leaflet.

sections.h: Who needs to be careful with which medicine?
sections.html:
• People with stomach ulcers, gastritis or a history of stomach bleeding: ibuprofen and naproxen can irritate the stomach; paracetamol is usually more suitable.
  • People on blood thinners: anti-inflammatories and aspirin increase the risk of bleeding. We cover dental care for heart patients in dental treatment for heart patients.
  • People with kidney disease, heart failure or high blood pressure: don't take anti-inflammatories without medical advice.
  • Pregnant women: painkillers in pregnancy should be chosen with your doctor; anti-inflammatories are generally avoided, especially in the second half of pregnancy. See dental treatment in pregnancy.
  • Breastfeeding mothers: most painkillers are compatible with breastfeeding, but check dose and duration in dental treatment while breastfeeding and with your doctor.
  • Children: aspirin is not given to children; doses are based on weight, so always ask a paediatrician or pharmacist.

Many cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol. Taking them with a painkiller can push you over the daily maximum without realising.

sections.h: Common mistakes: aspirin on the tooth, antibiotics for pain
sections.html:
• Putting aspirin on the tooth: it doesn't relieve the pain and causes a chemical burn and sore on the gum.
  • Trying to stop the pain with antibiotics: antibiotics are not painkillers and don't treat inflammation inside the tooth on their own. We explain when they are needed in antibiotics for toothache.
  • Raising the dose or switching medicines often: if the pain doesn't go, the answer is treating the cause, not more medicine.
  • Putting off treatment because the pain stopped: severe pain that suddenly stops can mean the nerve is dying; infection can progress quietly. See what is a dead tooth?

sections.h: What you can do at home alongside medicine
sections.html:
• Hold a cold compress on the outside of your cheek for 10–15 minutes; heat can make swelling worse.
  • Don't chew on the painful side; avoid very hot, very cold and sugary food.
  • Raise your head slightly when lying down; it can help pain that gets worse at night.
  • To tell whether the pain is coming from the tooth, sinus or ear, see can toothache cause ear pain? and can sinusitis cause toothache?

We've gathered the general steps in how to relieve toothache.

sections.h: When is it dangerous to keep waiting with painkillers?
sections.html:
In these situations don't try to manage with painkillers; see a dentist the same day:

  • swelling of the face, under the jaw or around the eye;
  • fever, feeling unwell, difficulty swallowing or opening your mouth;
  • pain lasting more than 2–3 days despite painkillers, or pain that wakes you up;
  • a pimple-like bump on the gum or a bad taste in the mouth.

Swelling spreading quickly across the face and neck, or difficulty breathing, needs emergency care. We explain swelling in dental abscess.

At Dent32 we find the source of the pain with an examination and X-ray and, where needed, carry out first treatment the same day to relieve it; we share the options for a lasting solution in writing. For evening and weekend options, see emergency toothache.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: What is the most effective painkiller for toothache?
faq.a: Because toothache is usually linked to inflammation, anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen work better for many people. Paracetamol is usually more suitable for people with stomach or kidney problems, those on blood thinners and pregnant women. Choose with your pharmacist or doctor.

faq.q: Can paracetamol and ibuprofen be taken together?
faq.a: Studies have shown that taking the two together works well for dental pain. Dose and suitability vary from person to person, so ask your pharmacist or doctor before combining them.

faq.q: Does aspirin on the tooth stop the pain?
faq.a: No. Placed on the tooth or gum, aspirin doesn't relieve pain and causes a chemical burn and sore in the tissue.

faq.q: Do antibiotics cure toothache?
faq.a: Antibiotics are not painkillers. A dentist may prescribe them in specific situations such as spreading infection and swelling; inflammation inside the tooth is treated with dental treatment such as a root canal or extraction.

faq.q: How many days can I take painkillers?
faq.a: Painkillers are for the short time until treatment. If you need them for more than 2–3 days, the cause needs treating; long-term use raises the risk of side effects and hides the problem.

title: What is dry socket (alveolar osteitis)? Severe pain after an extraction, symptoms and treatment
desc: Throbbing pain that gets worse 2–4 days after an extraction can be a sign of dry socket. How to recognise it, how long it lasts, how it's treated and when you can drink hot tea after an extraction.
seoTitle: What is dry socket (alveolar osteitis)? | Dent32
seoDesc: Throbbing pain that worsens 2–4 days after an extraction can be dry socket. How to recognise it, how long it lasts and how it's treated.
lead: Dry socket (alveolar osteitis) happens when the blood clot that should form in the socket after an extraction breaks down or never forms, leaving the bone exposed. Its most typical sign is throbbing pain that increases instead of easing 2–4 days after the extraction and radiates to the ear and temple. It is not an infection; once the dentist cleans the socket and places a soothing dressing, the pain usually eases quickly. This article explains how to tell dry socket from normal post-extraction pain and how to prevent it.

sections.h: How do you recognise dry socket?
sections.html:
Normal healingDry socket
How the pain progressesWorst on days 1–2, then easesStarts or clearly worsens on days 2–4
What the pain is likeMild to moderate, relieved by painkillersSevere, throbbing, spreading to the ear and temple; painkillers don't fully help
How the socket looksDark red clot, then whitish healing tissueEmpty-looking, or greyish-white bone
OtherMild swellingBad taste and smell in the mouth
In short

Pain that increases instead of easing 2–4 days after an extraction, radiates to the ear and isn't relieved by painkillers is the most typical sign of dry socket. Call your dentist; treatment is quick and brings relief.

sections.h: Why does it happen and who gets it more often?
sections.html:
It occurs after a small proportion of routine extractions and more often after surgical removal of lower wisdom teeth. The main risk factors are:

  • smoking and shisha: sucking dislodges the clot and blood flow is reduced. See smoking and your teeth;
  • a difficult or long extraction, especially of lower wisdom teeth. See wisdom tooth extraction;
  • frequent rinsing, spitting or using a straw in the first 24 hours;
  • taking the contraceptive pill, and having had dry socket before;
  • existing infection at the extraction site and poor oral hygiene.

1. The dentist gently rinses the socket and removes any food debris.
  2. A soothing dressing is placed in the socket; the pain usually eases noticeably within hours.
  3. If needed, the dressing is changed every 1–3 days and a suitable painkiller is advised.
  4. Because dry socket is not an infection, antibiotics are usually not needed; fever, increasing swelling or pus are assessed separately.

With treatment the pain settles within a few days, while the socket can take 7–10 days to close fully. For choosing a painkiller, see which painkiller works for toothache?

sections.h: Preventing dry socket in the first days
sections.html:
• Don't rinse, spit or use a straw for the first 24 hours.
  • Don't smoke or use shisha for at least 48–72 hours; ideally stop for the first week.
  • Have hot drinks lukewarm on the first day; from the second day you can drink tea and coffee at a normal temperature.
  • Choose soft, lukewarm food in the first days and don't chew on the extraction side.
  • After 24 hours, rinse very gently with warm salt water after meals; keep brushing your teeth but avoid the extraction site.
  • Put off strenuous exercise for 1–2 days.

For general care and eating after an extraction, read after a tooth extraction.

With dry socket there is usually no marked facial swelling or fever; the pain comes from the exposed bone in the socket. Swelling that increases days after the extraction, fever, pus or difficulty swallowing suggest infection and should be checked the same day. For gum inflammation around wisdom teeth, see pericoronitis.

At Dent32 we give patients written aftercare instructions for the first days after an extraction, and see them the same day if the pain doesn't follow the expected course. If your extraction was done elsewhere, you can still come to us for an examination and dressing if you suspect dry socket. For the process, see tooth extraction in Beylikdüzü.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How long does dry socket last?
faq.a: Untreated, the pain can last 7–10 days or sometimes longer. Once the dentist cleans the socket and places a dressing, the pain usually eases markedly within hours or a few days.

faq.q: Does dry socket heal on its own?
faq.a: The socket does eventually heal by itself, but the pain can be severe in the meantime. A dressing speeds up healing and relieves the pain quickly, so it's worth seeing a dentist.

faq.q: When can I drink hot tea after an extraction?
faq.a: Having hot drinks lukewarm on the first day helps protect the clot. From the second day you can drink tea and coffee at a normal temperature; avoid straws in the first days.

faq.q: How can I avoid dry socket?
faq.a: Avoid rinsing, spitting and straws for the first 24 hours; don't smoke for at least 48–72 hours; eat soft, lukewarm food and don't chew on the extraction side.

faq.q: Do I need antibiotics for dry socket?
faq.a: Dry socket is not an infection; it's treated by cleaning the socket and placing a dressing. If there are signs of infection such as fever, increasing swelling or pus, your dentist will assess whether antibiotics are needed.

title: Why do children grind their teeth? When does night-time grinding need treatment?
desc: Does your child grind their teeth at night? The causes of teeth grinding in children, the link with snoring and sleep apnoea, whether it damages teeth, and when to see a dentist or ENT doctor.
seoTitle: Why do children grind their teeth? | Dent32
seoDesc: Does your child grind their teeth at night? Causes, the link with snoring and sleep apnoea, effects on teeth and when to see a dentist.
lead: Teeth grinding at night (bruxism) is common in children and usually eases by itself as they grow. The main causes are brief awakenings during sleep, stress, the period when adult teeth come through and, in particular, breathing problems such as snoring or enlarged adenoids. If there is marked tooth wear, jaw or headache in the morning, snoring or mouth breathing, it should be assessed. This article answers the questions parents ask most.

sections.h: Is teeth grinding normal in children?
sections.html:
Teeth grinding is very common in preschool and school-age children; studies report it in roughly 15–40% of children. Because baby teeth are soft, mild wear is common at this age and usually causes no problems. Grinding generally decreases once baby teeth have been replaced by adult teeth and in adolescence.

In short

Night-time teeth grinding in children is usually temporary and eases with growth. If there is snoring, mouth breathing, morning headache or jaw pain, or marked tooth wear, see a dentist and, if needed, an ear, nose and throat (ENT) doctor.

sections.h: Causes of teeth grinding in children
sections.html:
• Brief awakenings during sleep: grinding often happens as sleep becomes lighter.
  • Breathing problems: enlarged adenoids or tonsils, allergic nasal congestion, snoring and sleep apnoea often go together with grinding.
  • Stress and anxiety: it can coincide with changes such as starting school, moving house or a new sibling.
  • Changing teeth: as new teeth alter the bite, children may grind as if settling their teeth. See when do baby teeth fall out?
  • ADHD and some medicines: grinding has been reported more often in these situations.
  • Caffeine and screens in the evening: cola, tea and late screen time disturb sleep quality.

In Turkey, grinding is popularly linked to intestinal worms; scientific evidence for this is weak. If you suspect worms (for example an itchy bottom), see your paediatrician; grinding on its own is not enough to suggest it.

sections.h: When should you see a dentist or ENT doctor?
sections.html:
• if teeth are noticeably flattened, chipped or sensitive;
  • if your child complains of jaw, face or headache in the morning;
  • if there is snoring, pauses in breathing during sleep, mouth breathing, night sweats or waking up tired (an ENT assessment is advisable);
  • if grinding continues during the day or adult teeth have started to wear;
  • if there is clicking, locking or pain when opening the jaw. See jaw joint pain

sections.h: How is teeth grinding treated in children?
sections.html:
For most children, treatment means finding the cause and monitoring:

  • a regular bedtime, a calm routine and switching screens off at least an hour before bed;
  • cutting down on cola, tea, energy drinks and chocolate in the evening;
  • an ENT examination if there is snoring or mouth breathing; grinding may ease once enlarged adenoids are treated;
  • talking about sources of stress and, if needed, child mental health support;
  • monitoring wear at six-monthly dental check-ups.

While the jaw is still growing, a night guard is usually not the first option for baby teeth. If adult teeth show marked wear, the dentist may suggest a soft guard that doesn't restrict growth. We cover clenching and night guards in adults in teeth clenching and night guards.

Mild grinding usually leaves no lasting harm on baby teeth, which will be replaced anyway. Prolonged, heavy grinding can wear enamel, cause sensitivity and chipping, and wear on adult teeth can't be reversed. Wear from grinding shouldn't be confused with erosion from acidic drinks; when both are present, wear speeds up. See dental erosion.

At Dent32 we record tooth wear with photographs during children's check-ups and compare them at follow-up visits; if there are signs suggesting a breathing problem, we refer the family for an ENT assessment. For a child's first visit, see children's dentist in Beylikdüzü.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Does teeth grinding in children go away on its own?
faq.a: In most children grinding decreases with growth, especially after baby teeth have been replaced. If there is snoring, pain or marked wear, it should be assessed.

faq.q: Is teeth grinding in children caused by worms?
faq.a: It's a common belief, but the scientific evidence is weak. The most common causes are brief awakenings during sleep, breathing problems, stress and the period of changing teeth.

faq.q: Should a child who grinds wear a night guard?
faq.a: During the baby-teeth years a night guard is usually not the first option. If adult teeth show marked wear, the dentist may suggest a soft guard suited to growth.

faq.q: Is there a link between grinding and snoring?
faq.a: Yes. Snoring, mouth breathing and sleep apnoea often occur together with grinding. If these signs are present, an ENT examination is advisable.

title: Jaw joint pain and a clicking jaw: causes, jaw locking and treatment
desc: Does your jaw click when you open your mouth, or does it hurt just in front of your ear? Symptoms and causes of jaw joint disorders, what to do if your jaw locks, and treatment options.
seoTitle: Jaw joint pain and a clicking jaw | Dent32
seoDesc: Does your jaw click, or does it hurt in front of your ear? Symptoms and causes of jaw joint disorders, what to do if it locks, and treatment.
lead: Jaw joint (temporomandibular joint, TMJ) disorders show up as pain just in front of the ear, clicking or grating when opening the mouth, tired jaw muscles when chewing and sometimes a locked jaw. The most common causes are clenching and grinding, muscle tension and a displaced disc inside the joint. A click without pain or limited opening often needs no treatment. Most symptoms improve with a soft diet, changing habits and, if needed, a night guard.

sections.html:
• pain just in front of the ear, at the temple or in the cheek, worse when chewing;
  • clicking, popping or grating when opening and closing the mouth;
  • not being able to open fully, or the jaw shifting to one side as it opens;
  • a locked jaw: the mouth won't open, or stays open and won't close;
  • a tired jaw in the morning and headaches at the temples;
  • a feeling of fullness or ringing in the ear (when an ear examination is normal).

Pain in front of the ear can also be confused with toothache. See can toothache cause ear pain?

In short

A clicking jaw on its own, without pain or limited opening, often needs no treatment. If there is pain, locking or difficulty opening your mouth, see a dentist.

sections.h: What causes jaw pain and clicking?
sections.html:
• Clenching and grinding: often at night and without realising; it tires the chewing muscles. See teeth clenching and night guards.
  • Muscle tension and stress: pressing the teeth together during the day is a common cause.
  • A displaced joint disc: the click is heard as the disc slips back into place when the mouth opens.
  • Straining habits: chewing gum for long periods, biting nails or pens, lying with your chin propped on your hand.
  • A blow or keeping the mouth open for long: an accident, sports injury or a long dental appointment can cause temporary strain.
  • Joint inflammation and wear: seen with rheumatic conditions and in older age.

sections.h: What to do if your jaw locks
sections.html: There are two kinds of locking. If the mouth won't open (closed lock), don't force it; with a warm compress, soft food and a painkiller the muscles relax and opening usually improves, but still see a dentist. If the mouth stays open and won't close (dislocation), don't try to force it shut; see a dentist or go to A&E the same day.

sections.h: What you can do at home
sections.html:
• Eat soft food for a few days; avoid hard, sticky food and large mouthfuls.
  • Stop chewing gum; support your jaw gently with your hand when you yawn.
  • Check during the day that your teeth aren't touching: lips together, teeth slightly apart, tongue on the roof of the mouth.
  • Use a cold compress for new pain, or a warm one for tired muscles, for 10–15 minutes.
  • A short course of painkillers can help; see which painkiller works for toothache?
  • Try not to sleep on your front or with your jaw resting on your hand.

sections.h: How are jaw joint disorders treated?
sections.html:
Most patients improve without surgery:

  • A night guard (stabilisation splint): a hard guard made from an impression spreads the clenching force and relaxes the muscles.
  • Physiotherapy and exercises: exercises that guide jaw movement, and muscle massage.
  • Medication: short courses of anti-inflammatories or muscle relaxants, on medical advice.
  • Bite and dental treatment: planned dental treatment if missing teeth or a faulty bite contribute.
  • Advanced cases: assessment by a jaw surgeon for persistent locking or joint damage.

We describe how we treat clenching and jaw joint problems in Beylikdüzü in teeth clenching and jaw joint.

At Dent32 we assess joint sounds, how wide you can open, the chewing muscles and tooth wear together, and request imaging if needed. If a night guard is needed, we make it from an impression and adjust it at follow-up visits.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Is a clicking jaw dangerous?
faq.a: Without pain or limited opening, a clicking jaw is usually harmless and doesn't need treatment. If pain, locking or reduced opening come with it, an examination is advisable.

faq.q: Does jaw joint pain go away on its own?
faq.a: For many people it settles within a few weeks with soft food, stopping gum and noticing and reducing clenching. If the pain persists, options such as a night guard and physiotherapy are considered.

faq.q: Can jaw joint problems cause ear pain?
faq.a: Yes. The jaw joint sits just in front of the ear, so pain can be felt in the ear, along with fullness and ringing. If an ear examination is normal, the jaw joint should be assessed.

faq.q: Will a locked jaw unlock?
faq.a: Most cases where the mouth won't open improve as the muscles relax. If the mouth stays open and won't close, don't force it; see a dentist or go to A&E the same day.

title: What causes a metallic or bitter taste in the mouth? Dental, medication and health causes
desc: A metallic or bitter taste in your mouth? Causes such as gum inflammation, medicines, pregnancy, sinusitis, reflux and metal fillings, and when to see a dentist or a doctor.
seoTitle: What causes a metallic or bitter taste in the mouth? | Dent32
seoDesc: A metallic or bitter taste in your mouth? Causes such as gum inflammation, medicines, pregnancy, sinusitis and reflux, and who to see.
lead: A metallic or bitter taste in the mouth usually has a temporary, harmless cause: bleeding from gum inflammation, a medicine you are taking, early pregnancy, sinusitis or reflux are the most common. A new metal filling or different metals touching in the mouth can also cause a short-lived metallic taste. If the change lasts more than two weeks or comes with other symptoms, the cause should be investigated. This article covers the possible causes and whom to see when.

sections.h: Causes in the mouth and teeth
sections.html:
• Gum inflammation and bleeding: gums that bleed when you brush, or on their own, leave a metallic taste like blood. See how to treat gum inflammation.
  • Tooth or gum infection: an abscess or fistula can cause a bitter, unpleasant taste. See a pimple on the gum.
  • Poor mouth and tongue hygiene: a coating on the tongue changes how things taste. See white tongue.
  • Dry mouth: with less saliva, tastes seem sharper and less pleasant. See causes of dry mouth.
  • Metal fillings and crowns: a new amalgam filling, or different metals touching in the mouth, can cause a brief metallic taste and a slight electric-shock feeling. See should amalgam fillings be removed?

Medicines are one of the most common causes of taste changes. Some antibiotics (especially metronidazole and clarithromycin), some blood pressure medicines, diabetes medicines, lithium, chemotherapy drugs, and iron, zinc and multivitamin supplements can cause a metallic or bitter taste. The taste usually returns to normal when the course ends.

In short

A metallic or bitter taste is usually down to bleeding gums, a medicine, pregnancy, sinusitis or reflux. Don't stop a medicine on your own; if the change lasts more than two weeks, see your dentist and GP.

Don't stop a medicine that changes your taste without advice; your doctor may adjust the dose or switch it. We cover mouth care during chemotherapy in dental care during chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

• Pregnancy: a metallic taste is common, especially in the first three months, and usually passes by itself. See dental treatment in pregnancy.
  • Sinusitis, colds and flu: a blocked nose and post-nasal drip change taste and smell. See can sinusitis cause toothache?
  • Reflux: stomach contents coming up into the oesophagus cause a bitter or sour taste, especially in the morning.
  • Taste changes after viral infections: after some infections, taste and smell can seem different for weeks.
  • Pine nuts: some people get a bitter, metallic taste starting 1–3 days after eating pine nuts and lasting from a few days to two weeks; it's harmless.
  • Less common causes: vitamin B12 or zinc deficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, kidney or liver disease and, rarely, chemical exposure.

sections.h: How to get rid of a metallic taste
sections.html:
• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, use floss and clean your tongue.
  • Drink plenty of water; sugar-free gum can ease the taste by increasing saliva.
  • If you've started a new medicine or supplement, talk to your doctor.
  • If you have reflux symptoms, avoid heavy meals late in the evening and see your GP.
  • If metal cutlery makes it worse, use plastic or wooden cutlery for a while.

sections.h: When to see a dentist and when to see a doctor
sections.html: If you also have bleeding gums, toothache, swelling in the mouth or bad breath, see a dentist first. If the change lasts more than two weeks, or comes with weight loss, tiredness, passing urine often, or yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, see your GP. We cover the causes of bad breath separately in bad breath.

At Dent32, when patients come in with a change in taste we check gum health, fillings and crowns, sources of infection and dry mouth; if there is no dental cause, we refer you to your GP.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: What causes a metallic taste in the mouth?
faq.a: The most common causes are bleeding gums, some medicines and supplements, early pregnancy, sinusitis or upper respiratory infections, and new metal fillings. If it lasts more than two weeks, the cause should be investigated.

faq.q: What causes a bitter taste in the mouth?
faq.a: Reflux, some medicines, dry mouth, tooth or gum infection and eating pine nuts are common causes of a bitter taste.

faq.q: Which illness can a metallic taste be a sign of?
faq.a: Usually it isn't a sign of serious illness. But a long-lasting change in taste can be linked to vitamin B12 or zinc deficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, or kidney or liver disease, so see your GP if it lasts more than two weeks.

faq.q: Is a metallic taste normal in pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes, it's common, especially in the first three months, and usually passes on its own. Gum bleeding can also increase in pregnancy, so take extra care with oral hygiene.

title: How to floss your teeth: step-by-step technique, bleeding and common mistakes
desc: How do you floss, and should you floss before or after brushing? Step-by-step technique, bleeding gums when flossing, common mistakes and alternatives such as interdental brushes and water flossers.
seoTitle: How to floss your teeth: step-by-step technique | Dent32
seoDesc: How do you floss, and before or after brushing? Step-by-step technique, bleeding gums, common mistakes and interdental brushes or water flossers.
lead: Floss cleans plaque from between the teeth where a toothbrush can't reach, and daily use is recommended. With the right technique, the floss is eased between the teeth with a gentle sawing motion, wrapped around the tooth in a C shape and wiped upwards from just below the gum line. A little bleeding is common at first and usually eases within a week or two of regular flossing. This article covers the technique step by step, common mistakes and alternatives to floss.

sections.h: How to floss, step by step
sections.html:
1. Cut about 40–45 cm of floss and wind the ends around the middle fingers of both hands.
  2. Hold the floss between your thumbs and index fingers, leaving 2–3 cm between them.
  3. Ease the floss between the teeth with small back-and-forth sawing movements; don't snap it onto the gum.
  4. Wrap the floss around one tooth in a C shape, slide it gently just below the gum line and wipe up the side of the tooth a few times.
  5. Do the same for the neighbouring tooth in the same gap.
  6. Use a clean section of floss for each gap, and don't forget the back surfaces of the last teeth.
In short

Floss once a day, wrapping it around each tooth in a C shape and wiping upwards from just below the gum line. A little bleeding at first can be normal; if it lasts more than two weeks, see your dentist.

sections.h: Should you floss before or after brushing?
sections.html: What matters most is flossing every day. That said, flossing before brushing clears plaque from the gaps and may help the fluoride from your toothpaste reach between the teeth. The most convenient time is usually your evening clean before bed. For brushing technique, see how to brush your teeth properly.

sections.h: Is it normal for gums to bleed when flossing?
sections.html: A little bleeding is common when you start flossing and is usually a sign of existing gum inflammation. If you keep flossing gently rather than stopping, bleeding usually decreases within 1–2 weeks. Bleeding that lasts more than two weeks, is heavy or happens on its own suggests gum disease and needs an examination. See bleeding and receding gums.

• Snapping the floss down between the teeth; it cuts and bleeds the gum.
  • Just passing it through the gap and pulling it out; it needs to be wrapped around and wiped along the tooth.
  • Using the same section of floss for every gap.
  • Only cleaning the front teeth; decay and gum problems are most common at the back.
  • Pulling the floss upwards around a temporary tooth or crown; in that case slide it out sideways.
  • Giving up because of some bleeding.

sections.h: What can you use instead of floss?
sections.html:
ToolWho is it for?
Waxed floss or tapePeople with tight contacts between teeth; it slides more easily
Floss picksPeople with limited dexterity, children, anyone wanting convenience
Interdental brushesWider gaps, receding gums, around bridges and implants
Floss threaders or super flossUnder bridges and with fixed braces
Water flosserExtra cleaning with braces, bridges and implants; it doesn't fully replace floss

For choosing an electric toothbrush or water flosser, see electric toothbrushes and water flossers; if food often gets stuck between your teeth, see food stuck between teeth. Tips for people with braces are in living with braces.

You can start cleaning between a child's teeth once two teeth touch each other. For young children, an adult should do it; floss picks are a practical start. Decay starting between the teeth is hard to see, so regular check-ups matter. See decay between teeth.

sections.h: Gum and mouth care in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At Dent32, after a scale and polish, we try out the right floss or interdental brush size for your gaps together in front of a mirror. For more on cleaning, see scale and polish.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How often should I floss?
faq.a: Once a day, ideally in the evening before bed, is enough. What matters is flossing every day with the right technique.

faq.q: Should I floss before brushing?
faq.a: Either order is acceptable, but flossing before brushing may help fluoride reach between the teeth.

faq.q: Why do my gums bleed when I floss?
faq.a: Bleeding is usually a sign of existing gum inflammation. With gentle, continued flossing it usually eases within 1–2 weeks; if it lasts more than two weeks, get it checked.

faq.q: Does flossing create gaps between teeth?
faq.a: Flossing with the right technique doesn't create gaps. A feeling of more space can come from swelling going down as inflammation settles, or from existing gum recession.

faq.q: Can a water flosser replace floss?
faq.a: A water flosser is useful extra cleaning, especially with braces, bridges and implants, but it doesn't fully replace floss for wiping away plaque stuck to the tooth surface.

title: Is fluoride harmful? Fluoride and fluoride-free toothpaste, the right amount and fluorosis
desc: Is fluoride in toothpaste harmful, and is fluoride-free toothpaste a good idea? How fluoride protects teeth, the right amount by age, fluorosis, the drinking water debate and hydroxyapatite.
seoTitle: Is fluoride harmful? Fluoride and fluoride-free toothpaste | Dent32
seoDesc: Is fluoride in toothpaste harmful, and is fluoride-free a good idea? How fluoride protects teeth, the right amount by age and fluorosis.
lead: Used in the recommended amount, the fluoride in toothpaste is safe and is the protection against decay with the strongest evidence. Fluoride strengthens enamel, helps early decay reverse and reduces acid production by bacteria. Concerns about harm mostly relate to high fluoride levels in drinking water, or to children taking in too much fluoride over long periods. This article explains the difference between fluoride and fluoride-free toothpaste and the right amount for each age.

sections.html:
• It makes enamel more resistant to acid.
  • It helps early decay on the enamel surface (a chalky white spot) to re-harden.
  • It reduces acid production by bacteria in plaque.

This is why the World Health Organization and dental organisations recommend fluoride toothpaste for children and adults. We explain how decay starts in signs and stages of tooth decay.

In short

Used in the recommended amount, fluoride toothpaste is safe and is the protection against decay with the strongest evidence. Adults should use a pea-sized amount of 1350–1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste, spit after brushing and not rinse with water.

AgeAmount of toothpasteFluoride level
First tooth to age 3A thin smear the size of a grain of riceAt least 1000 ppm
Ages 3–6Pea-sized1000–1500 ppm
Age 6 and over, adultsPea-sized1350–1500 ppm

Spit the toothpaste out after brushing but don't rinse with water, so the fluoride stays on the teeth longer. An adult should help children brush until about age 7–8 and make sure they don't swallow the toothpaste. We cover fluoride varnish and fissure sealants applied by the dentist in fluoride and fissure sealants for children.

• Fluorosis: if too much fluoride is taken in over a long period while teeth are forming (before about age 8), white lines and spots can appear on the teeth. Most cases are mild and purely cosmetic. The most common cause is young children swallowing toothpaste. We cover treating white spots in white spots on teeth.
  • Swallowing a lot at once: a small child swallowing most of a tube can cause nausea and vomiting. Keep toothpaste out of children's reach; if it happens, call the poison information line (114 in Turkey) or seek medical advice.
  • High fluoride in drinking water: in Turkey, fluoride isn't added to tap water, but some regions have naturally high-fluoride water. Fluorosis is more common in children in these areas.

Debates about fluoride's effects on the thyroid, brain development and bones are mostly based on studies of high fluoride levels in drinking water. Using toothpaste as recommended doesn't create exposure comparable to those levels.

Fluoride-free toothpastes clean and freshen the mouth but don't give the protection against decay that fluoride does. True allergy or sensitivity to fluoride is extremely rare. If you want to use a fluoride-free toothpaste, discuss your decay risk with your dentist.

  • Hydroxyapatite toothpastes: some studies show promising results in re-hardening early decay, but the evidence is not as strong as for fluoride.
  • Charcoal and “natural” toothpastes: most contain no fluoride and can be quite abrasive. See whitening and charcoal toothpaste.
  • Sensitivity and erosion: fluoride and sensitivity toothpastes help protect enamel. See tooth sensitivity and dental erosion.

sections.h: Who is advised to use more fluoride?
sections.html: For people at high risk of decay, those wearing braces, people with dry mouth and those with exposed root surfaces from gum recession, a dentist may suggest a high-fluoride prescription toothpaste, a fluoride mouthwash or fluoride varnish in the clinic. We explain how to use mouthwash correctly in can you use mouthwash every day?

At Dent32 we look at your decay history, eating habits and saliva together during the examination and suggest the toothpaste and fluoride support that suits you. For children's first visits, see a child's first dental visit.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Is the fluoride in toothpaste harmful?
faq.a: No, it's safe when used in the recommended amount. Adults are advised to use a pea-sized amount of 1350–1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste; young children use less and shouldn't swallow it.

faq.q: Is it a good idea to use fluoride-free toothpaste?
faq.a: Fluoride-free toothpastes don't give the protection against decay that fluoride does. If you want to use one, discuss your decay risk with your dentist.

faq.q: Can children use fluoride toothpaste?
faq.a: Yes. A rice-grain smear from the first tooth, and a pea-sized amount from age 3, is recommended. An adult should help with brushing and make sure the toothpaste isn't swallowed.

faq.q: What is fluorosis?
faq.a: White lines and spots on the teeth caused by taking in too much fluoride over a long period while teeth are forming. Most cases are mild and cosmetic; the most common cause is young children swallowing toothpaste.

faq.q: Should I rinse after brushing?
faq.a: Just spit the toothpaste out; not rinsing with water keeps fluoride on the teeth for longer.

title: What is a dead tooth? Why does a tooth turn dark, and what happens when the nerve dies?
desc: Has a tooth turned grey or dark? Signs of a dead tooth, why the nerve dies, what happens if it isn't treated, root canal treatment and options to restore the tooth's colour.
seoTitle: What is a dead tooth? Why a tooth turns dark | Dent32
seoDesc: Has a tooth turned grey or dark? Signs of a dead tooth, why the nerve dies, what happens if untreated, and ways to restore its colour.
lead: A dead tooth is one in which the tissue holding the nerve and blood vessels (the pulp) has lost its vitality. The most common causes are deep decay and a blow to the tooth, which can lead to this months or even years later. Typical signs are the tooth turning grey or dark, severe pain that suddenly stops, and a pimple-like bump on the gum. A dead tooth can usually be kept with root canal treatment rather than extracted, and its colour can be improved with internal bleaching or a crown.

sections.html:
• Colour change: the tooth turns grey, brown or blackish as blood products from the pulp pass into the inner tooth tissue.
  • How the pain progresses: first severe, throbbing pain, which may then suddenly stop. This can mean the nerve has died, not that it has healed.
  • Tenderness when biting: once infection reaches the root tip, pressing on the tooth hurts.
  • A bump on the gum: infection at the root tip can cause a draining pimple on the gum. See a pimple on the gum.
  • Bad taste and swelling: as infection spreads there may be a bad taste and swelling of the gum or face. See dental abscess.

Sometimes a dead tooth causes no symptoms at all and is spotted on a routine X-ray as inflammation at the root tip.

In short

A tooth that turns grey or dark, no longer reacts to cold, or whose severe pain suddenly stops may have died. A dead tooth can usually be kept with root canal treatment; left untreated it can lead to an abscess and bone loss.

• Deep decay: when bacteria reach the pulp, inflammation develops first, then loss of vitality. See stages of tooth decay.
  • A blow: a fall, sports injury or knock to the face can damage the tooth's blood vessels even without a fracture. See broken tooth.
  • Repeated large fillings and cracks: many procedures on the same tooth, and cracks, weaken the pulp. See cracked tooth syndrome.
  • Advanced gum disease: rarely, infection reaches the pulp through the root tip.

sections.h: How is a dead tooth diagnosed?
sections.html: The dentist checks the tooth's vitality with a cold test and, if needed, an electric pulp test, and checks the root tip for tenderness by tapping and pressing. An X-ray shows whether there is inflammation or a cyst at the root tip. A change in colour doesn't always mean a dead tooth; fillings, surface stains or old amalgam can also change colour. See black spots on teeth.

sections.h: How is a dead tooth treated?
sections.html:
1. Root canal treatment: the dead tissue inside the tooth is removed and the canals are shaped and filled. The tooth stays in the mouth. See root canal treatment.
  2. Restoring the colour: after root canal treatment, bleaching from inside the tooth (internal bleaching) can lighten it considerably. If the colour doesn't improve or the tooth is weak, veneers or crowns are considered. See laminate veneers and types of dental crowns.
  3. Teeth that can’t be saved: with a root fracture or advanced bone loss, the tooth is extracted and an implant or bridge is planned. See extraction or root canal?

sections.h: What happens if a dead tooth isn't treated?
sections.html: Even if the pain stops, infection in a dead tooth can progress at the root tip and cause an abscess, a cyst and loss of the surrounding bone. Rarely, infection can spread to the tissues of the face and neck. That's why a tooth that has changed colour or had a knock should be checked. We cover treating cysts at the root tip in tooth cysts and apicoectomy.

In children, a baby tooth that has had a knock can turn pink or grey temporarily and sometimes returns to normal by itself. If there is no swelling, gum bump or pain, the dentist may suggest monitoring. For more, see dental trauma in children.

sections.h: Examining a discoloured tooth in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
At Dent32 we find the cause of a discoloured tooth with vitality tests and X-rays, and set out options for keeping the tooth in writing. We describe the root canal process in Beylikdüzü in root canal treatment in Beylikdüzü.

Dent32 is at Barış Mah., Ginza Lavinya, E-5 Yanyolu No:30 D:179, 34520 Beylikdüzü, Istanbul and is open seven days a week. To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Should a dead tooth be pulled out?
faq.a: Usually not. A dead tooth can be cleaned and kept with root canal treatment. Extraction is needed when it can't be saved, for example with a root fracture or advanced bone loss.

faq.q: Will a dead tooth's colour come back?
faq.a: Internal bleaching after root canal treatment can lighten the colour considerably. If it doesn't lighten enough, veneers or crowns are considered.

faq.q: Does a dying nerve hurt?
faq.a: There is usually severe pain while the nerve is dying, which may then stop. As infection reaches the root tip, there may be pain on biting, swelling and a bump on the gum.

faq.q: Can a tooth die years after a knock?
faq.a: Yes. When a blow damages the tooth's blood vessels, loss of vitality can appear months or even years later. Teeth that have had a knock are best monitored with check-ups for a while.

faq.q: Can a dead tooth heal by itself?
faq.a: No. Dead pulp tissue doesn't heal on its own; left untreated, infection can progress at the root tip.

title: Whitening teeth at home: is baking soda, lemon, vinegar or hydrogen peroxide harmful?
desc: Does baking soda whiten teeth, and is it harmful? Can lemon or vinegar whiten teeth? How home methods affect enamel, safe options, and home whitening supervised by a dentist.
seoTitle: Whitening teeth at home: is baking soda harmful? | Dent32
seoDesc: Does baking soda, lemon or vinegar whiten teeth, and are they harmful? How home methods affect enamel and safe, dentist-supervised options.
lead: Most home whitening methods don't lighten the tooth's own colour; at best they reduce surface stains from tea, coffee and smoking. Acidic methods such as lemon, vinegar and strawberries wear away enamel and can make teeth look more yellow over time. Baking soda in toothpaste is low in abrasiveness and helps with surface stains, but using it neat, often and hard isn't recommended. The safe way to lighten tooth colour is home or in-clinic whitening supervised by a dentist.

sections.html:
MethodDoes it work?Risk
Baking soda (baking soda toothpaste)Can reduce surface stainsAbrasion if used neat and often; contains no fluoride
Lemon, vinegar, apple cider vinegarNoAcid wears enamel and causes sensitivity; the damage is permanent
Lemon + baking sodaNoAcid and abrasive together; one of the most harmful combinations
Hydrogen peroxide from the chemistLimited when used without supervisionGum irritation and burns, sensitivity
Activated charcoalLimited, for surface stainsCan be abrasive; contains no fluoride
Strawberries, turmeric, coconut oilNo evidenceThe acid in strawberries can soften enamel
In short

Home methods don't lighten the tooth's own colour, and acids such as lemon and vinegar wear enamel away permanently. Baking soda is only suitable in toothpaste and for surface stains. To lighten tooth colour safely, whitening needs to be supervised by a dentist.

sections.h: Is whitening with baking soda harmful?
sections.html:
Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is a mild abrasive. Toothpastes containing it are low in abrasiveness and have been shown to reduce surface stains. The problem is pouring neat baking soda onto a brush and scrubbing hard every day: this can increase wear and sensitivity, especially in people with receding gums and exposed roots. Neat baking soda also contains no fluoride, so it can't replace toothpaste.

If you want to try baking soda, use it once or twice a week alongside your fluoride toothpaste, with a soft brush and without pressing hard. Never mix it with anything acidic (lemon, vinegar).

sections.h: Why do lemon and vinegar make teeth look more yellow?
sections.html: Enamel softens on contact with acid and is then worn away by brushing. As enamel thins, more of the yellowish dentine beneath shows through, so acidic methods can make teeth look more yellow over time. This wear can't be reversed and causes sensitivity. We explain the effects of acid and wear in dental erosion and enamel wear.

sections.h: Can you whiten teeth with hydrogen peroxide?
sections.html: The ingredient that actually lightens tooth colour is hydrogen peroxide or related compounds, which are also in professional whitening gels. But the concentration, the application time and protecting the gums all matter. Under cosmetics rules in the European Union and Turkey, oral products sold over the counter may contain no more than 0.1% hydrogen peroxide; higher concentrations are used after an examination and under a dentist's supervision. Holding chemist's hydrogen peroxide in your mouth or putting it on a toothbrush can irritate and burn the gums and make teeth sensitive.

sections.h: What you can safely do at home
sections.html:
• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste; whitening toothpastes can reduce surface stains. See whitening and charcoal toothpaste.
  • Rinse with water after tea, coffee and cola; drink through a straw where possible.
  • Stop or cut down smoking; it causes some of the most stubborn stains.
  • Have a scale and polish every six months; for many people teeth look noticeably lighter. See scale and polish.
  • Home whitening with custom trays made by a dentist and a low-concentration gel is the genuine whitening method that can be used safely at home.

We explain why teeth turn yellow in why do teeth turn yellow?, and professional whitening in the clinic and at home in teeth whitening.

sections.h: Why is an examination needed before whitening?
sections.html:
• Decay and exposed root surfaces can cause severe sensitivity during whitening; they're treated first.
  • Fillings, crowns and veneers don't change colour with whitening, so a colour mismatch can appear on front teeth.
  • Root-filled or darkened teeth may need a different method. See dead tooth.
  • Whitening is usually postponed during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
  • If you have sensitivity, it can be prepared for in advance. See tooth sensitivity.
