faq.q: Does baking soda whiten teeth?
faq.a: Baking soda doesn't lighten the tooth's own colour; it can reduce surface stains. Baking soda toothpastes are considered safe, but using neat baking soda often and hard can cause wear.

faq.q: Does lemon whiten teeth?
faq.a: No. The acid in lemon softens and wears enamel; as enamel thins, teeth can look more yellow and become sensitive. The damage can't be reversed.

faq.q: Can I rinse with hydrogen peroxide?
faq.a: Holding chemist's hydrogen peroxide in your mouth or putting it on a brush can irritate and burn the gums. Peroxide whitening should be done under a dentist's supervision with the right concentration and timing.

faq.q: Is there a safe way to whiten teeth at home?
faq.a: Yes: home whitening with custom trays made by a dentist and a suitable gel. Beyond that, whitening toothpaste, regular scale and polish and cutting down on staining habits help with surface stains.

faq.q: Is charcoal whitening harmful?
faq.a: Activated charcoal can reduce surface stains to a limited extent but can be abrasive, and most products contain no fluoride. Regular use isn't recommended.

title: Can you use mouthwash every day? Chlorhexidine, alcohol and fluoride mouthwash compared
desc: Can you use mouthwash every day, and should you use it straight after brushing? The difference between chlorhexidine, alcohol, alcohol-free and fluoride mouthwash, staining, and use in children.
seoTitle: Can you use mouthwash every day? | Dent32
seoDesc: Can you use mouthwash every day, and right after brushing? Chlorhexidine, alcohol, alcohol-free and fluoride rinses, staining and children.
lead: Mouthwash doesn't replace brushing and flossing; chosen well, it adds extra protection. Fluoride and alcohol-free mouthwashes can be used daily by most people. Chlorhexidine mouthwashes are strong antiseptics, usually used for a short period on a dentist's advice after gum treatment or surgery; with longer use they can stain teeth brown and change taste. Using mouthwash at a different time of day, rather than straight after brushing, is more useful.

sections.h: Types of mouthwash and what they do
sections.html:
TypeWhat it doesHow long?
FluorideExtra protection against decay; useful with braces, dry mouth or exposed rootsCan be used daily
ChlorhexidineStrong antiseptic; plaque control after gum treatment and surgeryOn a dentist's advice, usually 1–2 weeks
Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) and essential oilsHelps reduce plaque and gum inflammationProducts suitable for daily use are available
Alcohol-basedCan have an antiseptic effectCan cause dryness and burning; not ideal for a dry mouth
Salt waterSoothing after extractions, for ulcers and gum irritationShort term
In short

Fluoride and alcohol-free mouthwashes can be used daily by most people, while chlorhexidine is used on a dentist's advice and usually for 1–2 weeks. Mouthwash doesn't replace brushing or flossing.

Using mouthwash straight after brushing can wash away the fluoride from your toothpaste. It's more useful at a different time of day, for example after lunch. If you use chlorhexidine, wait at least 30 minutes after brushing, because some foaming agents in toothpaste can reduce its effect. Don't eat or drink for about 30 minutes after using mouthwash.

Yes. With longer use it can cause brown staining on the teeth and tongue, changes in taste and more tartar build-up. The stains can usually be removed with a scale and polish. Because of these side effects, chlorhexidine should be limited to the period your dentist advises. We cover other causes of dark stains in black spots on teeth.

Alcohol-based mouthwashes can cause burning and dryness; people with a dry mouth, mouth ulcers or who should avoid alcohol are better off with alcohol-free products. A link between alcohol mouthwashes and mouth cancer has been studied without a clear conclusion; if you're concerned, choose alcohol-free. See causes of dry mouth and, for ulcers, mouth ulcers.

Mouthwash can mask bad breath for a few hours but doesn't remove the cause. The most common sources are the coating on the tongue, debris between the teeth and gum disease. A lasting solution needs tongue cleaning, flossing and, if necessary, gum treatment. See bad breath causes and treatment and how to floss.

sections.h: Who should use mouthwash, and who needs to be careful?
sections.html:
• People with braces and those at high risk of decay: fluoride mouthwash helps. See living with braces and is fluoride harmful?
  • After gum treatment or surgery: the chlorhexidine mouthwash your dentist recommends, for the stated period.
  • After an extraction: no mouthwash or rinsing for the first 24 hours; after that, rinse very gently with warm salt water. See dry socket.
  • Children: usually not recommended under age 6 because of the risk of swallowing; older children need products made for children and adult supervision.
  • Pregnant women and people with long-term conditions: check with a doctor before long-term use.

At Dent32 we advise in writing whether you actually need a mouthwash based on your gum health and decay risk and, if so, which type and for how long. For gum inflammation, see how to treat gum inflammation.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Can you use mouthwash every day?
faq.a: Fluoride and alcohol-free mouthwashes can be used daily by most people. Chlorhexidine mouthwashes are used on a dentist's advice and usually for short periods such as 1–2 weeks.

faq.q: Should I use mouthwash before or after brushing?
faq.a: Using it straight after brushing can wash away fluoride from your toothpaste. It's more useful at a different time of day; with chlorhexidine, wait at least 30 minutes after brushing.

faq.q: Does mouthwash stain teeth?
faq.a: Long-term use of chlorhexidine mouthwash can cause brown stains. They can usually be removed with a scale and polish.

faq.q: Can mouthwash replace brushing?
faq.a: No. Mouthwash doesn't mechanically remove plaque stuck to the teeth; it adds protection on top of brushing and flossing.

faq.q: Can children use mouthwash?
faq.a: It's usually not recommended under age 6 because of the risk of swallowing. Older children can use products made for children under adult supervision.

title: How to tell a dental practice in Türkiye is properly licensed: 8 checks before your first visit in Beylikdüzü
desc: Choosing a dental polyclinic or clinic in Beylikdüzü? Eight things you can check yourself: licence and type of practice, the dentist's title, sterilisation, written plan, consent and invoice.
seoTitle: How to tell a dental practice in Türkiye is properly licensed | Dent32
seoDesc: Choosing a dental practice in Beylikdüzü? Eight things to check yourself: licence, type of practice, the dentist's title, sterilisation and invoice.
lead: In Türkiye, private dental surgeries, polyclinics and oral health centres open under a licence issued under Ministry of Health regulations and are inspected by the provincial health directorates. In a licensed practice it is clear which dentist treats you and under what title, how procedures are recorded and whom to contact if there is a problem. You can run the eight checks below before or during your first visit to a dental practice in Beylikdüzü or anywhere else.

sections.h: Surgery, polyclinic, centre: what the name on the sign tells you
sections.html:
Private dental practices are classified by type: a surgery (muayenehane) opened by a single dentist in their own name, a polyclinic where several dentists can work, a larger oral and dental health centre, and a hospital with beds. The official name often includes the type, for example “… Ağız ve Diş Sağlığı Polikliniği” (oral and dental health polyclinic). In everyday Turkish they are all called “diş kliniği” (dental clinic).

That's why searches for a dental clinic and a dental polyclinic in Beylikdüzü usually show the same places. We explain the differences in dental polyclinic, clinic or surgery.

sections.h: 8 checks before and during your first visit
sections.html:
1. Official name and address: Do the sign, website, Google listing and invoice show the same name and address? A mismatch isn't always a problem, but it's worth asking.
  2. Licence and responsible dentist: Polyclinics and centres have a responsible manager dentist (mesul müdür). You are entitled to ask about the type of practice and who is responsible.
  3. Name and title of the dentist treating you: Specialist titles may only be used by dentists who have completed specialist training. Phrases such as “implant expert” or “smile specialist” based on a course or certificate are not an official specialty.
  4. Examination and imaging: A plan should follow a clinical examination and, where needed, X-rays or a CT scan, and the findings should be shown to you. See dental X-rays and CT scans.
  5. Written plan: Options, number of visits and cost should be given in writing. See written treatment plan.
  6. Consent: Before any invasive procedure the risks and alternatives should be explained and your consent obtained. See consent forms and patient rights.
  7. Sterilisation: Instruments in sealed pouches and single-use items opened in front of you. See sterilisation in a dental clinic.
  8. Invoice and records: You should receive an invoice for every payment, and procedures should be recorded. You can ask for a copy of your X-rays.
In short

In a licensed dental polyclinic the practice name, responsible dentist, the treating dentist's title, the written plan, consent and invoice are all clear. Asking about them isn't distrust; it's your right as a patient.

sections.h: The way a practice promotes itself is a clue too
sections.html: Türkiye's health promotion regulation, in force since 12 November 2025, bans advertising by healthcare providers. Price, discount or campaign announcements, superiority claims such as “the best”, promotion through patients' thanks and certificate-based “specialist” titles all fall under it. Non-compliant promotion doesn't by itself mean poor treatment, but it says something about how carefully a practice follows the rules. Details: dental advertising rules in Türkiye.

sections.h: Where to go with a question or complaint
sections.html:
• The practice itself first: talking to the treating or responsible dentist resolves most problems.
  • For complaints about healthcare providers, the Istanbul Provincial Health Directorate and the Ministry of Health communication centre (SABİM, ALO 184).
  • For matters of professional ethics, the regional chamber of dentists.
  • For disputes about fees, the consumer arbitration committees.

faq.q: Is a dental clinic the same as a dental polyclinic?
faq.a: In everyday language, yes. Officially a polyclinic is a type of licensed oral and dental health practice where several dentists can work; “dental clinic” is a general term.

faq.q: What does “implant specialist” mean in Türkiye?
faq.a: There is no official dental specialty called implantology. The specialties are oral and maxillofacial surgery, oral and maxillofacial radiology, paediatric dentistry, endodontics, orthodontics, periodontology, prosthodontics and restorative dentistry. Implants can be placed by dentists trained to do so.

faq.q: Where can I find a dentist's title?
faq.a: Ask the practice and the dentist directly; the practice website and sign should show each dentist's name and title. If a specialist title is used, it's reasonable to ask in which specialty.

title: Dental consent forms and patient rights: what to know before you sign
desc: What is informed consent before dental treatment and what should the form include? Your rights to information, to refuse treatment, to your records and to a second opinion.
seoTitle: Dental consent forms and patient rights | Dent32
seoDesc: What is informed consent before dental treatment and what should the form include? Your rights to information, refusal, records and a second opinion.
lead: Before a procedure such as an implant, extraction, root canal treatment or orthodontics, your dentist explains what will be done, the possible risks and the alternatives, and then asks for your consent. An informed consent form isn't just a piece of paper to sign: it shows that you were informed and made the decision freely. This article covers what a consent form should contain, your rights as a patient and questions you can ask before signing.

sections.html:
Under Türkiye's Patient Rights Regulation, patients have the right to be told about their condition, what the proposed treatment involves, its benefits, possible risks and side effects, any alternatives, and what may happen without treatment. Consent given after this explanation is called informed consent.

Verbal consent is enough for a simple examination. For invasive procedures such as extractions, implants, gum surgery, root canal treatment and orthodontics, written consent is common and good practice.

sections.h: What should a consent form include?
sections.html:
• Diagnosis: what the problem is, in plain language.
  • Planned procedure: which tooth, what will be done and over how many visits.
  • Possible risks: for example bleeding and dry socket after extraction, nerve or sinus risks with implants, or rare events such as an instrument separating during root canal treatment.
  • Alternatives: other options, and the possible consequences of doing nothing.
  • Afterwards: expected discomfort, care and follow-up visits.
  • Names and date: the patient's and the treating dentist's names, signatures and the date.

The cost usually appears in a separate written treatment plan rather than the consent form. See written treatment plan.

RightWhat it means in practice
InformationLearning your diagnosis, options and risks in language you understand
Consent and refusalDeclining a proposed treatment or withdrawing consent you gave
Access to recordsAsking for a copy of your X-rays and treatment records
PrivacyYour health information is protected as special-category personal data
Choice and second opinionGetting another dentist's view; see second opinion
In short

A consent form protects you: you know in advance what will be done, why and with what risks. If something is unclear, ask before signing; you also have the right to withdraw consent later.

1. What happens if this isn't done, and can it wait?
  2. Is there a less invasive option?
  3. What are the most common and the most serious risks, and how likely are they?
  4. What will I feel in the first days, and when should I contact you?
  5. Who will carry out the procedure and the follow-ups?

For more, see 12 questions to ask your dentist.

sections.h: Consent for children and with family support
sections.html: For patients under 18, consent is given by a parent or guardian, and the child is told what will happen in words suited to their age. For older patients or anyone who finds decisions difficult, having a relative at the appointment makes it easier to take in the information together. See dental treatment in later life.

For clinic details, our dentists and the full list of treatments, visit Dent32, dental clinic in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: Can I change my mind after signing a consent form?
faq.a: Yes, you can withdraw consent. If stopping a procedure that has already started would harm your health, the dentist will explain this clearly and you'll decide together.

faq.q: Does a signed consent form release the dentist from all responsibility?
faq.a: No. The form shows that you were informed; the dentist is still obliged to carry out treatment in line with professional standards.

faq.q: Can I get my X-rays and records?
faq.a: Yes. You can ask for a copy of your treatment records and X-rays; taking them to another dentist can reduce the need for repeat imaging.

title: Sedation and general anaesthesia for dental treatment: who needs it, where and how?
desc: Can dental treatment be done asleep? The differences between local anaesthetic, sedation and general anaesthesia, who they suit, how to prepare and other ways to manage dental anxiety.
seoTitle: Sedation and general anaesthesia for dental treatment | Dent32
seoDesc: Can dental treatment be done asleep? Local anaesthetic, sedation and general anaesthesia compared, who they suit and how to prepare.
lead: Most dental treatment is done with local anaesthetic alone: only the area being treated is numbed and you stay fully awake. Sedation or general anaesthesia may be considered for severe dental fear, very extensive treatment, young children with many cavities or patients with special needs. Because these methods need an anaesthesiologist and suitable equipment, they aren't carried out at every dental practice; who they suit and where they can be done is decided after an examination.

sections.h: Local anaesthetic, sedation and general anaesthesia
sections.html:
MethodAwarenessWho gives it?Typical use
Local anaestheticFully awake; only the area is numbDentistFillings, root canals, extractions, implants, scale and polish
Light or moderate sedationCalm and drowsy; responds when spoken toAnaesthesia team; some light methods under suitable conditionsLong or surgical procedures in anxious patients
Deep sedation and general anaesthesiaAsleep; no response to surroundingsAnaesthesiologistMany treatments in a young child, patients with special needs, extensive surgery

Local anaesthetic is usually given as well under sedation or general anaesthesia, which makes pain control afterwards easier.

• People whose dental fear is too severe for treatment under local anaesthetic
  • Young children who can't cooperate and need many teeth treated
  • People with intellectual or physical special needs
  • Long surgical procedures such as impacted teeth or several implants
  • Some situations where local anaesthetic doesn't work well enough

The dentist doesn't decide alone: general health, medicines and previous experiences of anaesthesia are assessed together with the anaesthesia team.

Sedation and general anaesthesia are given by a specialist anaesthesiologist in settings permitted by regulations, with equipment to monitor breathing and circulation and to handle emergencies. Not every dental practice has these facilities, so if treatment under sedation is needed, where it will take place is planned in advance.

1. Pre-anaesthetic assessment: chronic conditions, medicines and allergies are discussed.
  2. You'll need to avoid eating and drinking for some hours beforehand; the anaesthesia team will tell you how long.
  3. An adult escort is essential, and you mustn't drive that day.
  4. Rest on the day and the day after, avoiding heavy work.
  5. Children need close supervision for the first hours afterwards.
In short

Sedation and general anaesthesia are for specific situations such as untreatable fear or extensive procedures, and require an anaesthesiologist and suitable equipment. For most patients, a well-explained, unhurried local anaesthetic is enough.

sections.h: Other ways to reduce dental anxiety
sections.html: Not every fear needs sedation. Using the first appointment just to meet and examine, explaining each step in advance, agreeing a “stop” signal and splitting long procedures into shorter visits help most patients. More in step-by-step treatment for anxious patients. How long numbness lasts is covered in how long dental numbness lasts.

sections.html: At our polyclinic in Beylikdüzü, the first conversation covers your anxiety and the scope of treatment, and we assess together whether local anaesthetic will be enough. If sedation or general anaesthesia seems necessary, we explain clearly under what conditions and where it could be done.

faq.q: Will I be fully asleep under sedation?
faq.a: With light or moderate sedation you're drowsy and relaxed but still respond when spoken to. Being fully asleep is general anaesthesia, given by an anaesthesiologist.

faq.q: When are children treated under general anaesthesia?
faq.a: It's considered for young children who need many teeth treated and can't cooperate, or for children with special needs. A child-friendly approach is tried first, and the decision is made with the dentist, the family and the anaesthesia team.

faq.q: Can I drive after sedation?
faq.a: No. Don't drive or make important decisions on the day of sedation or general anaesthesia, and go home with an adult escort.

title: Why Turkish dental clinics don't show prices, “best” claims or reviews: the 2025 promotion regulation
desc: What did Türkiye's health promotion regulation of 12 November 2025 change for dental clinics? Rules on prices, campaigns, reviews, before-and-after photos and titles, and what patients can check.
seoTitle: Why Turkish dental clinics don't show prices, “best” claims or reviews
seoDesc: What did Türkiye's November 2025 health promotion regulation change for dental clinics? Rules on prices, reviews and before-and-after photos.
lead: Türkiye's Regulation on Promotion and Information Activities in Health Services was published in the Official Gazette (no. 33075) and came into force on 12 November 2025. It bans open or covert advertising by all healthcare providers, including dental clinics; providers may only give information within the rules. So on the website of a compliant dental clinic you won't find a price list, discounts, superiority claims such as “the best” or patients' thank-you messages. This article summarises the points that matter for patients and how you can use them when assessing a clinic.

sections.html:
• Advertising: open or covert advertising of health services is banned; only information within the rules is allowed.
  • Prices and campaigns: promotion may not include fees, discounts, campaigns or promotions; incentives such as gifts and prize draws are not allowed.
  • Superiority claims: wording such as “the best”, “the only” or “leading” that creates a sense of superiority or exploits a lack of knowledge may not be used.
  • Patient thanks: posts that use patients' or relatives' thanks and satisfaction as advertising are not allowed.
  • Steering: content that directly or indirectly steers patients to a particular dentist or provider is banned.
  • Sponsored listings: paid, sponsored or boosted search engine and social media listings are not allowed.
  • Titles: only recognised specialty titles may be used; certificate-based “specialist” titles may not.
  • Unproven methods: methods that are not scientifically proven or regulated by the Ministry may not be presented.

The regulation doesn't ban patient images outright, but it sets strict conditions:

  • A patient's image may not be used without their explicit consent, which can be withdrawn at any time.
  • A patient who refuses must see no change in diagnosis, treatment or fees, and no discount or gift may be offered for consent.
  • Images must not be misleading: no deceptive make-up and no retouching afterwards.
  • Before and after photos must be taken under the same conditions, with the procedure date and the date of the image stated.
  • It must be stated whether the image shows a real patient, and the source given if it's borrowed.

For domestic promotion, images must carry this warning (translated): “Results of any surgical or interventional procedure may vary from person to person. You are advised to obtain a detailed opinion from your doctor before the procedure.”

sections.h: What a clinic website may show
sections.html:
The regulation also defines what information is allowed. Providers may share their address, contact details, opening hours, the fields in which they accept patients and the titles of their dentists. Websites must clearly show when the information was last updated and how to contact the site editor. Providers that treat patients from abroad under health tourism must also publish their health tourism authorisation certificate.

In short

A compliant clinic won't offer you a price list, a “best” claim or patient testimonials. Instead it tells you who it is, where it is, which dentists work there and how treatment is carried out.

sections.h: How you can use these rules as a patient
sections.html:
1. Compare prices using the written plan given after an examination, not adverts; see what determines dental treatment prices.
  2. If a dentist is presented as a “specialist”, ask in which specialty; see how to tell a dental practice is licensed.
  3. Read reviews yourself on independent platforms rather than quotes chosen by the clinic; see how to read dental clinic reviews.
  4. Check before-and-after images for dates, consent and the warning text.
  5. You can report content you believe is advertising to the provincial health directorate.

sections.h: How Dent32's website follows these rules
sections.html: Instead of a price list or campaigns, we explain which factors determine the cost of treatment. We don't publish patient thanks or review quotes. We present our dentists with their titles and show the required warning next to before-and-after images. Every page shows the last update date and the site editor's contact details. Our articles are for information; the right treatment for you is decided after an examination.

To book, call or WhatsApp +90 555 011 33 68, or use our contact page. At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

For clinic details, our dentists and the full list of treatments, visit Dent32, dental polyclinic in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: Why don't dental clinics in Türkiye publish prices?
faq.a: The regulation bans fees, discounts and campaigns in promotion. Dental costs also depend on the number of teeth, materials and any additional procedures, so a realistic figure can only be given after an examination.

faq.q: Are patients' Google reviews banned too?
faq.a: Patients writing about their own experience on independent platforms isn't what the regulation addresses. It restricts providers from using thanks and satisfaction statements as advertising in their own promotion.

faq.q: When did the regulation come into force?
faq.a: It was published in the Official Gazette no. 33075 and came into force on 12 November 2025.

title: Dental treatment while breastfeeding: anaesthetic, X-rays, painkillers, antibiotics and whitening
desc: Can breastfeeding mothers have dental treatment? Does local anaesthetic pass into breast milk, is a pause needed, X-rays, painkillers and antibiotics, and which treatments can wait.
seoTitle: Dental treatment while breastfeeding | Dent32
seoDesc: Can breastfeeding mothers have dental treatment? Local anaesthetic and breast milk, X-rays, painkillers, antibiotics and treatments that can wait.
lead: Breastfeeding isn't a barrier to dental treatment. Fillings, root canal treatment, scale and polish and most extractions can be done during this time. Very little of the local anaesthetic used in dentistry passes into breast milk, and there's usually no need to pause breastfeeding. Dental X-rays have no effect on milk. For medicines, simply tell your dentist you're breastfeeding; non-urgent cosmetic treatments such as whitening are usually left until after breastfeeding.

sections.h: Does local anaesthetic pass into breast milk?
sections.html:
Local anaesthetics in dentistry are given in small doses to one area of the mouth. Very little reaches the blood and milk, and very little of that is absorbed by the baby's gut. So pumping and discarding milk or a long break from breastfeeding is usually unnecessary.

If it makes you feel more comfortable, you can feed your baby just before the appointment, so some time has passed before the next feed.
Yes. X-rays don't stay in the body and have no effect on milk. Dental X-ray doses are low, and they can be taken during breastfeeding when needed. See dental X-rays and CT scans.

MedicineGeneral position during breastfeeding
ParacetamolGenerally considered compatible with breastfeeding
IbuprofenGenerally considered compatible for short-term use
Penicillin-type antibiotics such as amoxicillinUsable in most cases; watch the baby for diarrhoea or nappy rash
Some antibiotics and painkillersNeed care with long-term use; your doctor may choose another option

This table is general information. Always take medicines at the dose and for the time your doctor advises, and mention at each visit that you're breastfeeding and how old your baby is. When antibiotics are needed is covered in do antibiotics and painkillers cure toothache?.

In short

Fillings, root canals, scale and polish and most extractions can be done while breastfeeding. Local anaesthetic and X-rays don't stop you feeding; medicines are chosen with breastfeeding in mind.

• Teeth whitening: safety data during breastfeeding are limited, so it's usually advised to wait until you've finished. See teeth whitening.
  • Extensive cosmetic treatment: planned work such as smile design can wait until sleepless nights and the intense care routine ease.
  • Major surgery: planned surgery such as several implants is possible but is timed with medicines and recovery in mind.

Pain, abscesses or broken teeth shouldn't wait, though: untreated infection is a bigger risk for the mother. See dental abscess.

Gum bleeding that increased during pregnancy often settles after the birth, but night feeds, frequent snacking and tiredness can make oral care slip. A dental check-up and scale and polish in the first months after the birth is a good start. We cover pregnancy separately in dental treatment in pregnancy.

If you mention that you're breastfeeding when booking, we'll plan to keep your waiting time short. If you're bringing your baby, having someone with you makes it easier to relax during treatment.

faq.q: When can I breastfeed after a dental injection?
faq.a: So little local anaesthetic passes into milk that you can usually feed straight away. Feeding your baby before the appointment is another option if it makes you more comfortable.

faq.q: Can I have a tooth extracted while breastfeeding?
faq.a: Yes. Extraction is done under local anaesthetic, and any painkiller or antibiotic afterwards is chosen knowing you're breastfeeding.

faq.q: Can I whiten my teeth while breastfeeding?
faq.a: Safety data are limited, so it's usually advised to wait until you've finished breastfeeding. Meanwhile a scale and polish can reduce surface stains.

title: Dental care before and during cancer treatment: chemotherapy and head and neck radiotherapy
desc: For people about to have chemotherapy or head and neck radiotherapy: why a dental check first matters, mouth sores and dryness, timing of extractions and caring for your mouth at home.
seoTitle: Dental care before and during cancer treatment | Dent32
seoDesc: Before chemotherapy or head and neck radiotherapy: why a dental check matters, mouth sores and dryness, extraction timing and home care.
lead: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy to the head and neck affect the tissues of the mouth directly: mouth sores (mucositis), dry mouth, a tendency to infection and faster decay are common. So a dental examination before cancer treatment starts is recommended, ideally with teeth that need extracting and sources of infection dealt with before treatment begins. During and after treatment, the dentist works in contact with the oncology team.

sections.h: A dental check before cancer treatment
sections.html:
The aim is to deal in advance with problems that could flare up during treatment. Decay, gum disease, infection at root tips and loose teeth are assessed, with a panoramic X-ray if needed.

  • Teeth that can't be saved or are a source of infection are removed before treatment, leaving time to heal; timing is agreed with the oncology team.
  • Sharp fillings and dentures are adjusted so they don't cause sores.
  • A scale and polish is done and home care explained.
  • Fluoride treatment may be planned for people having radiotherapy.
In short

A dental check before chemotherapy or head and neck radiotherapy lowers the risk of pain and infection during treatment. Book it as early as possible before treatment starts.

sections.h: What can happen in the mouth during treatment?
sections.html:
ProblemWhat can help
Mouth sores (mucositis)A soft brush, alcohol-free mouthwash, avoiding spicy and acidic food; pain relief as advised by your doctor
Dry mouthSipping water often, sugar-free gum, saliva substitutes; see dry mouth
Fungal infection (thrush)White patches on the tongue and palate; needs treatment
Tendency to bleed and infectionPlanned dental work is postponed while blood counts are low; urgent problems are managed together with the oncology team
Taste changesUsually improve gradually after treatment ends

If dental treatment is needed during chemotherapy, the timing is decided with your oncologist based on your blood counts.

The blood supply to the jawbone in the treated area can be reduced. After surgery such as an extraction there, the bone may fail to heal (osteoradionecrosis). So after radiotherapy, treatments that keep teeth are preferred over extraction, and any surgery is planned in advance.

With less saliva, decay can progress quickly. Regular check-ups, high-fluoride toothpaste or gels and cutting down sugary snacks are important. If opening the mouth becomes restricted, jaw exercises may be advised.

sections.h: Caring for your mouth at home
sections.html:
• Brush twice a day with a soft brush and fluoride toothpaste
  • Use floss or interdental brushes; check with your dentist if there's bleeding
  • Alcohol-free mouthwashes recommended by your doctor
  • Take dentures out and clean them every night
  • Avoid smoking and alcohol

For technique, see how to brush your teeth properly.

sections.h: A pre-treatment dental check in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:

Bringing a list of your medicines and recent blood test results makes the assessment easier.

faq.q: Can I see a dentist during chemotherapy?
faq.a: Yes, but planned treatment is timed with your oncologist according to your blood counts. For urgent problems such as pain or swelling, contact your dentist and oncology team without delay.

faq.q: Can teeth be extracted after radiotherapy?
faq.a: Extractions in the treated area are planned carefully because of the risk of the bone not healing. Treatments that keep the tooth are preferred where possible; if extraction is needed, precautions are discussed in advance.

faq.q: What helps mouth sores during chemotherapy?
faq.a: A soft brush, alcohol-free mouthwash, plenty of water and avoiding spicy and acidic food help. If sores stop you eating, your doctor can suggest treatments to reduce the pain.

title: Dental treatment with heart disease: stents, heart valves, bypass, pacemakers and blood thinners
desc: With a stent, prosthetic heart valve, bypass or pacemaker, what should you know before dental treatment? Who needs antibiotic cover, should medicines be stopped, and is anaesthetic safe?
seoTitle: Dental treatment with heart disease | Dent32
seoDesc: With a stent, heart valve, bypass or pacemaker, what should you know before dental treatment? Antibiotic cover, medicines and anaesthetic safety.
lead: Most people with heart disease can safely have fillings, root canal treatment, scale and polish, extractions and implants. What matters is that your dentist knows about your condition and medicines and, where needed, plans together with your cardiologist. You shouldn't stop blood thinners or antiplatelet medicines on your own, and in some situations, such as a prosthetic heart valve, preventive antibiotics may be needed before the procedure.

sections.html:
• Any heart attack, stent or bypass, and when
  • A prosthetic or repaired heart valve, or previous infective endocarditis
  • Congenital heart disease
  • A pacemaker or defibrillator (ICD)
  • All your medicines: anticoagulants, antiplatelets, blood pressure and rhythm medicines
  • Any recent chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations

This determines which procedure is done, when and how. Other conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure are covered in dental treatment with chronic conditions.

During procedures that make the gums or root tip area bleed, mouth bacteria can briefly enter the bloodstream. For most people this causes no problem. But for those at high risk of infective endocarditis, a single preventive dose of antibiotic is recommended beforehand. According to current guidelines this group mainly includes:

  • People with a prosthetic heart valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
  • People who have had endocarditis before
  • Some congenital heart conditions (particularly unrepaired ones or those recently repaired with prosthetic material)

A stent, bypass or pacemaker alone usually doesn't require antibiotic cover. Your doctor decides which medicine and dose; don't take antibiotics on your own.

In short

With a prosthetic heart valve, previous endocarditis or some congenital heart conditions, preventive antibiotics may be needed before procedures that make the gums bleed. A stent or bypass alone doesn't call for this.

Antiplatelet medicines after a stent and anticoagulants shouldn't be stopped without your cardiologist's approval, as stopping them can raise the risk of clots. Fillings, root canal treatment and most extractions can be done while you continue them, with local measures to control bleeding. For more extensive surgery, blood tests and the medicine schedule are planned with your cardiologist or prescribing doctor.

sections.h: Timing, anaesthetic and comfort in the chair
sections.html:
• Recent heart attack or stent: non-urgent treatment is usually postponed for a while; your cardiologist decides how long. Urgent problems such as pain and infection aren't postponed.
  • Local anaesthetic: the small amount of adrenaline in dental anaesthetics is used safely in most heart patients; the dose is adjusted to your condition.
  • Pacemakers: your dentist may take precautions with some electrical instruments, so always mention it.
  • Position: people with heart failure may struggle to lie flat; treatment can be done semi-upright.
  • Short, calm visits: stress and long sessions can strain the heart, so treatment can be split into shorter visits.

Studies have shown links between gum disease and cardiovascular disease. Regular scaling and gum treatment lower the inflammatory load in the mouth. For heart patients, keeping the mouth healthy is also one of the surest ways to avoid infections that need urgent treatment. See gum treatment.

sections.h: Planning for heart patients in Beylikdüzü

faq.q: Can someone with a stent have a tooth extracted?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases without stopping antiplatelet medicines, using local bleeding control. Don't stop them without your cardiologist's approval; if the stent is very recent, non-urgent work may be postponed.

faq.q: Is dental anaesthetic safe for heart patients?
faq.a: Yes. The small amount of adrenaline in dental anaesthetics is used safely in most heart patients, and the dentist adjusts the dose to your condition.

faq.q: Do I need antibiotics before dental treatment?
faq.a: Only in high-risk groups such as a prosthetic heart valve, previous endocarditis and some congenital heart conditions, before procedures that make the gums bleed. Your doctor decides.

title: Does dental treatment break the fast? Fillings, extractions, injections and brushing in Ramadan
desc: Can you have a filling, an extraction or a dental injection while fasting? What Türkiye's Presidency of Religious Affairs says, timing medicines and caring for your mouth during Ramadan.
seoTitle: Does dental treatment break the fast? | Dent32
seoDesc: Can you have a filling, an extraction or a dental injection while fasting? What Türkiye's religious authority says and mouth care in Ramadan.
lead: According to statements by Türkiye's Presidency of Religious Affairs (Diyanet), having a filling, having a tooth extracted and receiving a numbing injection for treatment don't break the fast, as long as no water, blood or medicine is swallowed. Even so, many people prefer to leave dental treatment until after iftar or after the Eid holiday. This article covers what can be done while fasting, situations that need medicine and caring for your mouth during Ramadan. For a definitive religious ruling, please consult Diyanet's current guidance.

sections.html:
SituationDoes it break the fast?
Having a fillingNo, if no water or material is swallowed
Having a tooth extractedNo, if no blood or medicine is swallowed
Numbing injection (local anaesthetic)No, as it isn't nourishment
Brushing teethNo, if toothpaste and water aren't swallowed; care is needed
Rinsing the mouthNo, if water isn't swallowed
Taking or swallowing medicineYes

This table summarises statements Diyanet has shared publicly. For your own situation you can contact Diyanet's ALO 190 line or official website.

sections.h: Having treatment while fasting: what matters in practice
sections.html:
• Water and suction: teeth are cooled with water during fillings and root canal treatment. Suction removes it; if you're worried, tell your dentist and breaks can be taken.
  • After an extraction: you may taste blood for a while; you bite on gauze and can spit rather than swallow. Since painkillers may be needed in the first days, bigger extractions can be planned close to iftar or after the holiday.
  • Hunger and dizziness: long procedures can be tiring after many hours without food. Extensive treatment may be more comfortable near iftar or after Ramadan.
  • Emergencies: swelling, an abscess or severe pain shouldn't wait until Ramadan ends. See dental abscess and facial swelling.

sections.h: If you need antibiotics or painkillers
sections.html:
Taking medicine breaks the fast. If antibiotics are prescribed, skipping doses or stopping early can make treatment fail. Tell your dentist you're fasting; where possible they may choose a twice-daily medicine that fits suhoor and iftar. Diyanet's guidance also notes that people who are ill and need medicine are permitted not to fast.

When antibiotics are needed is covered in do antibiotics and painkillers cure toothache?.

In short

According to Diyanet, fillings, extractions and dental injections don't break the fast; taking medicine does. If you need antibiotics, plan doses around suhoor and iftar with your dentist rather than stopping them.

sections.h: Bad breath and oral care in Ramadan
sections.html:
Saliva flow drops while fasting, more builds up on the tongue and bad breath becomes more noticeable. To reduce it:

  • Brush with fluoride toothpaste after suhoor and after iftar.
  • Clean your tongue with a brush or tongue scraper; see tongue cleaning.
  • Drink plenty of water between iftar and suhoor, and cut down sugary and acidic drinks.
  • Use floss or interdental brushes before bed.

Causes of persistent bad breath are covered in bad breath.

sections.h: A note for people with diabetes
sections.html: Blood sugar can fluctuate in people with diabetes who fast; it's important that it is under control before long or surgical dental procedures. Planning with chronic conditions is covered in dental treatment with chronic conditions.

faq.q: Does a dental injection break the fast?
faq.a: According to Diyanet, treatment injections that aren't nourishment don't break the fast, and dental numbing injections fall into this category.

faq.q: Can I have a tooth out while fasting?
faq.a: Yes; according to Diyanet the fast isn't broken as long as no blood or medicine is swallowed. Since painkillers may be needed afterwards, bigger extractions can be planned close to iftar.

faq.q: Can I brush my teeth while fasting?
faq.a: It's said not to break the fast as long as toothpaste and water aren't swallowed. Many people therefore brush after suhoor and after iftar.

title: Signs of mouth cancer: sores and patches on the tongue, cheek or palate that don't heal
desc: When do a mouth sore that won't heal in two to three weeks, a white or red patch, a lump or numbness matter? Mouth cancer risk factors, a self-check at home and the dental examination.
seoTitle: Signs of mouth cancer: sores and patches that don't heal | Dent32
seoDesc: When does a mouth sore that won't heal in 2–3 weeks, or a white or red patch, matter? Mouth cancer risk factors, self-checks and examination.
lead: The vast majority of mouth sores and patches have harmless causes such as ulcers, denture rubbing or biting, and heal within a week or two. A sore that hasn't healed in two to three weeks, a white or red patch, a hard area or unexplained numbness, however, should always be checked by a clinician. Mouth cancer found early has a good chance of successful treatment, and a routine dental examination covers not only the teeth but also the tongue, cheeks, palate and floor of the mouth.

sections.html:
• A sore or ulcer that doesn't heal within two to three weeks
  • A white (leukoplakia) or red (erythroplakia) patch that doesn't wipe off
  • A hard area, lump or thickening on the tongue, cheek, lip or floor of the mouth
  • Unexplained bleeding, or numbness of the tongue or lip
  • New difficulty chewing, swallowing or speaking
  • Teeth loosening without gum disease, or a denture that suddenly no longer fits
  • A lump in the neck that doesn't go away, or a hoarse voice
In short

If you have a mouth sore that hasn't healed in two to three weeks, a white or red patch that won't wipe off, or a hard area, get it checked. Early assessment usually finds a harmless cause; if not, early diagnosis makes treatment easier.

sections.h: How to tell harmless sores apart
sections.html:
Usually harmlessNeeds examination
Ulcer: painful, round, yellow-white base; heals in 7–14 daysA sore lasting more than two to three weeks, which may be painless
Sore from a denture or broken tooth edge: heals once the cause is removedA sore that doesn't heal after the cause is removed
Thrush: white plaques that wipe offA white or red patch that doesn't wipe off
Bite or burn from hot foodA hard area, lump or numbness

See mouth ulcers and white tongue for more.

• Tobacco: cigarettes, cigars, pipes, hookah and smokeless tobacco are the main risk factor.
  • Alcohol: raises the risk markedly, especially combined with tobacco.
  • HPV infection: linked particularly to cancers of the tonsils and base of the tongue.
  • Sun: long-term sun exposure plays a role in lower lip cancer.
  • Chronic irritation: sores repeatedly caused by an ill-fitting denture or sharp tooth should be assessed.

Having a risk factor doesn't mean you will get cancer, but people who smoke or drink regularly shouldn't skip mouth checks.

sections.h: A two-minute self-check once a month
sections.html:
1. Stand in front of a mirror in good light; take out any dentures.
  2. Look inside and outside your lips and at your gums.
  3. Gently pull your cheeks out with a finger and look inside.
  4. Stick out your tongue and look at the top, underneath and both sides; holding it with gauze makes the sides easier to see.
  5. Look at the floor of your mouth and the palate, and feel the soft tissues for hard areas.
  6. Feel your neck and under your jaw for lumps.

sections.h: What happens at a dental examination?
sections.html: A routine dental check includes the soft tissues of the mouth. If something suspicious is seen, any likely source of irritation is removed and you're reviewed shortly afterwards, or you're referred directly to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or an ear, nose and throat doctor. A definite diagnosis is made by examining a small tissue sample (biopsy). For how often to have check-ups, see dental check-ups.

If you've noticed a sore or patch that won't heal, mention it when booking; noting how long it's been there and any changes you've seen helps the assessment. We share our findings and, if needed, a referral recommendation in writing.

faq.q: When is a mouth sore dangerous?
faq.a: Sores that don't heal within two to three weeks, persist after the cause is removed, or come with a hard area or numbness should be checked. Most still turn out to have a harmless cause.

faq.q: Is mouth cancer painful?
faq.a: In the early stages it is often painless, so the absence of pain doesn't mean a sore is harmless. Painless sores that don't heal should be examined too.

faq.q: Can a dentist spot mouth cancer?
faq.a: A dental examination includes the tongue, cheeks, palate and floor of the mouth; if something suspicious is found, you're referred for further tests. A definite diagnosis needs a biopsy.

title: Gum infection around a wisdom tooth (pericoronitis): swelling, trouble opening the mouth and treatment
desc: Why does the gum over a partly erupted wisdom tooth get inflamed? Pericoronitis symptoms, what to do at home, when it's urgent, treatment and whether the tooth needs to come out.
seoTitle: Gum infection around a wisdom tooth (pericoronitis) | Dent32
seoDesc: Why does the gum over a partly erupted wisdom tooth get inflamed? Pericoronitis symptoms, home care, when it's urgent and treatment.
lead: Pericoronitis is inflammation of the gum partly covering a tooth that hasn't fully come through, most often a lower wisdom tooth. Food and bacteria trapped under the gum flap can't be cleaned away, so the area swells, hurts and tastes unpleasant; in severe cases opening the mouth and swallowing become difficult. A mild episode may settle in a few days but tends to come back. The lasting solution, depending on the tooth and gum, is cleaning the area, removing the gum flap or extracting the tooth.

sections.html:
• Pain and swelling around the last tooth
  • The upper tooth biting on the swollen gum, pain when chewing
  • A bad taste or smell, sometimes pus
  • Limited mouth opening, pain on swallowing
  • Pain spreading to the ear or throat; see can toothache spread to the ear?
  • In severe cases fever and swollen glands under the jaw

If swelling spreads to the cheek, under the jaw or into the neck, if swallowing or breathing becomes difficult, if you can barely open your mouth or have a high fever, see a dentist without delay, or a hospital emergency department at night or at the weekend. See dental abscess and facial swelling and emergency dentist.

In short

Pericoronitis usually affects the gum over a partly erupted lower wisdom tooth. Spreading swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing and high fever are emergencies; if mild episodes keep returning, a lasting solution should be planned.

sections.h: What you can do at home until you're seen
sections.html:
• Gently clean the area with a soft brush and rinse out food with warm water
  • Rinse with warm salt water several times a day
  • Take painkillers as directed on the leaflet
  • Drink plenty of water and eat soft food
  • Don't put heat on your face, and don't take antibiotics unless advised by a dentist

1. Cleaning and irrigation: the area under the gum flap is washed with an antiseptic solution and debris removed. Most mild episodes settle with this.
  2. Medicine if needed: with fever, spreading swelling or general symptoms, the dentist may prescribe antibiotics. See when antibiotics are needed.
  3. Adjusting the opposing tooth: if the upper wisdom tooth keeps biting on the swollen gum, it is assessed too.
  4. Lasting solution: once the inflammation settles, the tooth's position is checked on an X-ray. If it can come through properly, the gum flap can be removed; if there isn't room, it's tilted, or episodes keep recurring, extraction is advised.

For the extraction decision and recovery, see when should a wisdom tooth come out? and tooth extraction in Beylikdüzü.

Behind a wisdom tooth is hard to reach with a brush. A small-headed or single-tuft brush, rinsing after meals and regular check-ups can reduce episodes until a decision about extraction is made. Repeated episodes can also cause decay and bone loss on the neighbouring tooth, so putting it off isn't wise.

faq.q: Does pericoronitis go away on its own?
faq.a: A mild episode may settle in a few days with cleaning and rinsing, but because the cause remains it tends to return. You need an examination for a lasting solution.

faq.q: Is the tooth taken out straight away?
faq.a: Usually the inflammation is settled first, then extraction or removal of the gum flap is planned depending on the tooth's position. In emergencies the dentist decides the approach.

faq.q: Why does pericoronitis make it hard to open the mouth?
faq.a: The inflammation is close to the chewing muscles, which tighten and limit opening. This improves as the inflammation clears.

title: Dental specialties in Türkiye: what orthodontists, endodontists, periodontists and others do
desc: The 8 official dental specialties in Türkiye, what a general dentist is qualified to do, unofficial titles such as “implant specialist”, and when you may be referred to a specialist.
seoTitle: Dental specialties in Türkiye: who does what | Dent32
seoDesc: The 8 official dental specialties in Türkiye, what a general dentist can do, unofficial titles like “implant specialist” and when you're referred.
lead: In Türkiye every graduate of a dental faculty is qualified to diagnose and treat diseases of the mouth and teeth. Specialisation is additional training on top of that, entered by exam and lasting several years. Dentistry has eight official specialties, and only dentists who complete that training may use the title “specialist”. Here we explain what each specialty does, which treatments a general dentist takes on, and the unofficial titles you often see in promotion.

sections.h: Dentist and specialist dentist: the difference
sections.html:
Dental school in Türkiye takes five years. Graduates practise with the title “Dt.” and can carry out fillings, root canal treatment, extractions, dentures, crowns, gum treatment and implants to the extent of their training. Specialist training is entered through the national dental specialty exam (DUS) and completed at a university or training hospital, with a thesis and exams.

A dentist who completes it may use the title “specialist dentist” in that field. Specialisation doesn't mean a general dentist can't provide that treatment; it means deeper training and experience for complex cases.

SpecialtyMain areas
Oral and maxillofacial surgeryImpacted teeth, jaw cysts, advanced implant surgery, jaw fractures
Oral and maxillofacial radiologyInterpreting X-rays and CT scans, diagnosing oral lesions
Paediatric dentistry (pedodontics)Baby teeth and young permanent teeth, prevention, behaviour management
EndodonticsRoot canal treatment, retreatment, root-end surgery
OrthodonticsTooth and jaw irregularities, braces and clear aligners
PeriodontologyGum disease, gum surgery, gum grafts
ProsthodonticsCrowns, bridges, dentures, implant-supported prostheses
Restorative dentistryFillings, aesthetic restorations, wear and decay
In short

Türkiye has eight official dental specialties. The title “specialist” is only for dentists who have completed specialist training in one of them.

Implantology, cosmetic dentistry and smile design are not separate specialties in Türkiye. Courses, certificates and master's programmes exist in these areas, but they don't confer a specialist title. The health promotion regulation in force since 12 November 2025 also bans presenting certificate-based titles as “specialist”. Details: dental advertising rules in Türkiye.

Asking about a dentist's title is as natural as asking who will treat you. See how to tell a dental practice is licensed.

sections.h: When you may be referred to a specialty
sections.html:
Most treatment is provided by general dentists. In the situations below, the opinion of a dentist in the relevant specialty may be sought:

  • A wisdom tooth deep in bone or near the nerve, a large jaw cyst: oral and maxillofacial surgery. See wisdom teeth.
  • Curved or calcified canals, recurring infection at the root tip: endodontics. See tooth cysts and root-end surgery.
  • Skeletal jaw problems, guiding growth in children: orthodontics. See early orthodontics for children.
  • Advanced bone loss, loose teeth: periodontology. See gum pocket treatment.
  • Young children who struggle to cooperate with treatment: paediatric dentistry, with sedation or general anaesthesia if needed.

sections.h: Questions you can ask at the examination
sections.html:

  • Does my case need referral to a specialty, and why?
  • If so, which part of the treatment will be done where?
  • Will I get the whole plan in writing?

For more, see 12 questions to ask your dentist.

faq.q: Can a general dentist place implants?
faq.a: Yes. Implants can be placed by dentists trained to do so; implantology isn't a separate specialty in Türkiye. In complex situations such as limited bone, a surgical opinion may be sought.

faq.q: What are a pedodontist and an orthodontist?
faq.a: A pedodontist has completed specialist training in paediatric dentistry, an orthodontist in orthodontics. Only dentists with that specialty may use these titles.

faq.q: How do I know if a dentist is a specialist?
faq.a: Ask the practice and the dentist; specialists state their title together with the specialty. The website and sign should show each dentist's name and title.

faq.q: Is cosmetic dentistry a specialty?
faq.a: No. Cosmetic dentistry isn't an official specialty in Türkiye; aesthetic treatments fall within general dentistry and specialties such as restorative dentistry and prosthodontics.

title: Extract the tooth or save it with a root canal? 7 factors that decide
desc: Can a painful or infected tooth be saved with root canal treatment, or should it come out? Remaining tooth structure, root and bone condition, cracks, cost and what follows an extraction.
seoTitle: Extract the tooth or save it with a root canal? | Dent32
seoDesc: Can a painful or infected tooth be saved with a root canal, or should it come out? Remaining structure, root and bone, cracks, cost and options.
lead: For a tooth that hurts or has an abscess there are two routes: keep it with root canal treatment, or extract it and later fill the gap with an implant, bridge or denture. Saving a tooth that can be saved usually means fewer procedures and lower cost in the long run. But not every tooth can be saved; in a tooth cracked down the root, with no bone support left or very little sound structure, a root canal may not be a lasting solution. Here are the main factors behind the decision.

sections.html:
1. Remaining sound tooth structure: After root canal treatment there must be enough tooth above the gum line to support a filling or crown.
  2. A vertical crack or fracture in the root: A crack running down the root usually can't be saved. See cracked tooth syndrome.
  3. Bone support: In a clearly loose tooth that has lost bone to advanced gum disease, root canal treatment alone isn't enough.
  4. Size of the infection at the root tip: Most root-tip infections heal after root canal treatment; large lesions may need additional surgery. See tooth cysts.
  5. How important the tooth is: A molar that anchors a bridge or matters for chewing is worth more effort; a wisdom tooth with no opposing tooth is usually extracted.
  6. Previous root canal treatment: A failed root canal can often be redone. See root canal retreatment.
  7. General health, time and budget: Root canal treatment, the crown on top and check-ups should be weighed against extraction, healing and the implant process.

sections.h: Root canal and extraction side by side
sections.html:
Root canal + crownExtraction + implant or bridge
Your own toothKeptLost
TimeUsually 1–2 visits, then a crownSeveral months for extraction, healing and implant
Neighbouring teethUnaffectedA bridge needs them prepared; an empty gap lets teeth drift
BonePreservedBone shrinks after extraction; an implant slows this
Not suitable whenRoot crack, too little structure, advanced bone lossThere is a healthy, savable root

If extraction is chosen, plan from the start how the gap will be filled. See a single missing tooth and implant or bridge.

sections.h: Do you need a crown after root canal treatment?
sections.html: Root-filled teeth, especially molars, become more prone to fracture over time. So back teeth with significant loss of structure are usually given a crown or onlay after root canal treatment. Front teeth and teeth with little loss of structure may only need a filling. For sensitivity after treatment, see pain after root canal treatment.

sections.h: Before you say “just take it out”
sections.html:
Wanting a painful tooth out straight away is understandable. Yet most of the pain settles quickly once the nerve is cleaned out in the first stage of root canal treatment. Extraction can't be undone; it shouldn't be decided under the influence of pain, without an examination and X-ray. To ease pain temporarily, see the tips in how to relieve toothache.

In short

Keeping a savable tooth is usually the route with the fewest procedures. Insisting on a root canal for a tooth that can't be saved, on the other hand, costs time and money; the decision should rest on examination and imaging.

faq.q: Which is better, a root canal or an implant?
faq.a: If there is a healthy, savable root, saving the tooth with a root canal is usually considered first. An implant is a strong option for teeth that can't be saved, but it replaces your own tooth rather than coming before it.

faq.q: Can a tooth with an abscess be saved?
faq.a: Often, yes. An abscess usually heals once root canal treatment removes the source of infection. A root crack or advanced bone loss may mean extraction.

faq.q: What happens if I leave the gap empty?
faq.a: Neighbouring teeth can tilt into the gap, the opposing tooth can over-erupt and the bone in that area shrinks over time. That's why planning how to fill the gap after extraction is advised.

title: Tooth cysts and root-end surgery (apicoectomy): does a root canal clear them?
desc: Is the dark area at the root tip on your X-ray a cyst? Root-tip inflammation versus cysts, healing after root canal treatment, how an apicoectomy is done and recovery.
seoTitle: Tooth cysts and root-end surgery (apicoectomy) | Dent32
seoDesc: Is the dark area at the root tip on your X-ray a cyst? Inflammation versus cysts, healing after root canal treatment and apicoectomy.
lead: When an X-ray shows a dark, round area at the tip of a tooth's root, most patients call it a “cyst”. Most of these areas are root-tip inflammation caused by a dead or infected nerve, and they heal after root canal treatment. Some are true cysts; large lesions, lesions that don't heal or that persist despite a root canal may need root-end surgery (apicoectomy). Here we explain the difference, the treatment options and recovery.

sections.h: What is the dark area at the root tip?
sections.html:
When a tooth's nerve dies from decay, a fracture or a knock, bacteria in the root canal cause inflammation that spreads from the root tip into the bone. The body breaks down bone in that area, which appears dark on an X-ray. Most often this is inflamed tissue called a granuloma; less often a fluid-filled cyst with its own lining develops. X-rays can't always tell the two apart; a definite diagnosis needs the tissue to be examined.

Cysts can also form around impacted teeth, which is one reason impacted wisdom teeth need regular checks. See wisdom teeth.

• Often none at all; it's found on a routine X-ray.
  • Tenderness when biting or pressing on the tooth
  • A pimple-like bump on the gum, sometimes with a salty discharge. See a pimple on the gum.
  • Swelling, pain and fever during flare-ups. See dental abscess.
  • Discolouration of the tooth (a sign the nerve may have died)

For most root-tip lesions the first treatment is a root canal: the canals are cleaned, shaped and filled. Once the source of inflammation is gone, the bone gradually repairs itself. If the tooth has already had a root canal, retreatment is considered first.

Healing is followed with X-rays; bone usually fills in over 6–12 months, longer for large lesions. If there are no symptoms and the dark area is shrinking, treatment is on track.

In short

Most “cysts” seen on X-rays are root-tip inflammation and heal after a root canal. Root-end surgery is the second step, for cases where a root canal isn't enough or isn't possible.

It's used for lesions that don't heal despite a root canal, are very large or can't be reached through the canal. It's done under local anaesthetic:

  1. The gum over the root tip is opened.
  2. The inflamed tissue or cyst in the bone is removed.
  3. A few millimetres of the root tip are cut away.
  4. The root end is sealed with a biocompatible filling material that stops bacteria leaking.
  5. The gum is stitched; stitches usually come out after 7–10 days.

Removed tissue is sent for pathology when needed. In large cysts a bone graft may be used to help the bone heal.

• Mild swelling and bruising for the first 2–3 days are common; a cold pack helps on the first day.
  • Use the painkiller your dentist recommends; antibiotics are given only if needed.
  • Don't brush the stitched area for a few days; brush the other teeth as usual.
  • Smoking slows healing.
  • Bone healing is checked on an X-ray over the following months.

At Dent32 we assess the size of the lesion and whether the tooth can be saved with X-rays and, where needed, a CT scan. See dental X-rays and CT scans. We explain the options — root canal, retreatment, root-end surgery or extraction — in writing, and refer cases that need advanced surgery to the relevant specialty.

faq.q: Does a tooth cyst go away by itself?
faq.a: No. Because its source is an infected root canal, it won't heal until that source is removed by root canal treatment or surgery; it can grow over time even without symptoms.

faq.q: Should a tooth with a cyst be extracted?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Most root-tip lesions heal after a root canal. Extraction is considered if there's a root crack, too little tooth structure or advanced bone loss.

faq.q: Is an apicoectomy painful?
faq.a: It's done under local anaesthetic; afterwards there may be mild pain and swelling for a few days, usually controlled with painkillers.

title: A pimple-like bump on the gum (dental fistula): causes, should you pop it, how it heals
desc: A pimple-like bump on the gum that sometimes drains is usually the outlet of a chronic infection in a tooth. Causes, diagnosis, treatment and what not to do.
seoTitle: A pimple-like bump on the gum (dental fistula) | Dent32
seoDesc: A pimple-like bump on the gum is usually the drainage path of a chronic tooth infection. Causes, diagnosis, treatment and what not to do.
lead: A small, pimple-like bump on the gum, usually level with a tooth's root, is most often a fistula (sinus tract). It's a drainage channel created by inflammation collecting at the root tip or in a gum pocket. Because the pus drains through it, it often doesn't hurt; the bump goes down and comes back a few days later. No pain doesn't mean the problem has gone: until the source is treated the fistula keeps returning and bone loss can progress.

sections.html:
• A dead nerve and root-tip infection: The most common cause. The nerve dies after deep decay, old large fillings or a knock. See tooth cysts and root-tip inflammation.
  • A failed or incomplete root canal: A previously root-filled tooth can also develop a fistula. See root canal retreatment.
  • A gum pocket abscess: In advanced gum disease, pus can collect in deep pockets. See gum pockets.
  • A root crack: Cracks running down the root can cause a fistula too. See cracked tooth.
  • Inflammation around an implant: A similar bump can appear next to an implant. See implant lifespan and peri-implantitis.

sections.h: Fistula or another kind of sore?
sections.html:
SignFistulaMouth ulcerCold sore
AppearancePimple-like bump on the gumSore with a white-yellow base and red rimSmall blisters at the edge of the lip
DischargePus or a salty taste when pressedNoneBlisters burst and crust
CourseGoes down and returns in the same placeHeals in 7–14 daysHeals in 7–10 days
SourceAn underlying tooth or gum problemImmunity, stress, injuryA virus

For ulcers and mouth sores, see mouth ulcers. Any sore that hasn't healed in two weeks should be examined; see signs of mouth cancer.

The dentist first needs to find which tooth the fistula comes from; the bump doesn't always belong to the tooth right above it. Cold and tapping tests are done, gum pocket depths are measured and an X-ray is taken. If needed, a thin, X-ray-visible root canal filling cone is placed into the tract and an X-ray taken; the cone points to the source. In complex cases a CT scan helps. See dental X-rays and CT scans.

• Root canal treatment: For nerve-related fistulas, the tract usually closes within a few weeks once the source is cleaned.
  • Retreatment or root-end surgery: For teeth that have been treated before.
  • Gum treatment: Deep cleaning and, if needed, surgery for fistulas from gum pockets.
  • Extraction: If there's a root crack or the tooth can't be saved. See extraction or root canal.

Antibiotics may calm the bump temporarily but don't treat the source; once the course ends, the fistula returns. See do antibiotics cure toothache.

In short

A fistula isn't a disease in itself but a sign of an underlying infection. Even if the bump goes down, it won't heal until the source is treated.

• Don't prick or squeeze the bump; you can spread the infection.
  • Don't take antibiotics unless a dentist prescribes them.
  • Don't postpone treatment just because it doesn't hurt.
  • If you have facial swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing or breathing, see a dentist or go to A&E without delay. See dental abscess.

At Dent32 we find the source of the fistula with an examination and X-ray and explain the treatment options in writing. A fistula is usually not an emergency, but it shouldn't be put off; you can send a photo on WhatsApp to book.

faq.q: Will a pimple on the gum go away by itself?
faq.a: The bump goes down but usually returns in the same place. It won't go away for good until the underlying tooth or gum infection is treated.

faq.q: Is a fistula dangerous if it doesn't hurt?
faq.a: Because the infection drains through the fistula, there may be no pain; but the infection continues and can keep destroying the surrounding bone. No pain is no reason to delay treatment.

faq.q: When does a fistula close after root canal treatment?
faq.a: Usually within a few days to a few weeks. If it doesn't, the dentist reassesses the source.

title: Cracked tooth syndrome: sudden pain on biting, diagnosis and treatment
desc: A sharp pain when you bite something hard or release your bite can be a sign of a cracked tooth. Symptoms, why X-rays miss it, and crown, root canal and extraction options.
seoTitle: Cracked tooth syndrome: sudden pain on biting | Dent32
seoDesc: A sharp pain when you bite something hard can signal a cracked tooth. Symptoms, why X-rays miss it, and crown, root canal or extraction options.
lead: If you get a sharp, brief pain in a tooth when you bite on something hard or the moment you stop chewing, and you can't pinpoint exactly where it is, the tooth may be cracked. Cracked tooth syndrome is common in molars with large fillings and in people who clench their teeth. Because cracks often don't show on X-rays, diagnosis can be delayed. Cracks caught early can be protected with a crown; advanced cracks may need root canal treatment or extraction.

sections.html:
• Sharp pain when biting, especially when chewing at a certain angle
  • Pain the moment you release your bite (a typical sign of a cracked tooth)
  • Brief sensitivity to cold drinks and sweets
  • Not being sure exactly which tooth hurts
  • Avoiding chewing on that side

Constant, throbbing pain that wakes you at night can mean the crack has reached the nerve. For other causes of sensitivity, see tooth sensitivity.

• Large fillings: Wide fillings that thin the tooth's walls, especially old amalgam fillings. See should amalgam fillings be removed.
  • Clenching and grinding: High forces through the night. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • Hard foods: Ice, seeds, hard sweets, nuts in their shells, olive stones.
  • Root-filled teeth without a crown
  • Sudden hot–cold changes and knocks

TypeWhat it meansGeneral approach
Craze linesFine surface lines in the enamel onlyHarmless, no treatment needed
Fractured cuspA corner of the tooth breaks offFilling or crown
Cracked toothA crack running from the biting surface towards the rootCrown; root canal if it reaches the nerve
Split toothThe crack separates the tooth into twoUsually extraction
Vertical root fractureA crack that starts in and runs along the rootUsually extraction
In short

The earlier a crack is found, the easier the tooth is to save. Don't put off pain on biting just because it comes and goes.

Cracks are often as thin as a hair and don't show on X-rays. To diagnose them the dentist does a bite test on each tooth, shines a strong light through the tooth (a crack blocks the light), uses magnification and, if needed, removes an old filling to inspect the tooth. If a root crack is suspected, gum pocket depths and a CT scan help. See dental X-rays and CT scans.

• Crown or onlay: A restoration that wraps the tooth stops the crack opening and often ends the pain on chewing. See types of dental crowns.
  • Root canal and crown: If the crack has reached the nerve or pain continues after the crown. See root canal treatment.
  • Extraction: If the crack extends into the root or the tooth has split. See extraction or root canal.
  • Night guard: If you clench, it protects both the treated tooth and the others.

• Don't crunch ice, seeds or hard sweets.
  • Wear a night guard if you clench.
  • Don't delay crowning molars that have lost a lot of structure or had a root canal.
  • Repair broken fillings and chipped corners promptly. See what to do if you break a tooth.

At Dent32 we use bite tests, light examination and X-rays to find which tooth is cracked and how far the crack goes, and we explain the options for saving it in writing.

faq.q: Does a cracked tooth heal by itself?
faq.a: No. Unlike bone, tooth tissue can't repair a crack, and the crack can grow over time. Early on, a crown can protect the tooth.

faq.q: Do cracked teeth show on X-rays?
faq.a: Usually not. Diagnosis relies on bite tests, light examination and magnification; a CT scan can help with root cracks.

faq.q: Are the fine lines on my teeth cracks?
faq.a: Fine lines visible in the light on front teeth are usually harmless craze lines confined to the enamel. Without pain or sensitivity they need no treatment; if in doubt, have them checked.

title: A black spot or stain on a tooth: decay or staining? Causes and treatment
desc: Black marks in the grooves of molars, between teeth or at the gum line aren't always decay. Tea and coffee stains, tartar, old fillings and other causes, and how each is treated.
seoTitle: A black spot or stain on a tooth | Dent32
seoDesc: Black marks on molars, between teeth or at the gum line aren't always decay. Tea and coffee stains, tartar, old fillings and how each is treated.
lead: A black spot on a tooth makes most people think of decay first. Decay can indeed look black or brown, but staining in the grooves of molars, tartar, old metal fillings, a darkened tooth after a knock and bacterial stains in children can look similar. Only an examination and, where needed, an X-ray show which it is. Below we cover the most common causes and how each is handled.

sections.h: Possible causes of a black spot
sections.html:
CauseWhere it appearsClue
DecayMolar grooves, between teeth, at filling edgesSoft surface that catches; may be sensitive to sweets and cold
Arrested (inactive) decayUsually molar groovesHard, shiny dark spot that hasn't changed for years
Tea, coffee, tobacco stainingGrooves, gum line, between teethSuperficial; usually polishes off
TartarInner surfaces of lower front teeth, gum lineRough, hard deposit
Old amalgam fillingThe filling and surrounding toothGrey-black shadow
A tooth whose nerve has diedUsually a front tooth after a knockThe whole tooth turns grey-brown
Black stain in childrenA thin black line along the gumBacterial staining, not decay

Decay starts as a chalky white spot and over time turns brown and black. If the surface has softened and an instrument catches in it, the decay is active. Some decay hardens and stops over the years; it's dark but hard and shiny, and often only needs monitoring. Decay between teeth may not be visible from outside and needs an X-ray. Details: signs and stages of tooth decay, decay between teeth.

In short

What matters isn't the black colour but how hard the surface is and what the X-ray shows. A soft, growing spot needs treatment; a hard, unchanging one can be monitored.

Tea, coffee, red wine and smoking leave dark stains, especially in the deep grooves of molars and at the gum line. This staining isn't decay and largely polishes off at the clinic. Tartar forming below the gum line can look black when mixed with blood and causes gum inflammation; it's removed with a scale and clean. For overall discolouration, see why teeth turn yellow.

Old amalgam fillings darken over time and can give the surrounding tooth a grey shadow. If the filling is sound, that alone isn't a reason to remove it; if there's decay or a crack at its edge, it's replaced. See should amalgam fillings be removed.

A front tooth turning grey months or years after a knock can mean its nerve has died. Such teeth first need root canal treatment; the colour can then be corrected with internal whitening or a crown. See dental trauma.

Some children have a thin, dotted black line along the gum line. It's usually staining from certain mouth bacteria, not decay, and is often seen in children with low decay risk. It polishes off at the clinic but can come back. Iron supplements can also darken teeth; giving the syrup through a straw and rinsing afterwards helps. For decay in baby teeth, see baby bottle tooth decay.

• Polishing and professional cleaning: For staining and tartar.
  • Fissure sealants: To protect deep grooves that aren't decayed. See fluoride and fissure sealants.
  • Filling: For active decay. See white fillings.
  • Root canal plus internal whitening or a crown: For darkened teeth whose nerve has died.
  • Monitoring: For hard, unchanging arrested decay.

At Dent32 we determine with an examination and, if needed, an X-ray whether a spot is decay, and suggest only the treatment that's needed; we don't fill stains.
