faq.q: Will a black spot come off with brushing?
faq.a: Surface staining may fade a little, but staining in deep grooves and decay won't brush off. An examination is needed to tell what it is.

faq.q: Does a black spot need treatment if it doesn't hurt?
faq.a: Decay doesn't hurt at first. A soft or growing spot needs treatment; hard, unchanging spots can be monitored.

faq.q: My child has a black line on their teeth. Is it decay?
faq.a: A thin black line at the gum line is usually bacterial staining, not decay. It's still worth having it checked at an examination.

title: Should amalgam (metal) fillings be removed? Mercury, health, removal and replacements
desc: Do old metal fillings affect your health, and should they all be replaced? The mercury in amalgam, who needs extra care, reasons for removal, safe removal and replacement options.
seoTitle: Should amalgam (metal) fillings be removed? | Dent32
seoDesc: Do old metal fillings affect your health, and should they all be replaced? Mercury in amalgam, reasons for removal and safe replacement options.
lead: Amalgam is a silver-coloured filling material that has been used for more than a century and is about half mercury. That's why many people wonder whether their old metal fillings should come out. The shared view of scientific bodies is that a sound amalgam filling doesn't need removing just because it contains mercury, since removal both releases mercury vapour and sacrifices healthy tooth structure. When a filling does need replacing because of decay, a fracture or a crack, white fillings and ceramics are used today.

sections.h: What is amalgam, and why is it being phased down?
sections.html:
Amalgam is made by mixing silver, tin and copper powders with mercury. Durable and inexpensive, it was the standard filling for back teeth for many years. Its use is now falling for two reasons: aesthetic expectations and the environmental impact of mercury. Under the Minamata Convention on Mercury many countries are phasing it down; the European Union banned amalgam in new fillings from 1 January 2025, except where strictly medically necessary.

The main reason for these rules is the environment; they don't call for sound fillings to be removed.

sections.h: Is amalgam in your mouth harmful?
sections.html:
Amalgam fillings release very small amounts of mercury vapour, especially during chewing and grinding. Research hasn't shown this to cause health problems in healthy adults. Even so, for some groups other materials are advised for new fillings where possible:

  • Pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and those planning pregnancy. See dental treatment in pregnancy, dental treatment while breastfeeding.
  • Young children
  • People with impaired kidney function and some neurological conditions
  • People allergic to mercury

This advice is about new fillings. Even in these groups, removing sound fillings is generally not advised, because removal means brief exposure to more mercury vapour.

sections.h: When is an amalgam filling replaced?
sections.html:
• Decay at its edge or underneath: If seen on an X-ray or at the examination.
  • A broken filling or cracked tooth: Large amalgam fillings can weaken the tooth's walls. See cracked tooth syndrome.
  • Allergy or a reaction in the mouth: Persistent white-red lesions on the cheek or tongue where they touch the filling.
  • Appearance: Fillings visible when you smile and a grey shadow in the tooth. See black spots on teeth.
  • As part of a wider treatment plan: For example if the tooth is going to be crowned anyway.
In short

A sound amalgam filling with sealed edges isn't removed just because it contains mercury. Reasons to replace it are decay, fracture, a crack, allergy or your own aesthetic preference.

• Removing the filling in sections, generating as little heat as possible
  • Plenty of water cooling and strong suction
  • Isolating the tooth with a rubber dam where appropriate
  • Suitable masks for the dentist and assistant
  • Separating amalgam waste under medical waste rules

If several fillings are being replaced, the work can be split over several visits.

OptionWhen
Composite (white) fillingSmall and medium cavities
Inlay or onlay (ceramic or composite)Large cavities, weakened tooth walls
CrownVery large loss of structure, a crack or a root-filled tooth

Details: white (composite) fillings, types of dental crowns. Brief sensitivity after a filling is normal; see pain after a filling.

faq.q: Should I replace all my amalgam fillings?
faq.a: Replacing sound fillings just because they contain mercury isn't advised. Fillings with decay, fractures, cracks or an allergy are replaced; replacing for appearance is your choice.

faq.q: Can amalgam fillings be removed during pregnancy?
faq.a: Removing sound amalgam fillings in pregnancy isn't advised, as removal means brief exposure to more mercury vapour. If replacement is needed, it's usually planned for after the birth.

faq.q: Are white fillings that replace amalgam durable?
faq.a: Composite fillings placed for the right indication with good isolation can last many years. For very large cavities an onlay or crown is more durable.

title: Can your body reject a dental implant? Implant failure, titanium allergy and re-implantation
desc: Implant “rejection” isn't like organ rejection. Why an implant may not fuse with bone, signs of early and late failure, the facts on titanium allergy and placing a new implant.
seoTitle: Can your body reject a dental implant? | Dent32
seoDesc: Implant “rejection” isn't like organ rejection. Why implants may not fuse with bone, signs of failure, titanium allergy and re-implantation.
lead: Many people considering implants ask the same thing: “Will my body reject it?” Dental implants don't undergo immune rejection the way transplanted organs can. Titanium is biocompatible and allergy to it is very rare. The great majority of implants fuse with bone without problems; in a small number of cases an implant doesn't fuse or is lost over the years because of infection, bone quality, smoking, uncontrolled diabetes or overloading. These risks can usually be assessed in advance, and a failed implant can be replaced.

sections.html: After an implant is placed, the surrounding bone bonds to its surface over a few months; this is called osseointegration. If it doesn't happen, the implant stays loose and has to be removed. People often call this “rejection”, but it isn't an immune reaction; it's a problem in the healing process.

This is when the implant fails to fuse before loading or in the first months. Main causes:

  • Infection at the site
  • Too little bone, or bone that is very soft
  • The implant not being stable enough when placed
  • Loading the implant too early or too heavily while it heals
  • Smoking. See smoking after implants.
  • Uncontrolled diabetes and some medicines that affect healing. See who can have implants, osteoporosis medicines.

An implant that has fused and been in use can still be lost over the years. The most common cause is peri-implantitis: inflammation and loss of the gum and bone around the implant, similar to gum disease. Poor cleaning, missed check-ups, a history of gum disease and smoking raise the risk. Overloading from clenching or ill-fitting prostheses can also cause bone loss. Details: how long implants last, aftercare for implants.

In short

Implant failure isn't “rejection”; its causes are largely known. Smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, poor cleaning and missed check-ups are the main risks.

sections.h: Signs: when to see a dentist
sections.html:
• The implant or the tooth on it moving
  • Pain that doesn't settle after the first weeks, or comes back
  • Bleeding, swelling or pus around the implant
  • Receding gum with the implant threads showing
  • Discomfort when biting

A loose screw in the crown doesn't necessarily mean the implant itself is loose, but it should still be checked. See problems with implant-supported prostheses.

Hypersensitivity to titanium has been reported but is very rare. If you have a history of metal allergy (nickel, for example), discuss it with your dentist; if needed, allergy tests and metal-free zirconia implants can be considered. Almost all failures to fuse come from the causes above, not allergy.

An implant that hasn't fused is removed and the area cleaned. A few months are usually allowed for the bone to heal, with a bone graft at the same time or later if needed. A new implant can then be placed in the same area. Before the second attempt, the cause of the first failure (smoking, diabetes control, bone volume, load) must be addressed. See bone grafts and sinus lifts.

faq.q: What are the signs of implant rejection?
faq.a: Movement, pain that doesn't settle, bleeding, swelling or pus around the implant, and receding gum. If you notice these, see a dentist without delay.

faq.q: Can an implant be redone if it fails?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. The failed implant is removed and, once the area has healed, a new one can be placed, with a bone graft if needed.

faq.q: Could I be allergic to titanium?
faq.a: It's very rare. Tell your dentist if you have a history of metal allergy; allergy testing and zirconia implants can be considered if needed.

title: Osteoporosis medicines and tooth extraction or implants: what's the risk, should you stop them?
desc: Taking bisphosphonates or denosumab? What to know before extractions and implants: the risk of jaw osteonecrosis, osteoporosis versus cancer doses, and why not to stop the medicine yourself.
seoTitle: Osteoporosis medicines and tooth extraction or implants | Dent32
seoDesc: Taking bisphosphonates or denosumab? What to know before extractions and implants: jaw osteonecrosis risk and why not to stop the medicine.
lead: Bisphosphonates and denosumab, used to treat osteoporosis, slow down bone breakdown. In people taking them, the jawbone can rarely fail to heal after procedures that affect bone, especially extractions (medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw). At osteoporosis doses this risk is very low and most dental treatment can be done safely. At the high doses used in cancer treatment the risk is clearly higher. The key rule: don't stop these medicines yourself for dental treatment.

sections.html:
GroupExample active ingredientsHow it's taken
Bisphosphonates (oral)Alendronate, risedronate, ibandronateWeekly or monthly tablet
Bisphosphonates (intravenous)Zoledronic acid, ibandronateInfusion once a year or every few months
DenosumabDenosumabInjection every six months (osteoporosis) or monthly (cancer)

Some cancer medicines and drugs that block blood vessel growth can carry a similar risk. At your appointment, list every medicine you take, since when and at what dose.

sections.h: What is jaw osteonecrosis, and how big is the risk?
sections.html:
In medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, usually after an extraction, the jawbone is left exposed in the mouth and doesn't heal for weeks. Pain, swelling, discharge and numbness of the lip may follow.

The risk depends on the type of medicine, the dose, how long it has been taken and why. In people taking tablets or a yearly infusion for osteoporosis it's very low, rising somewhat with longer use (generally beyond a few years). In people on high doses for cancer that has spread to bone it's clearly higher. Steroids, diabetes, smoking and poor oral hygiene increase the risk.

In short

At osteoporosis doses the risk is very low; at the high doses used in cancer treatment it's higher. In both cases the most effective protection is getting your mouth healthy before starting the medicine.

sections.h: Before starting the medicine: a dental check
sections.html: Ideally, have a dental examination before starting. Extracting teeth that can't be saved, treating gum disease and adjusting ill-fitting dentures at this stage reduces later risk. For people about to start cancer treatment, see dental care before and during cancer treatment.

sections.h: Dental treatment while taking the medicine
sections.html:
• Fillings, root canals, scale and clean, crowns: Usually done safely. Where possible, saving a tooth with a root canal is preferred over extraction. See extraction or root canal.
  • Extraction: Done if needed, as gently as possible, with antiseptic mouthwash and antibiotics if required, and followed up until healed. See after a tooth extraction.
  • Implants: Can be considered at osteoporosis doses after a risk assessment; generally not advised for people on high doses for cancer. See who can have implants.
  • Dentures: Dentures that rub the gum should be adjusted; sore spots shouldn't be ignored.

No, not on your own. A break from the medicine (a “drug holiday”) can only be decided by the doctor who prescribes it, weighing up your fracture risk. In particular, skipping a planned denosumab dose or stopping it suddenly can increase the risk of spinal fractures. If you need dental treatment, your dentist will plan the timing with your prescribing doctor. For other long-term conditions, see dental treatment with chronic illness.

• A wound that hasn't closed 6–8 weeks after an extraction
  • Hard, white-yellow bone visible in the mouth
  • Pain, swelling or discharge in the jaw
  • Numbness of the lower lip or chin
  • Teeth becoming loose for no clear reason

Bring your medicine boxes or prescription to the appointment. At Dent32 we assess the risk according to the type and duration of your medicine, contact your doctor if needed and plan treatment accordingly.

faq.q: Can I have a tooth out while taking osteoporosis medicine?
faq.a: Yes, an extraction can be done when needed; at osteoporosis doses the risk is very low. It's done as gently as possible and followed up until healed. Don't stop the medicine yourself.

faq.q: Can people on osteoporosis medicine have implants?
faq.a: Implants can be considered for people taking it for osteoporosis, after a risk assessment. For people on high doses for cancer, implants are generally not advised.

faq.q: Should I pause my medicine for dental treatment?
faq.a: Only the prescribing doctor can decide. Stopping denosumab suddenly in particular can raise fracture risk, so don't pause it yourself.

title: Can you be allergic to dental anaesthetic? Local anaesthetic, latex and other allergies at the dentist
desc: Palpitations, dizziness or flushing after a dental injection: is it an allergy? How rare true local anaesthetic allergy is, the effect of adrenaline, latex, antibiotics and other allergies.
seoTitle: Can you be allergic to dental anaesthetic? | Dent32
seoDesc: Palpitations or flushing after a dental injection: is it allergy? How rare true local anaesthetic allergy is, adrenaline, latex and others.
lead: Many people who feel palpitations, trembling, dizziness or faintness after a dental injection assume they're allergic to local anaesthetic. In fact true allergy to the local anaesthetics used in dentistry is very rare. Most of these reactions are the brief effect of the adrenaline in the anaesthetic, anxiety, or a fainting reflex triggered by the needle. True allergies are more often to latex gloves, some antibiotics and painkillers. Telling them apart avoids needlessly avoiding treatment.

sections.html:
ReactionSymptomsWhen
Adrenaline effectPalpitations, trembling, restlessnessRight after the injection, lasting a few minutes
Fainting reflex (vasovagal)Pallor, sweating, nausea, dizziness, faintingDuring or right after the injection
Anxiety and fast breathingNumbness, tingling, feeling short of breathThroughout the appointment
True allergyHives, itching, swelling of the face or lips, breathlessness, wheezingWithin minutes to hours

Swelling from biting a numb lip can also be mistaken for allergy; see how long dental numbness lasts.

In short

Palpitations and trembling are usually the brief effect of adrenaline, not allergy. Hives, facial swelling or breathlessness, on the other hand, need urgent assessment.

Most anaesthetics used in dentistry today belong to the amide group, and true allergy to them is extremely rare. Allergy to the ester-type ingredients in some numbing gels applied to the gum is a little more likely. The preservative (sulphite) in adrenaline-containing solutions can cause problems for some people, especially sulphite-sensitive asthmatics.

If you believe you've had a true allergic reaction before, tell your dentist the details and the name of the medicine used. If needed, testing can be requested from an allergy and immunology doctor, and an anaesthetic from a different group or one without adrenaline can be chosen.

The small amount of adrenaline added to anaesthetics narrows blood vessels, making numbness last longer and reducing bleeding. It's used safely in most people with heart disease or high blood pressure; where needed, the dose is reduced or an adrenaline-free anaesthetic is chosen. Details: dental treatment with heart disease.

sections.h: Other allergies that can come up in dentistry
sections.html:
• Latex: Found in gloves and some materials. Tell us when booking if you're allergic; latex-free gloves and materials are used.
  • Antibiotics: Especially penicillins. A different antibiotic is chosen if you're allergic. See antibiotics and painkillers.
  • Painkillers: In some people, especially asthmatics, drugs such as ibuprofen can cause reactions.
  • Chlorhexidine: Found in mouthwashes and antiseptics; serious allergy has rarely been reported.
  • Metals: Nickel (some brace and denture alloys), rarely mercury. See amalgam fillings, living with braces.
  • Acrylic: Some denture materials can cause burning and redness in the mouth. See dentures.

sections.h: What to do before your appointment
sections.html:
• Mention all known allergies and past reactions at your first examination.
  • Bring any allergy test results or reports.
  • If you carry an adrenaline auto-injector, bring it with you.
  • Tell us if you're afraid of needles or tend to faint; treatment can be done lying back. See fear of the dentist.
  • Don't come on an empty stomach; low blood sugar increases the chance of fainting.

At Dent32 we record your allergy and medicine history at the first examination and choose the anaesthetic and materials accordingly. Options for very anxious patients are described in sedation and general anaesthesia.

faq.q: My heart raced after a dental injection. Am I allergic?
faq.a: Most likely not. Palpitations are usually the few-minute effect of the adrenaline in the anaesthetic. If you had hives, facial swelling or breathlessness, be sure to tell your dentist.

faq.q: Can local anaesthetic allergy be tested?
faq.a: Yes. If true allergy is suspected, an allergy and immunology doctor can carry out skin and challenge tests, and a safe anaesthetic is chosen based on the results.

faq.q: I'm allergic to latex. Can I have dental treatment?
faq.a: Yes. Mention it when booking; treatment is done with latex-free gloves and materials.

title: What smoking does to your teeth and gums: stains, gum disease and your mouth after quitting
desc: How cigarettes, e-cigarettes and shisha affect teeth, gums and healing: stains, gum disease that hides bleeding, implant risk, mouth cancer, and what changes after you quit.
seoTitle: What smoking does to your teeth and gums | Dent32
seoDesc: How cigarettes, e-cigarettes and shisha affect teeth, gums and healing: stains, gum disease, implant risk and what changes after you quit.
lead: Smoking's effect on the mouth goes far beyond yellow stains. Tobacco sharply increases the risk of gum disease while hiding its most important warning sign, bleeding. It slows healing after extractions, implants and gum treatment, and raises the risk of mouth cancer. E-cigarettes and shisha aren't harmless for the mouth either. The good news: once you quit, the tissues of the mouth start to recover and treatments have a better chance of success.

sections.h: Effects of smoking in the mouth
sections.html:
EffectWhat happens
StainingTar and nicotine leave yellow-brown stains on teeth
Gum diseaseHigher risk, faster progression, weaker response to treatment
Hidden bleedingNicotine narrows blood vessels, so gums bleed less even when diseased
Slow healingHealing after extractions, implants and surgery is delayed; dry socket is more likely
Bad breath and loss of tasteThe mouth dries out; taste and smell weaken
Mouth cancerTobacco is one of the main risk factors for mouth cancer
Changes on the palateWith pipes and heavy smoking, red dots on a white background on the palate

sections.h: Gums that don't bleed may not be healthy
sections.html:
In smokers, gum disease progresses quietly. Because nicotine reduces blood flow in the gums, they look paler and don't bleed when brushed, so the person assumes all is well. Bone loss may be continuing underneath. That's why regular gum measurements and X-ray checks matter even more for smokers. See gum inflammation, loose teeth in adults.

In short

In a smoker, gums that don't bleed aren't necessarily healthy. Nicotine suppresses bleeding, so gum disease can progress without symptoms.

• Extractions: Dry socket is more likely; don't smoke in the first days. See after a tooth extraction.
  • Implants: Higher risk of failure to fuse and of inflammation around the implant in later years. See smoking after implants, implant failure.
  • Gum treatment: Healing after deep cleaning is more limited; adding support to quit improves results.
  • Cosmetic treatment: Colour returns faster after whitening; composite fillings and bonding stain sooner. See why teeth turn yellow.

E-cigarettes contain no tar but do contain nicotine; they can cause dry mouth, gum irritation and delayed healing. Flavoured liquids may raise decay risk. Shisha adds the combustion products of charcoal to tobacco, and a single session involves inhaling smoke for much longer. None of these is considered a safe alternative for the mouth.

sections.h: What changes in your mouth after you quit
sections.html:
• Taste and smell start to improve within days.
  • As blood flow to the gums increases, they may bleed more when brushed for a while; this reveals the gums' real condition and isn't harm from quitting. It settles with a scale and clean and regular brushing.
  • Gum disease progresses more slowly and responds better to treatment.
  • Mouth cancer risk falls over time.

In Türkiye you can call the ALO 171 quit-smoking helpline or ask your family doctor for referral to a smoking cessation clinic.

• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and floss or use interdental brushes once a day. See how to brush properly.
  • Check-ups and a scale and clean every six months. See scale and clean.
  • Have any sore, white or red patch that hasn't healed in two weeks examined. See signs of mouth cancer.
  • Drink plenty of water and take steps against dry mouth. See dry mouth.

At Dent32 we follow gum measurements and the soft tissues more closely in patients who smoke, and plan implants and surgery around their smoking. Don't hesitate to tell us you smoke; the plan is safer for it.

faq.q: Why don't smokers' gums bleed?
faq.a: Nicotine narrows blood vessels and reduces blood flow in the gums. So even with gum disease, bleeding is limited and the disease can progress unnoticed.

faq.q: Why do my gums bleed more since I quit?
faq.a: As blood flow returns to normal, existing inflammation becomes visible. With a scale and clean and regular care, bleeding usually eases within a few weeks.

faq.q: Do e-cigarettes harm teeth?
faq.a: Yes. Although they contain fewer of some harmful substances than cigarettes, they contain nicotine and can cause dry mouth, gum irritation and delayed healing.

title: Food keeps getting stuck between my teeth: causes, harm and how it's fixed
desc: If food packs into the same gap after every meal, the cause may be an open contact, a filling or crown edge, receding gums or decay. What to do and how it's corrected.
seoTitle: Food keeps getting stuck between my teeth | Dent32
seoDesc: If food packs into the same gap after every meal, the cause may be an open contact, a filling edge, receding gums or decay. How it's fixed.
lead: Getting a bit of meat or fibre caught between teeth now and then is normal. But if food packs into the same spot at every meal, won't come out without a toothpick or floss and the area aches, the contact between the two teeth has broken down. Trapped food inflames the gum and leads to decay between the teeth and bad breath. The cause can usually be found and corrected.

sections.h: Why food always gets stuck in the same place
sections.html:
• An open contact: The tight contact between two teeth can loosen over time; floss slips through with no resistance.
  • A filling or crown edge: A filling or crown that doesn't touch the neighbouring tooth, overhangs or has chipped.
  • Decay between teeth: Decay breaks down the surface and creates a gap. See decay between teeth.
  • Receding gums: With gum and bone loss the spaces between teeth open up and fibrous food catches. See bleeding and receding gums.
  • Drifting teeth: Teeth next to a missing tooth tilt and gaps open. See a single missing tooth.
  • Between an implant and a natural tooth: Natural teeth keep moving very slightly throughout life while an implant doesn't; over the years a gap can open between the implant crown and its neighbour.
  • A crack or broken corner: See cracked tooth syndrome.

• Gum inflammation, swelling and a feeling of pressure; sometimes a gum abscess
  • Decay between the teeth
  • Bad breath. See bad breath.
  • Bone loss and gum pockets if it goes on for a long time
In short

A gap that traps food at every meal isn't something brushing will fix. Until the reason the contact opened is found, the problem continues.

• Use floss or an interdental brush of the right size to remove the trapped food gently. See water flossers and interdental brushes.
  • Don't press toothpicks into the gum; they can injure it and widen the gap.
  • Rinsing with warm salt water soothes the gum.
  • If it turns into pain, swelling or bleeding, have it examined without delay.

CauseSolution
Old filling with an open contactReplacing the filling so it contacts the neighbouring tooth
Ill-fitting crownReplacing the crown. See pain and odour under a crown
Decay between teethRemoving the decay and placing a filling
Receding gumsGum treatment; interdental brushes to keep the gap clean
Gap between implant and toothAdding a contact to the crown or replacing the crown
Drifting teethOrthodontics, or an implant or bridge for the missing tooth

When a filling or crown is redone, the contact is checked with floss; the aim is for the floss to pass with slight resistance. See dental fillings.

At Dent32 we examine the area with a floss test, a clinical check and a bitewing X-ray, and explain the cause and options in writing.

faq.q: Is it normal for food to get stuck between teeth?
faq.a: Occasionally, yes. If food packs into the same spot at every meal, the contact may have opened, a filling or crown may not fit, or there may be decay between the teeth.

faq.q: Are toothpicks harmful?
faq.a: Pressed into the gum and used often, they can injure it and open the gap. Floss or an interdental brush of the right size is safer.

faq.q: Why does food get stuck next to my implant?
faq.a: Natural teeth move very slightly over the years while an implant stays put, so the contact between them can loosen. It can be fixed by adding a contact to the crown or replacing the crown.

title: Should you go to the dentist on an empty stomach? Food, medicines and preparing for your appointment
desc: Can you eat before a filling, root canal, extraction or implant, and should you take your medicines? Preparation for people with diabetes, those on blood thinners and sedation; what to bring.
seoTitle: Should you go to the dentist on an empty stomach? | Dent32
seoDesc: Can you eat before a filling, root canal, extraction or implant, and take your medicines? Preparing with diabetes, blood thinners or sedation.
lead: For most dental treatment done under local anaesthetic you don't need to come on an empty stomach; on the contrary, a light meal beforehand lowers the risk of dizziness and fainting. Because numbness can last a few hours, you may not be able to eat straight after treatment. If sedation or general anaesthesia is planned, your dentist will give you separate fasting instructions. Don't stop your regular medicines yourself, especially blood thinners.

sections.html:
ProcedureBeforeAfter
Examination, scale and cleanNormal mealEat straight away; waiting 30 minutes after polishing is advised
Filling, root canalA light mealWait until the numbness wears off
Extraction, implantA light mealLukewarm, soft food once the numbness wears off
Sedation / general anaesthesiaThe fasting time your dentist givesAs instructed

Eating while numb can lead to biting your lip, cheek or tongue. Details: how long dental numbness lasts, after a tooth extraction.

In short

Don't come to treatment under local anaesthetic on an empty stomach; a light meal is enough. Fasting is only needed for sedation and general anaesthesia, and your dentist will tell you how long.

sections.h: Medicines: take them or stop them?
sections.html:
• Blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs: Don't stop them yourself. If needed, your dentist will plan with the prescribing doctor. See dental treatment with heart disease.
  • Blood pressure medicines: Take them at the usual time.
  • Diabetes medicines and insulin: Don't skip your meal or medicine; booking after a meal lowers the risk of low blood sugar. See dental treatment with chronic illness.
  • Osteoporosis medicines: Always tell your dentist. See osteoporosis medicines and extractions.
  • Preventive antibiotics: If advised, usually taken 30–60 minutes before the procedure.
  • Painkillers: Don't take them beforehand on your own; you can if your dentist advises it.

sections.h: If sedation or general anaesthesia is planned
sections.html:
• Follow the fasting time (usually several hours for solid food and less for clear fluids such as water; your dentist will give the exact times).
  • Bring someone with you, and don't drive afterwards.
  • Wear comfortable clothes; no jewellery or nail varnish.

Details: sedation and general anaesthesia for dental treatment.

• A list or the boxes of all your medicines
  • Any X-rays or CT scans taken in the last year. See dental X-rays and CT scans.
  • Reports on any long-term conditions
  • Your known allergies. See allergy to dental anaesthetic.
  • Any treatment plan from your previous dentist
  • A list of questions you'd like to ask. See questions to ask your dentist.

• Brush and floss your teeth.
  • Avoid alcohol; cutting down on caffeine can ease anxiety.
  • Tell us if you're pregnant or might be. See dental treatment in pregnancy.
  • If you're fasting, discuss in advance which procedures might affect your fast. See does dental treatment break the fast.
  • If you're anxious about the dentist, mention it when booking. See fear of the dentist.

faq.q: Can I eat before a tooth extraction?
faq.a: Yes. A light meal is advised before an extraction under local anaesthetic; coming hungry can increase the risk of dizziness and fainting. If sedation is planned, follow the fasting time you're given.

faq.q: I take blood thinners. Should I stop them before an extraction?
faq.a: Not on your own. Most extractions can be done while you continue them; if a change is needed, it's decided with your prescribing doctor.

faq.q: Can I take a painkiller before dental treatment?
faq.a: There's no need unless your dentist advises it. In some cases a painkiller may be suggested beforehand; take your regular medicines as usual.

title: When do baby teeth fall out and adult teeth come in? What if a tooth comes in behind?
desc: The order and ages at which baby teeth fall out, the six-year molar, an adult tooth coming in behind a baby tooth, pulling a wobbly tooth, and what to do if teeth are lost early or late.
seoTitle: When do baby teeth fall out and adult teeth come in? | Dent32
seoDesc: When baby teeth fall out and adult teeth come in, the six-year molar, a tooth coming in behind, and what to do if teeth are lost early or late.
lead: Children's baby teeth usually start to fall out around age 6, beginning with the lower front teeth, and the changeover is complete by about 12–13. The order and timing can vary by several months, even a year, from child to child. The two questions parents ask most are about adult teeth coming in behind baby teeth, and the six-year molar that doesn't replace any baby tooth. Below is the timetable and when to see a dentist.

sections.html:
Baby toothUsual age lostAdult tooth that replaces it
Central incisors6–7Central incisors
Lateral incisors7–8Lateral incisors
First baby molars9–11First premolars
Canines9–12Canines
Second baby molars10–12Second premolars

Lower teeth often change a little before the upper ones, and girls may start slightly earlier than boys. For the first baby teeth coming through, see teething in babies.

sections.h: The six-year molar doesn't replace a baby tooth
sections.html:
The first permanent molar (six-year molar) comes in around age 6 behind the last baby molar, without replacing any tooth. That's why parents often take it for a baby tooth. It's a permanent tooth for life, and it's prone to decay in its first years. Protecting it with a fissure sealant is advised. See fluoride and fissure sealants.

In short

The six-year molar is permanent; nothing replaces it. Pay particular attention to brushing and sealants while it's coming through.

sections.h: If an adult tooth comes in behind a baby tooth
sections.html:
Lower front adult teeth coming in behind the baby teeth (on the tongue side) is very common; they're sometimes called “shark teeth”. If the baby tooth is wobbly, it usually falls out by itself within a few weeks and the tongue gradually guides the adult tooth forward.

If the baby tooth isn't loose at all, or the adult tooth is fully through and the baby tooth hasn't come out within a few weeks, the dentist may need to remove it. If the adult tooth still doesn't move into line, an orthodontic assessment follows. See early orthodontics for children.

sections.h: A wobbly baby tooth: pull it at home?
sections.html:
• A child can wiggle a very loose tooth with the tongue or a finger; it usually comes out by itself.
  • Don't use forceful methods like tying string to a door; if the root hasn't dissolved yet the gum can tear or a piece of root can be left behind.
  • Once it's out, have the child bite on clean gauze for 10–15 minutes; bleeding stops quickly.
  • Avoid hot and hard food for the rest of that day.

• A baby tooth lost early to decay or a knock: Neighbouring teeth can drift into the gap; a space maintainer may be needed so the adult tooth has room. See decay in baby teeth, dental trauma.
  • A baby tooth that stays well past the usual age: An X-ray checks whether there's an adult tooth underneath; it may be congenitally missing or impacted. See congenitally missing teeth, impacted canines.
  • If a tooth on one side has changed but its partner hasn't after more than 6 months: Have it examined.

faq.q: At what age does the first baby tooth fall out?
faq.a: Usually around 6–7, starting with the lower central incisors. A few months earlier or later is normal.

faq.q: An adult tooth came in behind a baby tooth. What should I do?
faq.a: If the baby tooth is wobbly you can wait a few weeks; it usually falls out by itself. If it isn't loose or doesn't come out, see a dentist to have it removed.

faq.q: My child is 8 and hasn't lost a baby tooth yet. Is that normal?
faq.a: For many children it is. If there's a clear delay compared with peers, or a tooth on one side has changed but its partner hasn't, an X-ray check is advised.

title: Impacted canine (eye tooth): causes, diagnosis and bringing it into place with orthodontics
desc: Upper canines are among the teeth most often impacted. Signs, why early diagnosis matters, removing the baby canine, surgical exposure and orthodontic traction, and options for adults.
seoTitle: Impacted canine (eye tooth): causes and treatment | Dent32
seoDesc: Upper canines are often impacted. Signs, why early diagnosis matters, surgical exposure and orthodontic traction, and options for adults.
lead: After wisdom teeth, the tooth most often impacted is the upper canine (eye tooth), affecting roughly 1–2% of people. Because the canine forms the corner of the smile and plays an important role in chewing, an impacted canine is usually not extracted; orthodontic treatment tries to bring it into place. If it's spotted early, a simpler intervention can help it come in by itself. That's why dental check-ups between ages 10 and 12 matter.

sections.html:
• Lack of space in the jaw
  • The tooth developing in the wrong direction, especially towards the palate
  • The baby canine not falling out on time
  • A small or congenitally missing lateral incisor (the canine uses this tooth's root as a guide). See congenitally missing teeth.
  • Family tendency

• The baby canine still in place after age 13–14
  • One canine has come in but the other hasn't after more than 6 months
  • A hard bump on the palate or lip side
  • The lateral incisor tilting or shifting

Diagnosis is made on a panoramic X-ray; a CT scan is usually needed to see the tooth's exact position and its effect on neighbouring roots. See dental X-rays and CT scans.

sections.h: What happens if it isn't treated?
sections.html:
An impacted canine usually doesn't hurt, but as it tries to come through it can press on and dissolve the roots of the neighbouring incisors. This can progress unnoticed and lead to loss of the incisor. Cysts can also develop around teeth that stay impacted for a long time. See tooth cysts.

In short

An impacted canine can damage neighbouring roots without causing pain. Having canine position checked at age 10–12 gives a chance for early intervention.

sections.h: Early intervention: removing the baby canine
sections.html: Between about 10 and 13, if the permanent canine's direction isn't too far off, removing the baby canine can help the permanent tooth correct its path and come in by itself. An appliance to create space in the jaw may also be used. This doesn't work in every case, but when it does, surgery isn't needed. See early orthodontics for children, when baby teeth fall out.

1. Orthodontic treatment starts and space is created for the canine.
  2. Under local anaesthetic, a small surgical procedure uncovers the tooth and a small attachment is bonded to it.
  3. Using a fine chain or wire attached to it, the tooth is slowly pulled into place over several months.
  4. Once the tooth is in the arch, it's aligned with orthodontic treatment.

The whole process usually takes 1.5–2.5 years depending on the case. Retention is needed afterwards to keep the teeth in place. See retention after orthodontics.

Orthodontic traction can also be tried in adults, but with age the chance of the tooth fusing to the bone rises and success becomes less likely. If the tooth is badly positioned or fused, it's extracted, and the gap is closed orthodontically or filled with an implant or bridge. If the baby canine is sound with a good root, it can be kept for many years. See orthodontics for adults, a single missing tooth.

At Dent32 we follow canine position at children's and adults' check-ups, assess with X-rays and CT scans if in doubt, and explain the options in writing. For cases needing surgery we plan together with the relevant specialty. See orthodontics in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: Will an impacted canine come in by itself?
faq.a: Early on, removing the baby canine and creating space can help it come in by itself. At older ages and with badly positioned teeth, surgical exposure and orthodontic traction are usually needed.

faq.q: Should an impacted canine be extracted?
faq.a: Usually not; the canine is an important tooth and orthodontics tries to bring it into place. Very badly positioned teeth or teeth fused to bone may be extracted.

faq.q: At what age should it be treated?
faq.a: Diagnosis around age 10–12 is ideal, when simple interventions work best. Orthodontic traction can also be done in adolescence and adulthood, but success becomes less likely with age.

title: Congenitally missing teeth (agenesis): options when a lateral incisor or premolar never came in
desc: Some adult teeth never form, and it's common. The most often missing teeth, how it's noticed, keeping the baby tooth, closing the gap orthodontically, a bonded bridge and an implant after growth.
seoTitle: Congenitally missing teeth (agenesis) | Dent32
seoDesc: Some adult teeth never form. How it's noticed, keeping the baby tooth, closing the gap with orthodontics, a bonded bridge or a later implant.
lead: In some people one or more adult teeth never form; this is called tooth agenesis. Leaving wisdom teeth aside, studies put it at roughly 2–10% of people having at least one congenitally missing adult tooth. The teeth most often missing are the lower second premolars and the upper lateral incisors. It's usually noticed when a baby tooth doesn't fall out on time, or on an X-ray in childhood. The treatment option depends on age, which tooth is missing and the space in the jaw; ideally the decision is made before growth ends.

sections.html:
• A baby tooth that falls out much later than in peers, or never becomes loose. See when baby teeth fall out.
  • Unexpected gaps between the front teeth
  • A lateral incisor on one side but not the other, or one that is very small and pointed
  • No tooth bud visible on a panoramic X-ray

Diagnosis is confirmed by X-ray. Several missing teeth can be linked to certain syndromes, in which case a broader assessment is needed. A missing lateral incisor can also lead to an impacted canine; see impacted canines.

A baby tooth with no adult tooth beneath it, especially in the lower premolar area, can be used for many years, sometimes well into adulthood, as long as its root stays sound. It should be protected from decay and checked regularly. Over time its root may dissolve, it may loosen or sit lower than the teeth around it; other options are then considered.

In short

A sound baby tooth with no successor can be kept for as long as its root allows. A decision to extract it should be made together with the plan for afterwards.

OptionSuitable forNote
Closing the gap with orthodonticsCrowded mouths, especially in growing childrenIf a lateral incisor is missing, the canine can be moved forward and reshaped
Keeping the space for a later implantCases where the space is to be keptImplants are placed after growth, usually from 18
Bonded (winged) bridgeFront teeth, without cutting the neighboursUntil implant age in young people, or long term
Reshaping with bondingA small or pointed lateral incisorSize and shape corrected without cutting the tooth
Removable temporary dentureChildren who are still growingTemporary solution

Details: a single missing tooth, implant or bridge, what is bonding.

Deciding early in children keeps options such as orthodontic gap closure open. If the space is to be kept for an implant, the teeth mustn't drift into it and there must be enough room between the roots; this is usually achieved with orthodontics. An implant placed while the jaw is still growing can end up higher than the other teeth over time, because the natural teeth keep developing. That's why implants wait until growth is complete. See early orthodontics for children.

When the absence is noticed in adulthood or the baby tooth is lost, implants, bridges or orthodontics combined with an implant are considered. Bone in the gap may have thinned over the years; this is checked on a CT scan and a bone graft planned if needed. See dental implants in Beylikdüzü, orthodontics for adults.

faq.q: Which teeth are most often congenitally missing?
faq.a: Apart from wisdom teeth, the lower second premolars and upper lateral incisors are most often missing.

faq.q: Should the baby tooth in place of a missing adult tooth be extracted?
faq.a: If its root is sound and it works well, it's usually kept. If extraction is needed, the plan for afterwards (orthodontics, an implant or a bridge) should be decided first.

faq.q: Can my child have an implant?
faq.a: Implants aren't advised while the jaw is still growing; they usually wait until 18 or later. Until then a bonded bridge or temporary denture can be used.

title: Tongue-tie and lip-tie: breastfeeding in babies, speech in children and the gap between front teeth
desc: When do tongue-tie (ankyloglossia) and an upper lip-tie cause problems? Breastfeeding difficulty, speech, a gap between the teeth; assessment, and how a snip or frenectomy is done if needed.
seoTitle: Tongue-tie and lip-tie: feeding, speech and treatment | Dent32
seoDesc: When do tongue-tie and lip-tie cause problems? Breastfeeding difficulty, speech, a gap between the teeth, and how a frenectomy is done.
lead: The thin band of tissue under the tongue is the lingual frenum, and the band joining the upper lip to the gum is the labial frenum. Everyone has them; in some babies and children they are short, thick or attach very close to the teeth. A short tongue-tie (ankyloglossia) can make breastfeeding difficult in babies and some sounds harder for older children; a prominent lip-tie may be linked to a gap between the upper front teeth. Not every short frenum needs treatment; the decision depends on how the tongue and lip function.

sections.html:
• In babies: Difficulty latching, slow weight gain despite frequent long feeds, clicking during feeds; nipple pain and sores for the mother.
  • In children: The tongue can't stick out past the lips or forms a heart shape when it does, can't reach the palate, and some sounds (especially r, l, t, d) are difficult.
  • In adults: Restricted tongue movement, difficulty cleaning under the tongue, sometimes problems with denture fit.

Breastfeeding difficulties have many other possible causes; assessment should involve the paediatrician and a lactation consultant.

sections.h: Lip-tie and a gap between the front teeth
sections.html:
A gap between the upper front teeth as they come in is normal in children and usually closes by itself when the permanent canines erupt (age 11–13). If the lip-tie extends between the teeth and the gap persists after the canines are through, a lip-tie procedure may be considered along with orthodontic treatment. It's usually done after the gap has been closed orthodontically. For gaps in adults, see bonding and closing gaps between teeth.

In short

In children a gap between the upper front teeth is usually normal and closes when the canines come in. Lip-tie treatment generally waits until then.

What matters is less how the frenum looks than how freely the tongue and lip move: the tongue's movement forwards, upwards and sideways, and its function during sucking or speech. Observing a feed in babies and a speech assessment in children are important. If a frenum looks short but doesn't affect function, no treatment is needed.

sections.h: If treatment is needed, how is it done?
sections.html:
• Frenotomy (newborns and young babies): A quick snip that releases a thin frenum; it takes seconds, usually needs no stitches and the baby can feed straight afterwards.
  • Frenectomy / frenuloplasty (older children and adults): Releasing the frenum under local anaesthetic, with stitches if needed. Some centres use a laser.
  • Afterwards: Tongue and lip exercises are advised to stop the tissue reattaching; speech therapy may be added for speech problems.

Depending on the child's age, these procedures may be done by paediatric surgeons, ear, nose and throat surgeons or dentists. Don't decide on the basis of appearance alone.

• A short tongue-tie is not on its own a reason for late talking; late talkers need assessment by a paediatrician and speech therapist.
  • If there are breastfeeding problems, get support from a lactation consultant first.
  • Keep under the tongue and the front teeth clean; for brushing from the first teeth, see teething in babies.
  • Thumb-sucking and dummy habits can also affect how teeth line up. See dummies and thumb-sucking.

At Dent32 we assess the tongue and lip frenum at children's and adults' examinations, explain any functional restriction to the family and refer to the relevant doctor when needed. For children's check-ups, see dental care for children in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: What happens if a tongue-tie isn't cut?
faq.a: A tongue-tie that doesn't affect function causes no problems and needn't be cut. Treatment is considered if it clearly restricts feeding, speech or tongue movement.

faq.q: Does tongue-tie delay speech?
faq.a: A short tongue-tie can make some sounds harder but isn't on its own a cause of late talking. Late talkers need assessment by a paediatrician and a speech therapist.

faq.q: Is the gap between the front teeth caused by a lip-tie?
faq.a: In children it's usually part of normal development and closes when the canines come in. If it persists, an orthodontic assessment and, if needed, a lip-tie procedure are considered.

title: Do dummies and thumb-sucking damage teeth? When to stop and how to help your child quit
desc: How dummies and thumb-sucking affect teeth and jaws: open bite, crossbite, protruding front teeth. Up to what age it's fine, ways to stop and when to see a dentist.
seoTitle: Do dummies and thumb-sucking damage teeth? | Dent32
seoDesc: How dummies and thumb-sucking affect teeth and jaws: open bite, crossbite, protruding teeth. Up to what age it's fine and ways to stop.
lead: Sucking is a natural need for babies, and in the early years a dummy (pacifier) or thumb-sucking usually causes no lasting problem for teeth and jaws. When the habit continues past age 3, changes can appear: the front teeth not meeting (open bite), upper teeth pushed forward and a narrowing of the upper jaw. If the habit stops early these changes often correct themselves; if it continues after the adult teeth come in, orthodontic treatment may be needed.

sections.h: How sucking habits affect the teeth
sections.html:
ChangeWhat happens
Open biteThe front teeth don't meet when the mouth is closed. See open bite
Protruding upper teethThe thumb or dummy pushes the upper teeth forward and the lower teeth back
CrossbiteThe upper jaw narrows and the back teeth bite incorrectly
Tongue thrustThe tongue pushes between the front teeth when swallowing, keeping the gap open

How much effect there is depends on how long, how often and how hard the child sucks. A thumb or dummy in the mouth all night has more effect.

sections.h: Up to what age is it fine?
sections.html:
• 0–2 years: Sucking is natural and soothing. No lasting effect on the teeth is expected.
  • 2–3 years: Start cutting down.
  • After 3: The risk of changes to teeth and jaws rises; stopping is advised.
  • 6 and over (as adult teeth come in): Changes can become permanent; an orthodontic assessment is needed. See early orthodontics for children.
In short

Stopping the dummy or thumb-sucking around age 3 is advised. If it stops then, most of the changes correct themselves.

Dummies and thumb-sucking affect teeth in similar ways. The difference is how easy they are to give up: a dummy can be taken away at some point, but a thumb is always there, so thumb-sucking often lasts longer. There isn't enough evidence that dummies sold as “orthodontic” protect the teeth.

Don't dip dummies in honey, sugar or jam; it causes fast-spreading decay in baby teeth. See baby bottle tooth decay.

sections.h: Ways to help your child stop
sections.html:
• Cut down gradually: daytime first, then sleep times.
  • Notice when your child turns to sucking (boredom, tiredness, screen time) and offer something else to do.
  • Use praise and a reward chart; mark the days without sucking together.
  • Avoid punishment, teasing or shaming; they can reinforce the habit.
  • For thumb-sucking, a glove or plaster on the thumb at night can act as a reminder.
  • Don't push to stop during stressful times such as a new sibling, moving house or starting school.

• If the habit continues after age 4–5
  • If there's a gap between the front teeth or the upper teeth clearly stick out
  • If you notice a lisp or the tongue pushing between the teeth when swallowing

For thumb-sucking that continues after the adult teeth come in, an appliance fitted to the palate that reminds the child can be used. It isn't a punishment; the child's willingness makes success more likely.

faq.q: At what age should a dummy be stopped?
faq.a: Cutting down from around 2 and stopping around 3 is advised. If it stops then, changes in the teeth usually correct themselves.

faq.q: Does thumb-sucking ruin teeth?
faq.a: If it goes on long and often, it can cause a gap between the front teeth, protruding upper teeth and a narrow upper jaw. The effects can become permanent after the adult teeth come in.

faq.q: Is an orthodontic dummy better?
faq.a: There isn't enough evidence that orthodontic dummies protect the teeth. What matters isn't the shape but how long and how often it's used.

title: Dark gums and a black line around a crown: causes and solutions
desc: Why does a grey-black line or a bluish gum appear at the edge of a crown? Metal-ceramic crowns, gum recession, a darkened root, amalgam tattoo and metal-free solutions.
seoTitle: Dark gums and a black line around a crown | Dent32
seoDesc: Why does a grey-black line appear at the edge of a crown? Metal-ceramic crowns, gum recession, a darkened root and metal-free solutions.
lead: One of the most common complaints with crowns made years ago is a grey-black line where the crown meets the gum, or gum that looks purple-grey. Usually it's the metal framework of a metal-ceramic crown showing at the edge, or being exposed as the gum recedes. A darkened root in a root-filled tooth, gum inflammation and metal stains left from old amalgam fillings can look similar. Depending on the cause, gum treatment, replacing the crown with a metal-free one or gum aesthetic procedures may be needed.

sections.h: Causes of the black line and dark gums
sections.html:
CauseWhat it looks like
Metal-ceramic crownA thin grey-black line at the crown edge; light can't pass through metal, so the gum looks shadowed
Gum recessionThe crown edge and root surface that were under the gum become visible
Darkened rootThe root of a root-filled or dead tooth shows dark through thin gum
Metal postMetal inside the root gives thin gum a grey shadow
Gum inflammationRed, purple, bleeding gum at an ill-fitting crown edge
Amalgam tattooA permanent, flat, blue-grey patch on the gum (metal particles from old fillings or root canal work)

Natural pigmentation of the gum and brown patches in smokers also occur; these have nothing to do with the crown. See smoking and your gums.

If a crown edge overhangs, has a gap or is rough, plaque builds up and the gum becomes inflamed: red, purple, swollen and bleeding. This spoils the appearance and sets the stage for decay under the crown. The inflammation is treated first with gum treatment; then we look at whether the crown needs replacing. See gum treatment, pain and odour under a crown.

In short

Not every dark area at a crown edge is metal; inflamed gum also looks purple and dark. The cause has to be identified before the right treatment can be chosen.

• Replacing with a metal-free crown: Zirconia or all-ceramic crowns let light through, so there's no metal line at the edge. See zirconia or porcelain, types of dental crowns.
  • Masking a darkened root: An opaque framework, internal whitening of the root, or a fibre post instead of a metal one.
  • Gum graft: To thicken thin gum and cover a receded area. See gum grafts.
  • Correct placement of the crown edge: The new crown's margin is planned so it doesn't harm the gum.
  • Amalgam tattoo: Harmless; if needed for appearance, it can be corrected with a minor surgical procedure or a graft.

sections.h: What to watch for when a crown is replaced
sections.html:
• Once the old crown is off, the tooth and root are checked for decay and the root canal filling is assessed.
  • A temporary crown may be worn for a while to let the gum heal.
  • The shade is chosen with the neighbouring teeth, in daylight.
  • The new crown's fit at the edge and its contacts are checked. See sensitivity after a crown.

For how long zirconia crowns last, see how long zirconia crowns last.

faq.q: What causes the black line at the base of a crown?
faq.a: Most often it's the metal edge of a metal-ceramic crown showing, or exposed as the gum recedes. A darkened root and gum inflammation can look similar.

faq.q: Will dark gums go away?
faq.a: If the cause is gum inflammation, it improves with treatment. If it's metal or a darkened root, it won't go away unless the crown is replaced with a metal-free one or the root is masked.

faq.q: Can zirconia crowns show a black line?
faq.a: Zirconia has no metal framework, so there's no metal line. However, if the gum recedes the root surface can show, or a darkened root can cast a shadow through thin gum.

title: A hard bony bump on the palate or under the tongue (torus): is it dangerous, does it need removing?
desc: Hard, smooth swellings in the middle of the palate or inside the lower teeth are usually harmless bony growths called tori. Why they form, when they're removed and which swellings need checking.
seoTitle: A hard bony bump on the palate or under the tongue (torus) | Dent32
seoDesc: Hard, smooth bumps on the palate or inside the lower teeth are usually harmless bony growths called tori. Why they form and when they're removed.
lead: If you've felt a hard, smooth swelling with your tongue in the middle of your palate, or on the inner side of your lower front and premolar teeth, it's most likely a torus, a benign bony growth. Tori grow very slowly over the years, don't hurt and usually need no treatment. People often notice one by chance one day despite having had it for years. Still, not every new swelling in the mouth should be assumed to be a torus; swellings that grow quickly, are soft, painful or ulcerate should be examined.

sections.html:
TypeLocationFeatures
Palatal torusThe midline of the hard palateA single flat or lobulated bony bump
Mandibular torusTongue side of the lower premolars and caninesUsually rounded bumps on both sides
ExostosisOn the bone on the cheek side of the gumSmall, hard lumps

Tori are covered by normal lining of the mouth; pressed, they feel hard and don't move.

The exact cause isn't known; family tendency plays an important role. Habits that put high forces on the jaw, such as clenching and grinding, are thought to be linked especially to mandibular tori. See clenching and grinding. Tori aren't cancer and don't turn into cancer.

In short

A torus is a hard, smooth, benign bony growth that stays the same for years and doesn't become cancer. Treatment is only needed when it causes a problem.

• If a denture is planned: When a denture or a prosthesis covering the palate can't sit over it. See dentures.
  • If it keeps getting injured: When the thin lining over it is repeatedly hurt by hard food.
  • If it makes speaking, eating or cleaning difficult
  • If it's very large: When it restricts tongue movement.
  • For bone grafting: Occasionally, the removed bone can be used as a graft elsewhere.

Removal is a minor surgical procedure under local anaesthetic: the lining is opened, the bony bump is reduced and stitches are placed. There may be tenderness and swelling for a few days.

• A soft, painful swelling on the palate: It may be an abscess from a tooth. See dental abscess.
  • A soft, bluish blister inside the lip: It may be a mucocele from a salivary gland.
  • A swelling that grows fast, bleeds or ulcerates: Always have it examined. See signs of mouth cancer.
  • A pimple-like bump on the gum: It may be a fistula. See a pimple on the gum.
  • A one-sided hard swelling that's new and growing: It should be assessed with an X-ray.

• Chew hard, sharp-edged foods (toast crusts, fish bones) carefully.
  • A sore on a torus usually heals in 1–2 weeks; if it doesn't, have it checked. See mouth ulcers.
  • If you clench, a night guard protects both your teeth and your jaw joints. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • If a denture is planned, show the torus to your dentist beforehand.

At Dent32 we assess tori and other swellings during the oral examination and use an X-ray if needed. If a torus affects a denture plan or your daily life we explain the options, and refer cases needing surgery to the relevant specialty.

faq.q: Is a hard lump on my palate cancer?
faq.a: A hard, smooth swelling that doesn't hurt, in the midline of the palate that has been there for years is most likely a torus and not cancer. Swellings that are new, grow quickly, bleed or ulcerate should be examined.

faq.q: Does a torus go away?
faq.a: No; it's bone and doesn't disappear. But since it usually causes no problems, no treatment is needed.

faq.q: Does a torus need removing?
faq.a: Only if it prevents a denture fitting, keeps getting injured, or makes speaking, eating or cleaning difficult.

title: Dental treatment from Yakuplu: dental hospital or dental clinic? Getting to Dent32
desc: For people in Yakuplu looking for a dentist: the difference between a dental hospital, a polyclinic and a clinic, where to go in an emergency, and how to reach Dent32 on the E-5.
seoTitle: Dental treatment from Yakuplu: getting to Dent32 | Dent32
seoDesc: Looking for a dentist in Yakuplu? Dental hospital versus polyclinic and clinic, where to go in an emergency and how to reach Dent32 on the E-5.
lead: If you live in Yakuplu, you can reach Dent32 on the E-5 service road in Beylikdüzü quickly by bus, minibus or car. Many people searching for a "dental hospital" are actually looking for somewhere to have an examination, fillings, root canal treatment, crowns or implants, and most of these are also done at a private dental clinic. This article explains when a hospital is the right place, when a dental clinic is, and how to get from Yakuplu to Dent32.

sections.h: Dental hospital, public dental centre and dental clinic: the difference
sections.html:
In Turkey, places that provide dental care go by different names. On the public side there are oral and dental health centres and hospital dental departments; on the private side there are polyclinics, dental clinics and single-dentist practices. The core treatments are largely the same everywhere; the differences are mostly in waiting times, the number of dentists, opening hours and which procedures are done under one roof.

Where?When is it appropriate?
Hospital emergency departmentRapidly spreading facial swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing, high fever, a suspected broken jaw, bleeding that won't stop
Public dental centreTreatments covered by SGK; there may be a wait depending on the booking system
Private dental clinic / polyclinicExaminations, fillings, root canals, extractions, crowns, implants, orthodontics and aesthetic treatment, with weekend and evening appointments

We explain the difference between a polyclinic and a clinic in more detail in dental polyclinic, clinic or practice in Beylikdüzü.

title: When can you smoke after a dental implant? E-cigarettes, shisha and healing
desc: How many days after an implant can you smoke, why smoking puts implants at risk, and are e-cigarettes and shisha any different? A practical timeline for before and after surgery.
seoTitle: When can you smoke after a dental implant? | Dent32
seoDesc: How soon after an implant can you smoke, why smoking puts implants at risk, and are e-cigarettes or shisha different? A practical timeline.
lead: After an implant, the later you start smoking again the better: don't smoke at all for the first 72 hours, stop for the first two weeks, and ideally quit for the first 2–3 months while the implant fuses with the bone. Smoking reduces blood flow, which slows both wound healing and the implant's integration into the bone. This article gives smokers a practical plan for before and after implant surgery.

sections.h: How does smoking affect an implant?
sections.html:
An implant succeeds when the bone fuses to its surface (osseointegration). Nicotine narrows blood vessels, and the carbon monoxide in smoke reduces the oxygen reaching the tissues. As a result:

  • the stitched area heals more slowly and the risk of infection rises;
  • the implant may integrate with the bone more slowly, or not at all;
  • in the long term, inflammation and bone loss around the implant (peri-implantitis) are more common.

Studies have found clearly higher implant failure rates in smokers than in non-smokers. That doesn't mean smokers can't have implants, but the risk needs to be understood and reduced. See can smokers have dental implants?

PeriodAdviceWhy?
1–2 weeks before surgeryStop, or cut down significantlyBlood supply to the tissues improves
First 72 hoursDon't smoke at allThe blood clot and early healing are most vulnerable
First 2 weeksDon't smokeUntil the stitches are out and the wound has closed
First 2–3 monthsQuit if you canThe period when the implant fuses with the bone
After the final tooth is fittedCut down and keep up check-upsTo lower the risk of peri-implantitis
In short

Don't smoke for at least 72 hours after an implant, preferably two weeks; the safest option is to stop for the first 2–3 months while the implant integrates.

sections.h: Are e-cigarettes, heated tobacco and shisha less harmful?
sections.html: E-cigarettes and heated tobacco products also contain nicotine, which narrows blood vessels. With shisha, the amount of smoke and the length of exposure are usually greater than with cigarettes. The sucking action can also dislodge the blood clot in the wound in the first days. So the same rules apply to these products during healing.

sections.h: If you can't stop smoking, how to reduce the risk
sections.html:
• Tell your dentist honestly how much you smoke before surgery; the plan is made accordingly.
  • Don't drink through a straw or spit in the first days; sucking and spitting can disturb the clot.
  • Rinse your mouth with water after smoking and clean the implant area as your dentist shows you.
  • Your GP or a stop-smoking service can help with support such as nicotine patches.
  • Keep up check-ups after the final tooth is fitted; inflammation around an implant is easier to treat when caught early.

We cover general care in the first days in the first days after an implant.

sections.html:
At the examination we assess smoking, gum health and bone together. If necessary, gum treatment comes first; the number of implants and the healing time are planned with this in mind. The process is explained step by step in implant treatment in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: How many days after an implant can I smoke?
faq.a: Don't smoke at all for at least 72 hours; waiting until the stitches are out, about two weeks, is safer. Stopping for the first 2–3 months while the implant integrates improves the chance of success.

faq.q: Can smoking make an implant fail?
faq.a: Smoking makes it harder for the implant to fuse with the bone and increases the risk of losing it. Not every smoker loses an implant, but the risk is higher than for non-smokers.

faq.q: Can I vape after an implant?
faq.a: E-cigarettes also contain nicotine, which affects healing. The rules for cigarettes during healing apply to e-cigarettes too.

faq.q: Does shisha harm implants?
faq.a: Yes. Exposure to smoke is usually longer with shisha, and the sucking action can put strain on the wound in the first days. Avoid it during healing.

title: How long do zirconia crowns take? Number of visits, try-ins and temporary teeth
desc: Zirconia crowns usually take 3–4 appointments over about 1–2 weeks. What happens at each visit, how long a try-in takes, living with temporary teeth and what can make it take longer.
seoTitle: How long do zirconia crowns take? | Dent32
seoDesc: Zirconia crowns usually take 3–4 visits over 1–2 weeks. What happens at each visit, try-ins, living with temporaries and what causes delays.
lead: For most patients, zirconia crowns are completed in 3–4 appointments over about 1–2 weeks. At the first session the teeth are prepared and an impression is taken; the crown made in the lab is then tried in once or twice, and cemented at the final visit. A root canal, gum treatment or a large number of teeth can lengthen the process. This article explains what happens at each stage.

sections.html:
AppointmentWhat happens?Approx. length
1. Examination and planX-rays, photos, discussing shade and shape expectations30–60 min
2. Preparation and impressionLocal anaesthetic, controlled shaping of the teeth, digital or conventional impression, temporary teeth1–2 hours (depending on the number of teeth)
3. Try-inChecking the framework or unfinished crown for fit, bite and shade30–60 min
4. CementationFinal checks, permanent cementation, bite adjustment45–90 min

There are usually a few days between lab stages. When the examination and preparation can be done on the same day, the total comes down to three appointments.

In short

Zirconia crowns usually take 3–4 appointments over about 1–2 weeks; the number of try-ins and any treatment needed first determine the time.

sections.h: Why the try-in matters and how long it takes
sections.html: At the try-in we check that the crown sits exactly at the gum line, its contacts with neighbouring teeth, the bite and the shade. Front teeth may need a second try-in for shade and shape; for back teeth one is usually enough. Each try-in typically takes 30–60 minutes. If you don't like something you see at the try-in, that's the time to say so; changes are difficult once the crown is cemented.

• Temporary teeth are fixed with a weak cement; avoid hard and sticky foods (chewing gum, Turkish delight, nuts).
  • If a temporary comes off, keep it and call the clinic; it can usually be refitted the same day.
  • Prepared teeth may be sensitive to hot and cold; this usually eases once the final crown is fitted.
  • When flossing around temporaries, slide the floss out sideways rather than pulling it up.

For sensitivity after crowns, see sensitivity and care after crowns.

sections.h: What can make it take longer
sections.html:
• A tooth that needs a root canal: the root canal is completed first.
  • Gum inflammation: an accurate impression can't be taken on bleeding gums; gum treatment comes first.
  • Many teeth / full mouth: if the bite height changes, it is tested with temporaries for a while.
  • Crowns on implants: the implant needs to heal first. See how long implant treatment takes.
  • Front teeth with a difficult shade match: an extra try-in may be needed.

sections.h: Do digital impressions shorten the process?
sections.html: A digital impression taken with an intraoral scanner removes the waiting time for impression material, makes rescanning easy and reaches the lab quickly. What really determines the total time, though, is the lab work and the number of try-ins. More: digital dentistry at Dent32.

We explain who zirconia crowns suit in zirconia crowns in Beylikdüzü and how long they last in how long zirconia crowns last.

title: Full-mouth implants: how many implants do you need for a full set of teeth? Options and cost factors
desc: A toothless mouth does not need 32 implants. Options using 2–8 implants per jaw, fixed and removable solutions, timing, and the factors that determine the cost of full-mouth implants.
seoTitle: Full-mouth implants: how many implants do you need? | Dent32
seoDesc: A toothless mouth doesn't need 32 implants. Options with 2–8 implants per jaw, fixed and removable solutions, timing and cost factors.
lead: When all the teeth are missing, an implant is not placed for each tooth; a full set of teeth can usually be restored with 4–8 implants per jaw. For removable dentures held by implants, 2–4 implants per jaw may be enough. How many you need depends on bone volume, bite force, the type of prosthesis and your health. This article explains the options and what affects the cost.

sections.html: A jaw normally has 14–16 teeth, but a fixed implant bridge can carry 10–14 teeth on a few implants. The largest back molars are also often not replaced, without a significant loss of chewing efficiency. So "32 implant teeth" really means treatment with a total of 8–16 implants for both jaws.

For full-mouth implants, fixed teeth usually need 4–8 implants per jaw and an implant-retained denture 2–4; the number depends on your bone and the type of prosthesis.

sections.h: What determines the cost of full-mouth implants
sections.html:
The cost can't be given accurately without an examination and CT scan. The main factors are:

  • the number of implants and the implant system used
  • additional surgery such as bone grafting or a sinus lift
  • the number of teeth to be extracted and treatment of infection
  • whether temporary fixed teeth are made
  • the material of the final prosthesis: acrylic, composite, zirconia on a titanium bar, or full zirconia
  • CT scanning and digital planning

For details, see what affects implant prices and zirconia on a titanium bar. At Dent32 the plan and cost are given in writing, item by item, after the examination.

If there is enough bone, the implants can be placed in one session, and in suitable cases temporary fixed teeth are fitted within a few days. The bone usually needs 3–6 months to integrate with the implants, after which the final prosthesis is made. Bone grafting or a sinus lift lengthens the process. See same-day implants and immediate loading.

Age alone is not a barrier. Well-controlled diabetes and blood pressure usually don't rule out implants; heavy smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, radiotherapy to the head and neck and certain bone medicines need extra assessment. More: who can have implants, safe dental treatment with chronic conditions.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many implants are needed for all the teeth?
faq.a: For fixed teeth, usually 4–8 implants per jaw, 8–16 in total for both jaws. An implant-retained removable denture can use 2–4 implants per jaw.

faq.q: Why does the cost of full-mouth implants vary from person to person?
faq.a: The number of implants, the need for extra surgery, the number of extractions, temporary teeth and the material of the final prosthesis all vary, so the cost is only clear after an examination and CT scan.

faq.q: Can full-mouth implants be done in one day?
faq.a: If the bone is suitable, the implants can be placed in one session and temporary fixed teeth fitted shortly after. The final prosthesis usually follows after 3–6 months.

title: Who is All-on-6 or All-on-8 for? How they differ from All-on-Four and how to choose
desc: All-on-6 and All-on-8 are fixed-teeth treatments using 6 or 8 implants per jaw. How they differ from All-on-Four, who they suit, their advantages, the process and maintenance.
seoTitle: Who is All-on-6 or All-on-8 for? | Dent32
seoDesc: All-on-6 and All-on-8 use 6 or 8 implants per jaw for fixed teeth. How they differ from All-on-Four, who they suit, the process and upkeep.
lead: All-on-6 and All-on-8 place 6 or 8 implants in a toothless jaw and fix a bridge on top. They are chosen for patients with enough bone, a strong bite, or who want the bridge made in sections. Compared with All-on-Four, the load is spread over more implants, and if one implant has a problem the bridge can usually still be used. This article explains which option suits whom.

sections.html:
All-on-FourAll-on-6All-on-8
Implants per jaw468
Bone neededLess; back implants angledModerateMore, across a wider area of the jaw
BridgeOne pieceOne piece or sectionedOften possible in 2–3 sections
If one implant is lostThe bridge may need replanningUsually still usableUsually still usable
Likelihood of extra surgeryLowerDepends on boneBone grafting / sinus lift more common
In short

All-on-6 and All-on-8 spread the load over more implants in patients with enough bone and a strong bite; All-on-Four reduces extra surgery when bone is limited.

sections.h: Who are All-on-6 and All-on-8 for?
sections.html:
• People with enough bone in both the front and back of the jaw
  • People who clench or grind (bruxism) or have a strong bite
  • Patients whose upper jaw bone is softer and needs more support
  • People who want the bridge in sections, making cleaning and future repairs easier
  • People who want a wider chewing area at the back

On clenching: teeth grinding and night guards.

sections.h: When does All-on-Four make more sense?
sections.html: If there is very little bone at the back, All-on-6 or All-on-8 may need bone grafting and a sinus lift. With All-on-Four, the back implants are angled, which often avoids this extra surgery and shortens treatment. Which option is suitable is decided by measuring the bone on a CT scan. More: All-on-Four, bone grafting and sinus lift.

1. Planning with an examination, CT scan and intraoral scan
  2. Any extractions and placement of the implants
  3. Temporary fixed teeth shortly afterwards in suitable cases
  4. A healing period of 3–6 months
  5. Impression, try-in and fitting of the final bridge
  6. Regular check-ups and professional cleaning

We explain how many implants a full mouth needs in full-mouth implants.

The underside of a fixed bridge should be cleaned with interdental brushes and a water flosser. Sectioned bridges are easier to clean. A check-up and professional clean every six months help catch inflammation around implants early. For people who grind, a night guard may be advised to protect the bridge. See how long implants last.
