At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Is All-on-8 better than All-on-Four?
faq.a: They suit different situations. With enough bone, All-on-6 or All-on-8 spreads the load over more implants; with little bone, All-on-Four reduces extra surgery. The decision is made by measuring the bone on a CT scan.

faq.q: Who is All-on-6 not suitable for?
faq.a: Patients with very little bone who don't want grafting or a sinus lift, people with conditions that impair healing such as uncontrolled diabetes, and those on certain bone medicines need extra assessment; other options are discussed with them.

faq.q: Is the All-on-8 bridge made in sections?
faq.a: Eight implants often allow the bridge to be made in 2–3 parts, which makes cleaning and any future repair of one section easier.

title: Problems with implant dentures: looseness, sore spots, worn clips, breakage and odour
desc: Common problems with implant-supported dentures and their causes: a loose denture, sore spots on the gums, worn clips (locators), loose screws, fractures, odour and inflammation around implants.
seoTitle: Problems with implant dentures | Dent32
seoDesc: Common problems with implant dentures: looseness, sore spots, worn clips, loose screws, fractures, odour and inflammation around implants.
lead: The most common problems with implant dentures are looseness as the clips wear, sore spots on the gums, loose screws in fixed bridges, chipped or broken teeth, and odour and inflammation where cleaning is difficult. Most are solved with simple adjustments or part replacement, and coming in early protects both the denture and the implants. This article covers the signs and what to do.

sections.html:
SignLikely causeWhat is usually done?
Removable denture doesn't hold as wellWorn clip (locator) insertsReplacing the plastic inserts
Denture rubs the gum in one spotGradual change in bone and gum shapeAdjusting the fitting surface or relining
Clicking or slight movement in a fixed bridgeLoose screwChecking and tightening or replacing the screw
Chipped or cracked denture toothExcess force, grinding, hard foodRepair; a night guard if needed
Bad smell, bleedingBuild-up under the bridge, inflammation around implantsProfessional cleaning, treating inflammation, improving home care
Pain or swelling at an implantPeri-implantitis or infectionExamination, X-ray and treatment
In short

Most implant denture problems are solved by replacing clips, checking screws, adjusting the denture or professional cleaning; pain, swelling and bleeding can signal inflammation around an implant.

In implant-retained removable dentures, the plastic parts that provide grip wear a little each time the denture is taken out and put in. Depending on use, they usually need replacing every 6–18 months. It's a quick procedure and doesn't require a new denture. Taking the denture out at night and cleaning it also protects both the gums and the parts. More: what is an implant-supported denture.

sections.h: Loose screws and breakage in fixed bridges
sections.html: In screw-retained fixed bridges, a slight clicking or movement when chewing usually means a screw has loosened. Don't wait when you notice it: a loose screw can eventually break or strain the implant components. Teeth break more often on acrylic bridges than on zirconia; for people who grind, a night guard lowers the risk. On materials: zirconia on a titanium bar.

sections.h: Odour, bleeding and inflammation around implants
sections.html: If the underside of a fixed bridge and the area around the implants aren't cleaned well, food debris and plaque build up. The first signs are odour, bleeding when brushing and redness of the gums. Left untreated, bone loss around the implants (peri-implantitis) can develop. Interdental brushes, a water flosser and superfloss, plus a professional clean every six months, greatly reduce this risk. See how long implants last and peri-implantitis.

sections.h: When to come in without waiting
sections.html:
• Swelling, pus or fever at an implant
  • The denture suddenly becoming noticeably loose
  • Part of a fixed bridge coming off
  • A feeling that one implant is moving on its own

We can also examine and maintain dentures made at another clinic; if possible, bring documents showing the implant brand and sizes.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Why is my implant denture loose?
faq.a: In removable dentures the most common cause is worn clip inserts; in fixed bridges, a loose screw. Both are usually fixed with a short procedure.

faq.q: How often do the clips need replacing?
faq.a: Usually every 6–18 months, depending on use. Replacing them doesn't require a new denture.

faq.q: Can you maintain an implant denture made elsewhere?
faq.a: Yes. Examination, cleaning and many adjustments are possible. Replacing parts requires knowing the implant brand and size, so bring any documents you have.

faq.q: There's a smell from under my fixed bridge. What should I do?
faq.a: There may be build-up under the bridge or gum inflammation. You need a professional clean and examination; using interdental brushes and a water flosser at home prevents it coming back.

title: How to relieve toothache: what to do at home, what to avoid and when it's urgent
desc: First aid for toothache at home: painkillers, salt water, cold compresses. Why putting aspirin on the tooth, hot compresses and self-prescribed antibiotics do harm. Urgent warning signs.
seoTitle: How to relieve toothache at home, and when it's urgent | Dent32
seoDesc: First aid for toothache: painkillers, salt water, cold compresses. Why aspirin on the tooth and self-prescribed antibiotics do harm, and urgent signs.
lead: You can ease toothache temporarily at home: a suitable painkiller taken as directed on the leaflet, rinsing with warm salt water, cold on the outside of the cheek if it's swollen, and lying with your head raised all help. But none of these removes the cause; decay, nerve inflammation or an abscess can only be treated by a dentist. This article covers what is safe to do at home, what to avoid and when to seek help straight away.

sections.h: What you can safely do at home
sections.html:
1. Painkiller: take a painkiller you have used before without problems, without exceeding the dose on the leaflet. If you have stomach, kidney or heart problems, take blood thinners or are pregnant, ask a pharmacist or doctor which medicine is suitable first.
  2. Warm salt water: add half a teaspoon of salt to a glass of warm water and rinse gently; it clears away food debris.
  3. Floss: food trapped next to the painful tooth can make pain worse; remove it gently.
  4. Cold: if your cheek is swollen, wrap ice in a cloth and apply it to the outside for 10–15 minutes at a time.
  5. Head raised: propping your head up on a pillow at night can reduce throbbing.
In short

Painkillers, warm salt water and, if there's swelling, cold on the outside give temporary relief; to remove the cause you need to see a dentist.

• Putting aspirin on the tooth or gum: it causes a chemical burn in the mouth.
  • Hot compresses on the cheek: if there is infection, they can help swelling spread.
  • Antibiotics on your own: antibiotics don't relieve pain from nerve inflammation, and unnecessary use encourages resistance. More: do antibiotics cure toothache?
  • Alcohol or long-term clove oil: they can irritate the gums and mask the problem.
  • Cancelling your appointment because the pain stopped: pain can stop when the nerve dies, while the infection carries on quietly.

sections.h: What the type of pain tells you
sections.html:
Type of painPossible cause
A twinge with cold or sweet things that fades in secondsDecay, exposed root surface, sensitivity
Long-lasting throbbing that gets worse with heat and wakes you at nightNerve inflammation (pulpitis); often needs root canal treatment
Pain on biting, the tooth feeling 'longer'Inflammation at the root tip, cracked tooth
An ache in several upper back teeth that worsens when you bend downPossibly sinusitis. See can sinusitis cause toothache?
Pain spreading to the ear or templeReferred pain. See can toothache spread to the ear?

See sensitivity to hot and cold and signs and stages of tooth decay.

sections.h: When to seek help without waiting
sections.html:
• Swelling growing in the face, under the eye or in the neck
  • Fever, feeling unwell
  • Difficulty swallowing or breathing (go to a hospital emergency department immediately)
  • Pain that painkillers don't control and that keeps you awake
  • A broken or loosened tooth after an injury

For nights and weekends: toothache at night or at the weekend, dental abscess and facial swelling.

Dent32 is open seven days a week. If you're in pain, message or call us and we'll try to make room to see you the same day. At the examination we find the source of the pain and, if needed, do the first step to relieve it in the same session.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: What relieves toothache fastest?
faq.a: Taking a suitable painkiller at the leaflet dose and rinsing with warm salt water gives temporary relief. The cause can only be treated by a dentist.

faq.q: Will antibiotics help my toothache?
faq.a: Antibiotics don't relieve pain caused by nerve inflammation; they are only given when a dentist decides they are needed, for example for spreading infection. Don't take antibiotics on your own.

faq.q: Does toothache go away by itself?
faq.a: Sometimes, but that often means the nerve has died. The infection can progress quietly into an abscess, so you still need an examination.

faq.q: What should I do about toothache at night?
faq.a: Take a painkiller, lie with your head raised and don't use hot compresses. If you have spreading facial swelling, fever or difficulty breathing, go to a hospital emergency department; otherwise see your dentist the next day.

title: Can sinusitis cause toothache? Telling sinus pain from tooth pain
desc: Is pain in your upper back teeth from sinusitis or from a tooth? Symptoms, how to tell them apart, sinusitis caused by a tooth, and when to see a dentist or an ear, nose and throat doctor.
seoTitle: Can sinusitis cause toothache? | Dent32
seoDesc: Is pain in your upper back teeth from sinusitis or a tooth? Symptoms, how to tell them apart, and whether to see a dentist or an ENT doctor.
lead: Yes, sinusitis can cause toothache. The roots of the upper molars and premolars sit very close to the sinus, so when the sinus is inflamed you can feel aching and pressure in these teeth. Sinus pain is usually felt in several upper back teeth at once, gets worse when you bend forward and comes with a blocked nose. Clear pain in one tooth that worsens with hot or cold or wakes you at night is more likely to come from the tooth itself.

sections.h: Why does sinusitis make teeth hurt?
sections.html: The maxillary sinus lies just above the upper back teeth. In some people only a thin layer of bone separates the root tips from the sinus floor. When the sinus is inflamed and pressure builds, pain is felt in teeth supplied by the same nerves, even if there is nothing wrong with the teeth.

SignMay be from the sinusMay be from a tooth
How many teeth?Several upper back teeth togetherUsually one tooth
With movementWorse when bending forward or going downstairsNo clear change
Hot and coldUsually no effectSensitivity or lingering pain
Other symptomsBlocked nose, discharge, facial pressure, reduced sense of smellSwollen gum, visible decay or fracture
TimingAfter a cold or allergyWhen eating, at night
In short

Pain in several upper back teeth that worsens when you bend forward and comes with a blocked nose points to sinusitis; pain in one tooth that worsens with hot, cold or at night points to the tooth. An examination and X-ray settle it.

It can also work the other way round: infection in an upper back tooth can spread from the root tip into the sinus and cause one-sided, recurring sinusitis. Especially with one-sided, foul-smelling discharge and sinusitis that doesn't clear with treatment, the teeth should be checked. In that case the sinusitis may not fully clear until the tooth infection is treated. A panoramic X-ray or CT scan helps with the diagnosis. See dental X-rays and CT scans.

sections.h: Dentist or ear, nose and throat doctor?
sections.html:
• If the pain is in one tooth, worsens with hot or cold, or there is a visible problem with the tooth, see a dentist first.
  • If a blocked nose, discharge and fever are the main symptoms, see your GP or an ENT doctor first.
  • If pain continues despite sinusitis treatment, or recurs on one side, have a dental examination.
  • If you're not sure, a dental examination quickly shows whether the pain is coming from a tooth.

sections.h: What you can do in the meantime
sections.html: Drinking plenty of fluids, inhaling steam and rinsing the nose with saline can relieve sinus pressure. Use painkillers as directed on the leaflet. Don't take antibiotics unless a doctor advises it. For general advice see how to relieve toothache.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Which teeth does sinusitis affect?
faq.a: Mostly the upper molars and premolars, the upper back teeth. The pain is usually felt in several teeth together.

faq.q: How long does sinus toothache last?
faq.a: It eases as the sinusitis clears, usually within a few days to two weeks. If the pain continues after the sinusitis has gone, you need a dental examination.

faq.q: Can tooth decay cause sinusitis?
faq.a: Infection at the root tip of an upper back tooth can spread into the sinus and cause sinusitis. With one-sided, recurring sinusitis the teeth should be checked as well.

title: Can toothache spread to the ear, head and jaw? Referred pain and warning signs
desc: Why does pain spread from lower molars to the ear and from upper teeth to the temple? Telling tooth, jaw joint and ear pain apart, and warning signs of heart-related jaw pain.
seoTitle: Can toothache spread to the ear, head and jaw? | Dent32
seoDesc: Why does pain spread from lower molars to the ear or from upper teeth to the temple? Telling tooth, jaw joint and ear pain apart.
lead: Yes, toothache can spread to the ear, temple, head and jaw. Because the teeth and these parts of the face share the same main nerve (the trigeminal nerve), the brain can't always tell exactly where pain comes from; this is called referred pain. Problems in the lower molars and wisdom teeth in particular can feel like earache. The reverse also happens: jaw joint and ear problems can be felt as toothache.

sections.html:
SourceWhere pain may be felt
Lower molars and wisdom teethEar, in front of the ear, angle of the jaw, neck
Upper molarsTemple, cheek, under the eye, upper jaw
Upper front teethBridge of the nose, around the eye
Jaw joint (clenching)In front of the ear, temple, a general ache in the teeth
SinusSeveral upper back teeth
In short

Problems in the lower back teeth often refer pain to the ear, and upper back teeth to the temple and under the eye; an examination and X-ray show the source.

• From a tooth: worse with hot, cold or biting; you can often point to a tooth; may throb at night.
  • From the ear: a full feeling in the ear, reduced hearing, discharge, fever; starts after a cold.
  • From the jaw joint: pain in front of the ear when opening and closing, clicking, tired jaw in the morning, a clenching habit. See clenching and jaw joint pain.
  • From a wisdom tooth: swelling of the gum at the back, difficulty opening, a bad taste. See wisdom teeth.

sections.h: Caution: jaw pain can also come from the heart
sections.html: A heart attack or angina can sometimes be felt as pain in the left lower jaw or teeth. If jaw or tooth pain comes with chest pressure, breathlessness, cold sweats, pain spreading to the arm or nausea, especially if it started during exertion, call emergency services (112 in Turkey) straight away. This should not wait for a dental appointment.

At the examination each tooth is checked and X-rays are taken if needed. If a dental problem such as decay, nerve inflammation or a wisdom tooth is found, it is treated and the referred pain settles too. If no cause is found in the teeth, the jaw joint is assessed or you are referred to an ENT doctor. For first aid at home, see how to relieve toothache.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Why does toothache spread to the ear?
faq.a: The teeth and the area around the ear share the same main nerve, so pain from the lower back teeth can be felt in the ear. This is called referred pain.

faq.q: Can toothache cause headaches?
faq.a: Yes. Inflammation in the upper back teeth in particular can spread to the temple and head. Clenching can also cause morning head and jaw pain.

faq.q: How can I tell if my earache is coming from a tooth?
faq.a: If it gets worse with hot, cold or biting and there is no fullness or discharge in the ear, it may be a tooth. A dental examination, and if needed an ENT examination, will tell for sure.

title: How long does dental numbness last? Eating, drinking and what to watch after local anaesthetic
desc: Dental local anaesthetic usually lasts 1–3 hours in the upper jaw and 3–5 hours in the lower jaw. Eating while numb, lip biting in children, palpitations and numbness that doesn't wear off.
seoTitle: How long does dental numbness last? | Dent32
seoDesc: Dental anaesthetic usually lasts 1–3 hours in the upper jaw and 3–5 in the lower. Eating while numb, lip biting in children and lasting numbness.
lead: Local anaesthetic for dental treatment usually lasts 1–3 hours in the upper jaw and 3–5 hours in the lower jaw. In the lower jaw the main branch of the nerve is numbed, so the lip, tongue and half the chin can stay numb for longer. Not eating or drinking hot drinks until the numbness wears off prevents accidental lip or cheek biting.

sections.h: How long does the numbness last?
sections.html:
Type of anaestheticWhere?Approx. duration of numbness
InfiltrationMost upper teeth, lower front teeth1–3 hours
Nerve blockLower back teeth3–5 hours (lip and tongue)
Intraligamentary / single toothProcedures limited to one toothShorter

The duration depends on the drug used, the amount, your metabolism and the area.

In short

Dental numbness usually lasts 1–3 hours in the upper jaw and 3–5 hours in the lower jaw; don't eat or drink anything hot until it wears off.

• Don't eat until the numbness wears off; you could bite your cheek, tongue or lip without noticing.
  • Avoid hot tea and coffee; you can't feel the temperature and could burn your mouth.
  • You can drink water and cool or lukewarm drinks; take care on the numb side.
  • When you can eat after a filling depends on the type of filling. See dental fillings.

sections.h: Children: watch for lip and cheek biting
sections.html: Children may chew their lips or cheeks out of curiosity about the numb feeling, which shows up the next day as swelling and a sore. Watch your child after treatment and don't give food until the numbness has gone. For our approach with children, see dental care for children.

Most dental anaesthetics contain adrenaline, which narrows blood vessels and prolongs the effect. Some people feel a brief racing heart or shakiness, which usually passes within minutes. If you have heart disease, high blood pressure or a thyroid problem, are pregnant, or have reacted to an anaesthetic before, always say so before treatment; the drug and dose are chosen accordingly. See safe dental treatment with chronic conditions.

sections.h: If the numbness doesn't wear off
sections.html: Numbness lasting into the next day is rare. If numbness, tingling or loss of feeling lasts more than 24 hours, tell the dentist who treated you. Changes in sensation after procedures close to a nerve (such as removing a lower wisdom tooth) usually resolve by themselves within weeks, but they must be followed up.

Before starting treatment we ask about your health and any medicines you take. If you can still feel anything during the procedure, just tell us; we don't continue until the anaesthetic has taken full effect. If you're anxious about the dentist, see for people with dental anxiety.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many hours does dental numbness last?
faq.a: Usually 1–3 hours in the upper jaw and 3–5 hours in the lower jaw. It varies with the drug, the amount and the person.

faq.q: Can I drink water while I'm numb?
faq.a: Yes, water and cool or lukewarm drinks are fine. Avoid hot drinks and food until the numbness wears off.

faq.q: Can I have a dental anaesthetic while breastfeeding?
faq.a: Yes. Local anaesthetics used in dentistry are generally considered safe during breastfeeding; tell your dentist that you're breastfeeding.

faq.q: What if I'm still numb the next day?
faq.a: If numbness or loss of feeling lasts more than 24 hours, tell the dentist who treated you; it needs to be followed up.

title: Is pain after root canal treatment normal? How long it lasts and when to go back
desc: Mild pain and tenderness on biting for 2–3 days after a root canal is normal. Why it happens, how long it lasts, the second visit, temporary fillings, the final restoration and warning signs.
seoTitle: Is pain after root canal treatment normal? | Dent32
seoDesc: Mild pain and tenderness on biting for 2–3 days after a root canal is normal. Why it happens, how long it lasts and the warning signs.
lead: For a few days after root canal treatment, mild to moderate pain and tenderness, especially when biting, is normal and is usually controlled with painkillers. For most patients it eases noticeably within 2–3 days and is gone within a week. Pain that keeps getting worse, facial swelling or fever is not expected, and you should go back to your dentist.

sections.h: Why is there pain after a root canal?
sections.html: Root canal treatment removes the inflamed nerve tissue inside the tooth, but the tissues around the root tip can be affected by the procedure. If there was inflammation at the root tip beforehand or the tooth was very painful, tenderness afterwards may be a little more noticeable. This doesn't mean the treatment has failed; it's the tissues' healing response.

TimeWhat to expectWhat to do
First 24 hoursAn ache once the numbness wears off, tenderness on bitingPainkiller, don't chew on that side
Days 2–3Tenderness eases noticeablySoft foods
1 weekMost patients have no symptomsAppointment for the final filling or crown
6–12 monthsIf there was an inflamed area at the root tip, the bone healsFollow-up X-ray
In short

Mild pain that is worse on biting for 2–3 days after a root canal is normal; go back to your dentist if pain increases or you have swelling or fever.

Root canal treatment can be done in one or two visits. With two visits, the canals are cleaned and a temporary medicine is placed at the first; at the second they are filled permanently. The second visit is usually more comfortable than the first, and local anaesthetic is given again if needed. For the number of visits and the process, see root canal treatment in Beylikdüzü.

• Don't eat until the numbness wears off.
  • Don't chew hard food on that side until the final filling or crown is done; a root-treated tooth is fragile.
  • The temporary filling may wear a little; if it falls out or a large piece breaks off, call the clinic.
  • Don't delay the final restoration. Even a well-treated tooth can be lost to leakage or fracture if it isn't sealed.

sections.h: When to go back to your dentist
sections.html:
• Pain is getting worse instead of better
  • Swelling has appeared in the gum or face
  • You have a fever
  • Severe throbbing even without touching the tooth
  • The tooth feels 'high' when you bite (the bite may need adjusting)

If a root-treated tooth starts hurting again months or years later, see root canal retreatment.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many days does pain last after a root canal?
faq.a: Mild pain and tenderness on biting usually ease noticeably within 2–3 days and are gone within a week. Increasing pain or swelling is not normal.

faq.q: How long does a root canal take to heal?
faq.a: Pain and tenderness settle within a few days. If there was an inflamed area at the root tip, the bone can take 6–12 months to heal, which is checked with a follow-up X-ray.

faq.q: Do I need antibiotics after a root canal?
faq.a: Usually not. Your dentist will prescribe them if needed for spreading infection, swelling or fever.

faq.q: Do I need a crown after a root canal?
faq.a: For back teeth and teeth that have lost a lot of structure, a crown is often advised to prevent fracture. For front teeth with little loss, a filling may be enough.

title: Pain and sensitivity after a filling: how long it lasts and when it isn't normal
desc: Sensitivity to cold for a few days to two weeks after a filling is common. Pain on biting, the risk of nerve inflammation with deep decay, a high filling and when to go back.
seoTitle: Pain and sensitivity after a filling | Dent32
seoDesc: Cold sensitivity for a few days to two weeks after a filling is common. Pain on biting, a high filling, nerve inflammation and when to go back.
lead: Mild sensitivity, especially to cold, is common after a filling and usually settles by itself within a few days to two weeks. Pain when biting is usually caused by the filling being slightly high and is fixed with a quick adjustment. With deep decay, though, nerve inflammation can develop after a filling; pain that starts on its own, lingers or wakes you at night is the sign.

sections.h: What is normal after a filling?
sections.html:
SignPossible causeWhat is done?
A twinge with cold that fades in secondsPost-treatment sensitivity of the toothUsually eases in 1–2 weeks; a sensitivity toothpaste can help
Sharp pain on biting, tooth feels 'high'The filling is slightly above the biteA bite adjustment at a short appointment
An ache in the neighbouring toothContact point or referred sensitivityMonitored for a few days
Pain that starts on its own, lingers or wakes you at nightNerve inflammation (pulpitis)Examination; root canal treatment may be needed
In short

Sensitivity to cold for a few days to two weeks after a filling is usually normal; pain on biting suggests a high filling, and pain that wakes you at night suggests nerve inflammation.

sections.h: Why pain can continue with deep decay
sections.html: The closer the decay is to the nerve, the more likely the nerve is already inflamed. In this case the dentist places a protective liner near the nerve and monitors the tooth. Some teeth settle after the filling; in others the inflammation doesn't resolve and root canal treatment is needed. That's why your dentist may follow you up for a while after a deep filling. More: stages of tooth decay, when root canal treatment is needed.

sections.h: When can I eat after a filling?
sections.html: A white (composite) filling is hardened with a light, so it is set by the end of the procedure; you can eat once the numbness wears off. Avoiding very hot, very cold and very hard foods in the first days reduces sensitivity. More: dental fillings in Beylikdüzü, what is a white filling.

• Use a toothpaste for sensitive teeth; its effect builds over a few weeks.
  • Avoid hard-bristled brushes and brushing too hard.
  • Cut down on acidic drinks (fizzy drinks, lemon water).
  • Come for a check if sensitivity hasn't eased in two weeks or is getting worse.

For general causes of sensitivity, see sensitivity to hot and cold.

sections.h: When to come in without waiting
sections.html:
• Pain starts on its own and lasts for minutes
  • It wakes you from sleep
  • There is swelling of the gum or a fever
  • The filling has broken or fallen out. See my filling fell out

faq.q: How long does sensitivity last after a filling?
faq.a: Usually it eases within a few days to two weeks. Sensitivity lasting longer than two weeks or getting worse needs checking.

faq.q: Why does my filled tooth hurt when I bite?
faq.a: The most common reason is that the filling is slightly high. It's adjusted at a short appointment and the pain usually eases straight away.

faq.q: Will I need a root canal after a filling?
faq.a: Usually not. If the decay was very close to the nerve and the inflammation doesn't resolve, root canal treatment may be needed.

title: Pain and smell from a crowned tooth: how to spot decay under a crown and what's done
desc: What do a smell from under an old crown, a dark line at its edge, pain and bleeding gums mean? Decay under crowns, nerve inflammation, cracked roots and replacing a crown.
seoTitle: Pain and smell from a crowned tooth | Dent32
seoDesc: What do a smell from under an old crown, a dark edge and pain mean? Decay under crowns, nerve inflammation, cracked roots and replacement.
lead: Pain, a smell or darkening at the edge of a crowned tooth that starts months or years later usually points to decay starting at the crown margin, nerve inflammation in the tooth beneath, or a gum problem. A crown doesn't protect a tooth completely; if its edge isn't kept clean, the tooth underneath can decay. Caught early, the tooth can usually be saved; left untreated, it may be lost.

sections.h: Possible causes of pain and odour in a crowned tooth
sections.html:
SignPossible cause
Odour or bad taste at the crown edgeDecay at the margin, washed-out cement, trapped food
Darkening at the crown edge, a dark line at the gumAn edge exposed by gum recession, or decay
Pain with hot or cold, or at nightNerve inflammation in the tooth under the crown
Pain on biting, swollen gumInflammation at the root tip, a cracked root
Odour under a bridgeBuild-up under the false tooth, inadequate cleaning
The crown feels looseWashed-out cement, loss of tooth structure beneath
In short

Odour and darkening at a crown edge usually point to decay starting at the margin, and night pain to nerve inflammation in the tooth beneath; an early examination improves the chance of saving the tooth.

sections.h: How is decay under a crown detected?
sections.html: You can't see under a crown. At the examination the margin is checked with a probe, the gums are measured and an X-ray is taken. Metal-based crowns can partly hide the tooth underneath on an X-ray, so symptoms and examination findings are assessed together. See dental X-rays.

• Small decay at the edge: sometimes repaired with a margin filling while the crown stays in place.
  • Extensive decay underneath: the crown is removed, the decay cleaned out, the tooth built up with a filling if needed, and a new crown made.
  • Nerve inflammation: root canal treatment is needed; sometimes it can be done through the crown, but a new crown is often advised afterwards.
  • Cracked root: saving the tooth is often not possible; implant or bridge options are discussed.

For crown options see types of dental crowns; for implants see a single missing tooth.

sections.h: Protecting the tooth under a crown
sections.html:
• Brush the crown edge with the bristles angled towards the gum.
  • Use floss or interdental brushes every day; for under a bridge, use superfloss or a water flosser.
  • Have the margins checked with an examination and X-ray at least once a year.
  • If you grind your teeth, a night guard protects crowns. See teeth grinding and night guards.

For how long crowns last, see how long zirconia crowns last.

We can also examine and treat crowns made at other clinics.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Why does my crown smell?
faq.a: The most common causes are decay at the crown margin, washed-out cement and food trapped under a bridge. An examination and X-ray find the cause.

faq.q: Why does a crowned tooth hurt?
faq.a: Nerve inflammation in the tooth under the crown, inflammation at the root tip, decay at the edge or a cracked root can all cause pain.

faq.q: Can a root canal be done without removing the crown?
faq.a: Sometimes it can be done through the crown. If there is decay underneath or the crown would be weakened, replacing the crown is usually advised.

faq.q: Is a dark line at the crown edge decay?
faq.a: Not always; a metal margin exposed by gum recession can also look dark. An examination tells the difference.

title: How to get rid of gum inflammation: symptoms, home care, sore gums and treatment
desc: Gum inflammation (gingivitis) starts with bleeding when brushing, redness and swelling, and fully reverses in its early stage. What to do at home, why gums get sore and when you need treatment.
seoTitle: How to get rid of gum inflammation | Dent32
seoDesc: Gingivitis starts with bleeding when brushing, redness and swelling, and fully reverses early on. Home care, sore gums and when to get treatment.
lead: Gum inflammation (gingivitis) is the gums' reaction to bacterial plaque building up on the teeth: the gums turn red, swell and bleed when you brush. Caught early, it usually reverses completely within 1–2 weeks with proper brushing, cleaning between the teeth and, if needed, a scale and polish. Left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, where the attachment between gum and bone is lost.

sections.html:
• Bleeding when brushing, flossing or biting into an apple
  • Redness and a shiny, swollen look at the gum line
  • Tender gums that ache when touched
  • Bad breath and a bad taste in the mouth
  • The gum edge looking slightly detached from the tooth

Gum disease often starts without pain, so it can go unnoticed. Bleeding shouldn't be dismissed as 'brushing too hard'.

sections.h: How to get rid of gum inflammation at home
sections.html:
1. Keep brushing even if it bleeds: bleeding shows plaque has built up there. Brush twice a day for at least two minutes with a soft brush angled at 45 degrees to the gum line.
  2. Clean between your teeth: use floss or interdental brushes every day. Bleeding may increase in the first days, then eases within a week.
  3. Use mouthwash sensibly: chlorhexidine mouthwashes are used short-term on a dentist's advice; long-term use can stain teeth. Mouthwash doesn't replace brushing.
  4. Cut down on smoking: smoking masks bleeding and slows healing.

For the right technique: how to brush your teeth properly.

In short

Gum inflammation usually settles within 1–2 weeks with proper brushing and daily cleaning between the teeth; if there is tartar, a professional clean is needed.

CauseExplanation
Plaque and tartarThe most common cause; inflammation makes the gums tender
Brushing too hardIrritates the gums and can cause recession
Hormonal changesGums inflame more easily in pregnancy and puberty. See dental treatment during pregnancy
DiabetesUncontrolled blood sugar speeds up gum disease
Some medicinesCan cause gum overgrowth or a dry mouth
Poorly fitting fillings, crowns or denturesPlaque collects at the edges

sections.h: When should you see a dentist?
sections.html: If bleeding continues despite two weeks of regular care, if there is tartar, or if the gums are receding or teeth are loose, you need an examination. Tartar doesn't come off with a toothbrush; it needs a professional clean. If gum pockets have deepened, deep cleaning (root planing) is done. More: scale and polish, bleeding and receding gums, gum pockets and bone loss.
Gum disease has been linked with heart and blood vessel disease and with diabetes control. You can read more in the summary of Dr. Hüseyin Aşçı's DHA interview.

For the treatment process, see gum treatment in Beylikdüzü.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: How many days does gum inflammation take to clear?
faq.a: Early inflammation usually settles within 1–2 weeks with regular brushing and cleaning between the teeth. If there is tartar, a professional clean is needed.

faq.q: My gums bleed. Should I stop brushing?
faq.a: No. Bleeding shows there is plaque there; keep brushing gently and regularly with a soft brush. If it hasn't stopped in two weeks, have an examination.

faq.q: Which mouthwash helps gum inflammation?
faq.a: Chlorhexidine mouthwashes can be used short-term on a dentist's advice. Mouthwash doesn't replace brushing and cleaning between the teeth.

faq.q: Can gum inflammation make teeth fall out?
faq.a: Early inflammation doesn't. But left untreated it can progress to periodontitis, which causes bone loss and loose teeth.

title: How to heal mouth ulcers (canker sores): how long they last, causes and when to get checked
desc: Mouth ulcers usually heal by themselves in 7–14 days. Triggers, soothing remedies at home, sores caused by dentures or broken teeth, and warning signs for sores that don't heal in two to three weeks.
seoTitle: How to heal mouth ulcers (canker sores) | Dent32
seoDesc: Mouth ulcers usually heal in 7–14 days. Triggers, soothing remedies, sores from dentures or broken teeth, and warning signs for ones that linger.
lead: Mouth ulcers (aphthous ulcers, canker sores) are small, painful sores with a white-yellow centre and a red border, found on the cheek, the inside of the lip or the side of the tongue. Small ulcers usually heal without a trace in 7–14 days. Home remedies ease the pain while they heal. A sore that hasn't healed in two to three weeks, feels hard or doesn't hurt at all should always be examined.

sections.html:
• Minor injuries such as biting your cheek, brushing hard or sharp food
  • Stress and lack of sleep
  • Iron, vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency
  • Certain foods in some people (acidic fruit, chocolate, nuts)
  • Hormonal changes
  • Systemic conditions such as coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and Behçet's disease (investigated with frequent recurrences)

• Rinsing with warm salt water several times a day
  • Protective gels or pastes from the pharmacy that cover the sore
  • Avoiding acidic, spicy and hard foods for a few days
  • Using a soft brush; for some people toothpastes without sodium lauryl sulfate reduce recurrences
  • A painkiller as directed on the leaflet if pain is significant
In short

Small mouth ulcers heal by themselves in 7–14 days; salt water and protective gels reduce pain. A sore that hasn't healed in three weeks should be examined.

sections.h: Sores caused by teeth or dentures
sections.html: A sore that keeps coming back in the same place is often caused by a broken tooth edge, a rough filling, a brace bracket or a spot where a denture rubs. In that case it heals once the cause is removed. For a broken tooth see my tooth broke: what to do; for denture sores see dentures and problems with implant dentures.

Warning signWhy it matters
A sore that hasn't healed in 2–3 weeksOther causes need to be ruled out
A sore with hard, raised edges, or one that doesn't hurtCan be an early sign of mouth cancer
A white or red patch in the mouth that won't wipe offLeukoplakia / erythroplakia needs assessment
Many ulcers that recur frequentlyVitamin deficiencies and systemic conditions should be investigated
Fever, feeling unwell, difficulty swallowingViral infection or widespread inflammation

In people who smoke or drink alcohol, sores in the mouth that don't heal should be watched more carefully. A dental examination includes the soft tissues of the mouth; if needed, you are referred to an oral surgeon or the relevant doctor.

faq.q: How long do mouth ulcers last?
faq.a: Small ulcers usually heal by themselves in 7–14 days. Larger ones can take longer; any sore lasting more than three weeks should be examined.

faq.q: Are mouth ulcers contagious?
faq.a: No. Cold sores, the blisters on the edge of the lip, are caused by a virus and are contagious; the two are different.

faq.q: What should I do if I get ulcers often?
faq.a: With frequent ulcers, iron, B12 and folic acid levels and some systemic conditions should be checked; your GP can help. If a tooth is causing irritation, a dentist can fix it.

title: Why do adult teeth become loose? Gum disease, injury, clenching and treatment
desc: A loose tooth in an adult is often a sign of advanced gum disease. Other causes: injury, clenching, abscess, pregnancy. Can a loose tooth be saved, what is splinting and when is it urgent?
seoTitle: Why do adult teeth become loose? | Dent32
seoDesc: A loose adult tooth is often a sign of advanced gum disease. Other causes such as injury and clenching, splinting, and when it's urgent.
lead: The most common reason for a loose tooth in an adult is loss of the bone that holds it, caused by gum disease (periodontitis). Injury, clenching, an abscess at the root tip and hormonal changes in pregnancy can also make teeth mobile. If the cause is found and treated early, many loose teeth can be kept; waiting allows more bone to be lost.

sections.html:
CauseClues
Advanced gum disease (periodontitis)Movement in several teeth, receding gums, bleeding, bad breath, gaps opening between teeth
InjuryOne tooth after an accident or fall, sometimes displaced
Clenching / grindingWorn teeth, tired jaw in the morning, cracked crowns
Abscess at the root tipPain, swollen gum or a fistula (a pimple-like draining spot)
PregnancyTemporary slight movement with gum inflammation
During orthodontic treatmentSlight movement is expected and settles after treatment
In short

The most common cause of a loose adult tooth is bone loss from gum disease; treated early, most teeth can be kept.

If gum inflammation isn't treated, bacteria move below the gum line, pockets form between tooth and gum, and the supporting bone is gradually lost. This usually happens without pain; by the time a tooth is loose, bone loss is often advanced. Treatment involves measuring pocket depths, assessing the bone on X-rays, deep cleaning and, if needed, gum surgery. More: gum pockets and bone loss, gum inflammation.

sections.h: Can a loose tooth be saved?
sections.html:
• Treating the cause: a tooth won't firm up until gum inflammation, an abscess or excess force is dealt with.
  • Splinting: loose teeth are bonded to their neighbours on the back surface with a thin wire or fibre, spreading the chewing load.
  • Bite adjustment and night guard: load is reduced for people who clench and for teeth that hit first when biting. See teeth grinding and night guards.
  • Extraction and replacement: if bone loss is very advanced, the tooth may not be saveable; implant, bridge or denture options are discussed. See implant or bridge.

sections.h: When to come in without waiting
sections.html:
• A tooth displaced, pushed forwards or backwards, or knocked out after an injury (bring a knocked-out tooth in cold milk)
  • A loose tooth with facial swelling or fever
  • Mobility increasing quickly over a few days

For first aid after an injury, see the first 30 minutes after a fall or blow.

For the treatment process, see also gum treatment in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: Will a loose tooth tighten by itself?
faq.a: Temporary looseness after a minor knock or in pregnancy can settle by itself. Looseness from gum disease won't improve without treatment.

faq.q: Can a loose tooth be replaced with an implant?
faq.a: The tooth first has to be extracted and the gum disease brought under control. Whether the tooth can be saved is assessed first.

faq.q: How long does a splint last?
faq.a: Once the cause has been treated, a splint can be used for years with regular check-ups and cleaning.

title: Teething in babies: signs, order of teeth, how to soothe and caring for first teeth
desc: A baby's first tooth usually comes through around six months. Signs of teething, which symptoms shouldn't be blamed on teeth, safe ways to soothe, first brushing and the first dental visit.
seoTitle: Teething in babies: signs and how to soothe | Dent32
seoDesc: A baby's first tooth usually appears around six months. Teething signs, what not to blame on teeth, safe soothing, first brushing and first visit.
lead: A baby's first tooth usually appears around six months, most often one of the lower front teeth; anywhere between 4 and 12 months is considered normal. Dribbling, putting hands and toys in the mouth, fussiness and swollen gums are common signs. High fever, diarrhoea or a cough should not be put down to teething; ask your paediatrician. Start brushing as soon as the first tooth appears.

sections.h: In what order do baby teeth come in?
sections.html:
TeethApproximate age
Lower central incisors6–10 months
Upper central incisors8–12 months
Lateral incisors9–16 months
First baby molars13–19 months
Canines16–23 months
Second baby molars23–33 months

Timing varies between children; a few months early or late is usually fine. A child with no teeth at all by 18 months should be assessed. By about three years old, all 20 baby teeth are through.

• More dribbling and a dribble rash on the chin
  • Putting hands and toys in the mouth, wanting to bite
  • Fussiness and disturbed sleep
  • Swollen, red gums where a tooth is coming
  • A slight temperature (below 38 °C)

A temperature of 38 °C or more, diarrhoea, vomiting, a cough or refusing all feeds should not be blamed on teething; see your paediatrician.

In short

The first baby tooth usually appears around six months; dribbling, chewing and fussiness are normal, but high fever and diarrhoea should not be put down to teething.

• Gently massaging the gum with a clean finger or damp gauze
  • A teething ring chilled in the fridge (not frozen)
  • If pain is significant, a fever/pain medicine recommended by your paediatrician

Not recommended: amber teething necklaces and bracelets carry a risk of choking and swallowing. Numbing teething gels are not advised for young babies. Frozen, very hard teethers can damage the gums.

sections.h: Care once the first tooth arrives
sections.html:
1. Start brushing twice a day with a soft baby toothbrush as soon as the first tooth shows.
  2. Up to age three, use a smear of fluoride toothpaste the size of a grain of rice; from three to six, a pea-sized amount.
  3. Give only water after the last brush at night.
  4. Avoid putting your baby to sleep with a bottle. See bottle tooth decay.

sections.h: When is the first dental visit?
sections.html: The first visit is recommended when the first tooth appears, or by the first birthday at the latest. It's usually a short get-to-know-you and check: the teeth and gums are examined and parents get advice on brushing, diet and fluoride. More: when to take your child to the dentist for the first time, dental care for children in Beylikdüzü.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: At what age does a baby's first tooth come through?
faq.a: Usually around six months; anywhere between 4 and 12 months is normal. If there are no teeth by 18 months, an assessment is needed.

faq.q: Does teething cause fever?
faq.a: There may be a slight rise in temperature, but 38 °C or more should not be blamed on teething; ask your paediatrician.

faq.q: When should I start brushing my baby's teeth?
faq.a: As soon as the first tooth appears. Brush twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste.

title: Bottle tooth decay and cavities in baby teeth: signs, treatment and why baby teeth are treated
desc: Night-time bottles and frequent sugary drinks cause rapid decay in baby teeth. Early signs, whether baby teeth need fillings or root treatment, space maintainers after early loss, and prevention.
seoTitle: Bottle tooth decay and cavities in baby teeth | Dent32
seoDesc: Night-time bottles and sugary drinks cause rapid decay in baby teeth. Early signs, fillings and root treatment, space maintainers and prevention.
lead: Bottle tooth decay (early childhood caries) is fast-spreading decay that starts on the upper front baby teeth, especially in children who fall asleep drinking milk, formula or juice from a bottle. The first sign is chalky white marks along the gum line. Even though baby teeth will eventually fall out, they should be treated: they are needed for chewing, speech and holding space for adult teeth, and infection can affect the adult tooth beneath.

sections.h: How does bottle tooth decay start?
sections.html:
1. Dull, chalky white marks along the gum line of the upper front teeth
  2. The marks turning yellow-brown and the surface breaking down
  3. Teeth chipping and darkening, and the child reacting to cold or sweet things
  4. In advanced stages, pain, swollen gums or an abscess

Early white marks can be stopped with fluoride, so it's important to have them checked as soon as you notice them.

In short

Bottle tooth decay starts with white marks on the upper front teeth; early on it can be stopped with fluoride, while advanced decay needs fillings or root treatment of the baby tooth.

• Falling asleep with a bottle of milk, formula or juice (saliva drops during sleep and sugar stays on the teeth)
  • Frequent sugary drinks or snacks throughout the day
  • Dipping a dummy in honey or sugar
  • Teeth not being brushed regularly
  • Decay bacteria passing from parent to baby through shared spoons

SituationTreatment
White marks (early)Fluoride varnish, changes to diet and brushing
Limited decayFilling
Decay reaching the nerveBaby tooth root treatment (pulpotomy / pulpectomy)
Extensive tooth lossCrown for a baby tooth
A tooth that can't be savedExtraction; a space maintainer if needed

If a baby tooth is lost early, neighbouring teeth can drift into the gap and leave no room for the adult tooth. A space maintainer may be advised. For how we help children get used to treatment, see dental care for children in Beylikdüzü.

• Give only water after the last brush at night; don't put your child to sleep with a bottle.
  • Start moving to a cup from around one year old.
  • Limit fruit juice and sugary drinks, and cut down on snacks between meals.
  • From the first tooth, brush twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste.
  • Have the first check-up when the first tooth appears or by age one.

On fluoride and fissure sealants: fluoride and fissure sealants for children. On teething: teething in babies.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Baby teeth fall out anyway. Do they really need treating?
faq.a: Yes. Baby teeth help with chewing and speech and hold space for adult teeth. Untreated decay causes pain and infection and can affect the adult tooth underneath.

faq.q: Can breastfeeding cause decay?
faq.a: Breast milk alone is not the main cause of decay, but frequent and prolonged night feeds after teeth have come through can raise the risk if teeth aren't brushed. Regular brushing once teeth appear is important.

faq.q: Can a baby tooth have root canal treatment?
faq.a: Yes. When decay reaches the nerve, root treatment suited to baby teeth (pulpotomy or pulpectomy) can keep the tooth until it is due to fall out.

title: Fluoride varnish and fissure sealants for children: what they do, at what age and how often
desc: Fluoride varnish strengthens enamel and fissure sealants seal the grooves of back teeth against decay. At what age, how often, whether they are safe and what the visit is like.
seoTitle: Fluoride varnish and fissure sealants for children | Dent32
seoDesc: Fluoride varnish strengthens enamel and fissure sealants protect molar grooves from decay. At what age, how often, and are they safe?
lead: Fluoride varnish strengthens tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to decay; fissure sealants cover the deep grooves on the chewing surfaces of back teeth with a thin layer of filling material so food and bacteria can't settle there. Both are quick preventive treatments that need no anaesthetic and no drilling. Fluoride varnish is usually applied every six months depending on the child's decay risk; fissure sealants are placed when the adult molars come through, at around 6 and 12 years old.

sections.h: What is fluoride varnish and how is it applied?
sections.html:
Fluoride varnish is a concentrated fluoride material painted onto the teeth that sets quickly. It takes a few minutes and most children tolerate it easily. Afterwards, avoid hard foods for a few hours and don't brush that evening; normal brushing resumes the next day.

TopicInformation
When does it start?After baby teeth come through, depending on decay risk
How often?Usually every six months; more often for children at high risk
Is it safe?The amount is small and the varnish sticks to the teeth, limiting what is swallowed; it is safe under a dentist's supervision

The chewing surfaces of back teeth have grooves (fissures) narrower than a toothbrush bristle, and much decay starts in them. A fissure sealant covers these grooves with a flowable filling material. The tooth isn't drilled and no anaesthetic is needed: the tooth is cleaned and dried, the material is applied and hardened with a light.

ToothWhen it's done
First adult molars (six-year molars)About 6–7 years
Second adult molarsAbout 11–13 years
Deeply grooved baby molarsDepending on decay risk
In short

Fluoride varnish strengthens enamel and is usually applied every six months; fissure sealants seal the grooves of molars and are placed when the adult molars arrive, at about 6 and 12 years.

• Children who have had decay before
  • Children with deep grooves in their molars
  • Children who find brushing difficult or wear braces
  • Children who often eat sugary foods
  • Children with special care needs

sections.h: How long do fissure sealants last?
sections.html: Sealants can stay in place for years, but they can wear or partly chip off over time. They're checked at every visit and topped up if needed. A sealed tooth still needs regular brushing, and sealants don't protect between the teeth. For decay between teeth: decay between teeth.

sections.h: Fluoride at home: how much toothpaste
sections.html:
• Up to age 3: a smear the size of a grain of rice
  • Ages 3–6: a pea-sized amount
  • Spit after brushing; rinsing with lots of water washes the fluoride away
  • Parents should brush or supervise brushing until about age 7–8

For technique, see how to brush your teeth properly.

For children's check-ups and preventive care, see dental care for children in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: At what age is fluoride varnish applied?
faq.a: It can start once baby teeth have come through, depending on the child's decay risk. It is usually repeated every six months.

faq.q: Do fissure sealants damage the tooth?
faq.a: No. They are a flowable material applied without drilling, and no anaesthetic is needed.

faq.q: Is fluoride harmful?
faq.a: Fluoride varnish used in dentistry is safe at the right amount and frequency. At home, use the right amount of fluoride toothpaste for your child's age.

faq.q: Can adults have fissure sealants?
faq.a: Yes, on deeply grooved molars without decay in adults at high risk of decay.

title: Electric or manual toothbrush? Can a water flosser replace dental floss?
desc: Do electric toothbrushes remove more plaque, which type to choose and who benefits most? What a water flosser does and why it matters for people with implants, bridges and braces.
seoTitle: Electric or manual toothbrush? | Dent32
seoDesc: Do electric toothbrushes remove more plaque, and which to choose? What a water flosser does and why it helps with implants, bridges and braces.
lead: Used with good technique, a manual brush cleans teeth well; but studies show that electric brushes, especially those with rotating-oscillating heads, reduce plaque and gum inflammation slightly more than manual brushes. An electric brush is particularly helpful for people with limited dexterity, people with braces and those who brush too hard. A water flosser doesn't fully replace floss, but it is a great help around implants, bridges and braces, where cleaning is difficult.

sections.html:
Manual brushElectric brush
Plaque removalGood if technique is rightUsually slightly more effective
Depends on techniqueHeavilyLess; the brush does the movement
Risk of brushing too hardYesPressure-sensor models warn you
TimingNoneMost have a 2-minute timer
CostLowDevice and replacement heads
In short

With good technique both work; an electric brush usually removes slightly more plaque and makes technique easier. A water flosser complements floss and is especially useful around implants and bridges.

sections.h: Who benefits most from an electric brush?
sections.html:
• People with braces (cleaning around brackets)
  • People with arthritis or limited dexterity
  • People who brush hard and have receding gums (with a pressure sensor)
  • Children and teenagers who brush too briefly (with a timer)

• Soft bristles and a small head
  • A pressure sensor and a 2-minute timer
  • Replace the head about every three months, or when the bristles splay
  • Don't press the brush against the teeth; hold it on each tooth for a few seconds and move on

sections.h: What does a water flosser do?
sections.html:
A water flosser uses a pressurised jet of water to remove food debris from between the teeth and along the gum line. It doesn't remove sticky plaque from tooth surfaces as well as floss, so it's best used together with floss or interdental brushes where possible. For people who can't use floss, it's a good alternative.

  • Implants and implant bridges: under the bridge and around the implants. See caring for All-on-6 and All-on-8.
  • Fixed bridges: under the false tooth.
  • Braces: around brackets and wires. See living with braces.
  • Gum pockets: care after gum treatment.

sections.h: Which is best for cleaning between teeth?
sections.html: Floss works best in tight gaps; interdental brushes are more effective in wider gaps and where gums have receded. We can show you which suits you at your examination. More: guide to brushing, flossing and interdental brushes.

sections.h: Scale and polish and check-ups in Beylikdüzü
sections.html:
Tartar doesn't come off with a toothbrush; a check-up every six months and a professional clean if needed are recommended. See scale and polish in Beylikdüzü.

faq.q: Can an electric toothbrush damage the gums?
faq.a: Not when used properly. Use a soft head without pressing; pressure-sensor models warn you if you press too hard.

faq.q: Can a water flosser replace floss?
faq.a: Not entirely. A water flosser is good at flushing out debris, but floss or interdental brushes remove sticky plaque better. Using both is ideal.

faq.q: Can children use electric toothbrushes?
faq.a: Yes, there are models with small heads designed for children. An adult should still supervise brushing.

title: Do whitening toothpastes and charcoal toothpaste work? Enamel damage and real whitening
desc: Whitening toothpastes reduce surface tea and coffee stains but don't change tooth colour. The risks of charcoal, peroxide and blue-pigment pastes, and dentist-supervised whitening.
seoTitle: Do whitening toothpastes and charcoal toothpaste work? | Dent32
seoDesc: Whitening toothpastes reduce surface stains but don't change tooth colour. The risks of charcoal and other pastes, and dentist-supervised whitening.
lead: Whitening toothpastes can reduce the surface stains left by tea, coffee and smoking, thanks to abrasive particles and some chemicals, but they don't change the tooth's own (internal) colour. Charcoal toothpastes have not been shown to whiten teeth, and very abrasive ones can damage enamel. To genuinely lighten tooth colour, you need whitening supervised by a dentist.

sections.html:
TypeEffectCaution
Abrasive (silica etc.)Mechanically reduces surface stainsHighly abrasive pastes can wear enamel over time
Low-concentration peroxideSlight lightening; limited because contact time is shortCan cause sensitivity
Blue pigmentLeaves a thin film for an instant optical whiteningThe effect is temporary
CharcoalClaimed to reduce surface stains; evidence is lackingCan be abrasive; most contain no fluoride
In short

Whitening toothpastes reduce surface stains but don't change the tooth's internal colour; charcoal toothpastes are unproven and can wear enamel.

• Abrasive particles can wear enamel and especially exposed root surfaces, which can make teeth look more yellow and cause sensitivity.
  • Most charcoal toothpastes contain no fluoride, so protection against decay is weaker.
  • Charcoal particles can lodge at filling edges and the gum line and look grey.
  • There are no reliable studies showing a whitening effect.

sections.h: Why toothpaste alone can't change tooth colour
sections.html: A tooth's colour comes largely from the dentine beneath the enamel. With age, enamel thins and dentine darkens; some medicines and a dead nerve can also discolour a tooth from inside. Toothpaste can't change this internal colour. For the causes of discolouration: why teeth turn yellow.

The gels used in in-clinic or at-home whitening penetrate the tooth and lighten its colour. Before treatment there is an examination, decay and receding gums are assessed, the gums are protected and sensitivity is managed. Fillings, crowns and veneers don't whiten, so the plan takes any restorations on front teeth into account. More: teeth whitening: in-clinic or at home, teeth whitening in Beylikdüzü.

sections.h: Choosing a toothpaste for everyday use
sections.html:
• Choose a fluoride toothpaste (usually 1000–1450 ppm for adults).
  • If you have sensitivity, use a toothpaste for sensitive teeth.
  • Consider using whitening toothpaste occasionally rather than all the time.
  • Avoid hard brushes and brushing too hard.

faq.q: Does whitening toothpaste whiten teeth?
faq.a: It can reduce surface stains from tea, coffee and smoking, but it doesn't change the tooth's own colour. For real lightening you need dentist-supervised whitening.

faq.q: Is charcoal toothpaste harmful?
faq.a: Highly abrasive ones can wear enamel and exposed roots, and most contain no fluoride. A whitening effect hasn't been shown scientifically.

faq.q: Do baking soda and lemon whiten teeth?
faq.a: Lemon acid dissolves enamel and baking soda is abrasive. The mixture can damage teeth and isn't advised.

title: Dental erosion (enamel wear): acidic drinks, reflux, symptoms and prevention
desc: Fizzy and energy drinks, lemon water and reflux dissolve tooth enamel. Signs of erosion, why you shouldn't brush straight after acidic drinks, prevention and treatment options.
seoTitle: Dental erosion: acidic drinks, reflux and prevention | Dent32
seoDesc: Fizzy drinks, lemon water and reflux dissolve enamel. Signs of erosion, why not to brush straight after acidic drinks, prevention and treatment.
lead: Dental erosion is enamel being dissolved directly by acids, without bacteria. Fizzy and energy drinks, lemon water, vinegar, acidic fruit juices and stomach acid (reflux, frequent vomiting) are the most common causes. The first signs are translucent edges on the front teeth, yellowing and sensitivity. Lost enamel doesn't grow back, but changing habits can stop erosion and worn teeth can be repaired.

sections.html:
• Translucent, glassy edges on the front teeth
  • Yellowing as thinning enamel reveals the dentine beneath
  • Sensitivity to cold, heat and sweet things
  • Cupping on the chewing surfaces of back teeth; old fillings looking raised above the tooth
  • Teeth getting shorter, small chips at the edges
In short

Erosion is acid dissolving enamel directly; it shows as translucent front teeth, yellowing and sensitivity. Lost enamel doesn't grow back, but the damage can be stopped.

SourceExamples
DrinksCola and fizzy drinks, energy and sports drinks, fruit juices, water with lemon or vinegar, wine
FoodsCitrus fruit, sour sweets, pickles and vinegar-based sauces
Stomach acidReflux, frequent vomiting, morning sickness
HabitsHolding drinks in the mouth, sipping all day, brushing hard straight after acid
Dry mouthSaliva can't neutralise acid. See dry mouth

1. Cut down on acidic drinks; if you have them, drink with meals and through a straw, and don't sip all day.
  2. Rinse your mouth with water after acidic food or drink.
  3. Wait 30–60 minutes before brushing; enamel softened by acid wears more easily if brushed straight away.
  4. Use a fluoride toothpaste and a soft brush, and don't brush hard.
  5. Foods such as cheese or milk, and sugar-free gum, increase saliva and help neutralise acid.
  6. If you have reflux symptoms (heartburn, sour liquid in the mouth), see your doctor; erosion continues until reflux is treated.

• Early stage: fluoride and sensitivity treatment, changing habits.
  • Loss at edges and surfaces: rebuilding with bonding (composite). See what is bonding.
  • Significant loss on front teeth: laminate veneers. See laminate veneers.
  • Advanced loss on many teeth: crowns and, if needed, restoring bite height. See full-mouth rehabilitation.

If wear comes with clenching, a night guard may also be needed. See teeth grinding and night guards.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Does eroded enamel grow back?
faq.a: No, enamel can't regenerate. But early on, fluoride and changed habits can stop it progressing, and lost areas can be repaired with bonding, veneers or crowns.

faq.q: Should I brush straight after an acidic drink?
faq.a: No. Rinse with water first and wait 30–60 minutes before brushing; acid-softened enamel wears more easily if brushed straight away.

faq.q: Can reflux damage teeth?
faq.a: Yes. Stomach acid can cause erosion, especially on the inner surfaces of the upper front teeth and on the molars. Treating reflux also protects your teeth.

title: What causes dry mouth? Medicines, conditions, effects on teeth and what helps
desc: Medicines are the most common cause of dry mouth. Less saliva means more decay, bad breath and denture problems. Causes, effects on teeth, what you can do at home and when to see a doctor.
seoTitle: What causes dry mouth? Causes and what helps | Dent32
seoDesc: Medicines are the most common cause of dry mouth; less saliva means more decay and bad breath. Causes, effects on teeth and what helps at home.
lead: Dry mouth (xerostomia) is reduced saliva causing stickiness, burning and difficulty swallowing and speaking. The most common cause is medicines: some blood pressure, antidepressant, allergy and water tablets can reduce saliva. Diabetes, Sjögren's syndrome, radiotherapy to the head and neck and mouth breathing can also cause it. Because saliva protects teeth, dry mouth markedly increases the risk of decay.

sections.html:
CauseExamples
MedicinesSome blood pressure medicines, antidepressants, allergy medicines, water tablets, bladder medicines; taking several medicines
ConditionsDiabetes, Sjögren's syndrome, some rheumatic diseases
TreatmentsRadiotherapy to the head and neck, some chemotherapy
HabitsMouth breathing, snoring, smoking, alcohol, not drinking enough water
TemporaryAnxiety, feverish illness, dehydration

Age alone doesn't cause dry mouth; it is more common in older people mainly because of the medicines they take. See dental treatment in later life.

sections.h: What does dry mouth do to teeth?
sections.html:
• Decay risk rises, especially at the gum line and on exposed roots
  • Bad breath becomes more noticeable. See bad breath
  • Oral thrush develops more easily
  • Dentures hold less well and sore spots are more common
  • Taste is reduced, and swallowing and speaking become harder
In short

Medicines are the most common cause of dry mouth; less saliva means more decay, bad breath and denture problems. Plenty of water, sugar-free gum and fluoride care protect the teeth.

1. Drink small sips of water often through the day.
  2. Sugar-free gum or lozenges (preferably with xylitol) stimulate saliva.
  3. Saliva substitute gels and sprays from the pharmacy give relief.
  4. Avoid alcohol-based mouthwashes; choose alcohol-free ones.
  5. Cut down on caffeine, alcohol and smoking.
  6. A humidifier in the bedroom can reduce dryness at night.
  7. Don't try to keep your mouth moist with sugary sweets or drinks; they increase decay risk.

With dry mouth, brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between the teeth matter even more. Your dentist may suggest a higher-fluoride toothpaste or regular fluoride varnish, and check-ups may be more frequent depending on decay risk. If you think a medicine is drying your mouth, don't stop it yourself; talk to the doctor who prescribed it.

• Dry mouth lasting for weeks
  • Dry eyes and joint pain as well (to check for Sjögren's)
  • Excessive thirst and frequent urination (to check for diabetes)
  • Many new cavities in a short time

faq.q: What condition can dry mouth be a sign of?
faq.a: It can be a sign of conditions such as diabetes and Sjögren's syndrome, but the most common cause is medicines. See your GP if it lasts a long time.

faq.q: What helps dry mouth?
faq.a: Sipping water often, sugar-free gum, saliva substitute gels and sprays, alcohol-free mouthwash and a humidifier all help.

faq.q: Does dry mouth cause tooth decay?
faq.a: Yes. Saliva neutralises acids and repairs enamel; when it's reduced, decay risk rises significantly.

title: What causes a white tongue? Coating, oral thrush and how to clean your tongue
desc: A white tongue coating is usually bacteria and food debris that clear with cleaning. How it differs from thrush and patches that won't wipe off, and how to use a tongue cleaner.
seoTitle: What causes a white tongue? Coating and oral thrush | Dent32
seoDesc: A white tongue coating is usually bacteria and food debris that clear with cleaning. How it differs from thrush, and using a tongue cleaner.
lead: A white tongue is usually caused by bacteria, dead cells and food debris building up between the small projections (papillae) on its surface. Dry mouth, smoking, mouth breathing and feverish illness make this build-up worse. Regular tongue cleaning and plenty of water usually clear it. A white coating that leaves red, raw areas when wiped suggests thrush, and white patches that won't wipe off at all need to be examined.

sections.html:
ConditionAppearanceWhat to do
Coated tongue (build-up)White-yellowish coating on the back and middle of the tongue that wipes offTongue cleaning, water, treating dry mouth
Oral thrush (fungal)Red underneath when wiped, sometimes burning; after antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures, diabetesExamination and antifungal treatment
LeukoplakiaA white patch with clear edges that won't wipe offAlways examine; biopsy if needed
Geographic tongueShifting red areas with white bordersUsually harmless; monitored
In short

A white coating that wipes off is usually build-up and clears with cleaning; patches that bleed when wiped or won't wipe off at all should be examined.

1. Place a tongue scraper or soft brush at the back of the tongue.
  2. Draw it forward with light pressure; don't press hard.
  3. Rinse the cleaner after each stroke; 3–5 strokes are enough.
  4. Do it once a day, ideally with your morning brush.
  5. If you gag easily, hold your breath, stick your tongue out and make short strokes.

Much of the odour-causing compounds in bad breath are produced by bacteria on the back of the tongue, so regular tongue cleaning can reduce bad breath noticeably. If it persists, other causes such as gum disease, decay or build-up under crowns should be looked for. See causes and treatment of bad breath.

• A white coating that hasn't cleared in two weeks despite cleaning
  • Patches that won't wipe off or bleed when wiped
  • Burning, pain or a sore on the tongue
  • New white or red patches in people who smoke or drink alcohol

If you have a dry mouth, see dry mouth for causes.

At the examination we share the findings, the options and the approximate cost in writing; you are under no obligation to start treatment afterwards.

faq.q: Why is my tongue white?
faq.a: The most common cause is bacteria, dead cells and food debris building up on the tongue's surface. Dry mouth, smoking and feverish illness make it worse. Tongue cleaning and plenty of water usually clear it.

faq.q: Tongue scraper or toothbrush?
faq.a: A tongue scraper cleans a wider area with less gagging; a soft toothbrush also works if you don't have one. What matters is gentle, regular cleaning.

faq.q: How can I tell if my white tongue is thrush?
faq.a: With thrush, the white coating leaves a red, tender surface when wiped and often follows antibiotics, steroid inhalers or denture use. An examination is needed to be sure.

title: Life with braces: soreness, food, cleaning, loose brackets and poking wires
desc: Soreness for the first few days after braces are fitted is normal. Which foods to avoid, how to clean around brackets, what to do if a bracket comes off or a wire pokes, and how often check-ups are.
seoTitle: Life with braces: soreness, food and cleaning | Dent32
seoDesc: Soreness for a few days after braces is normal. Foods to avoid, cleaning around brackets, a loose bracket or poking wire, and check-ups.
lead: After braces are fitted, and after each adjustment, 3–5 days of aching and tenderness when chewing is normal and settles with painkillers and soft food. Brackets can irritate the cheeks and lips in the first weeks, and orthodontic wax reduces this. Avoiding hard, sticky and bite-into foods prevents brackets coming off. Because decay and white spots are more likely around brackets, cleaning matters more than ever.

sections.h: The first days: soreness and irritation
sections.html:
• A feeling of pressure and tenderness when chewing for the first 3–5 days is normal.
  • A painkiller taken as directed and soft foods (soup, yoghurt, pasta, mash) help.
  • Put orthodontic wax where brackets rub your cheek; the tissue gets used to them within a few weeks.
  • Rinsing with warm salt water soothes irritation in the mouth.
In short

Soreness for 3–5 days after braces is normal; avoid hard, sticky and bite-into foods, and clean carefully around the brackets every day.

AvoidHow you can eat them
Hard: nuts, ice, hard sweets, roasted chickpeasSofter alternatives; nuts crushed
Sticky: caramel, chewing gum, Turkish delightBest avoided
Bite-into: apples, carrots, corn on the cob, crusty breadCut into small pieces and chew with the back teeth
Very sugary and acidic drinksCut down; rinse with water afterwards

sections.h: How to clean teeth with braces
sections.html:
1. Brush after every meal, at least twice a day.
  2. Angle the brush downwards over the top of the brackets and upwards under them.
  3. Clean between the wire and the teeth with an interdental brush.
  4. For flossing, use orthodontic floss or a floss threader; a water flosser helps a lot.
  5. Use a fluoride toothpaste, and add a fluoride mouthwash if your dentist recommends it.

If cleaning isn't thorough enough, white spots (enamel demineralisation) can form around the brackets. See white spots on teeth, electric brushes and water flossers.

sections.h: If a bracket comes off or a wire pokes
sections.html:
• Loose bracket: usually not an emergency. Keep the bracket and call the clinic; you'll be given an appointment to re-bond it.
  • Wire end poking your cheek: cover it with orthodontic wax, or gently push the wire in with the clean rubber end of a pencil; call the clinic.
  • Broken elastic: fit a new one if you have spares; otherwise it's replaced at your next appointment.
  • Severe pain, swelling or a break after a knock: call the clinic without waiting.

Check-ups are usually every 4–8 weeks; keeping them is important for finishing on time. After the braces come off, a retainer keeps the teeth in place. See retainers after braces, clear aligners or braces, orthodontics in Beylikdüzü.
